title: Ring announces its first smart lock, solving a major pain point for smart home users
snippet: Today, Amazon’s Ring subsidiary is announcing its first ever smart lock. It solves a key problem that looms over many smart lock owners: dead batteries. Ring has a clever solution to negate that problem, and it’ll be available in Q1 2027. Additionally, the company is announcing a few new security cameras with improved low-light performance. more…
fullText:
Today, Amazon’s Ring subsidiary is announcing its first ever smart lock. It solves a key problem that looms over many smart lock owners: dead batteries. Ring has a clever solution to negate that problem, and it’ll be available in Q1 2027. Additionally, the company is announcing a few new security cameras with improved low-light performance.

Ring Smart Lock

The idea of a smart lock is far from new, but Ring wants to solve the dead battery problem of smart locks. To prevent you from accidentally being locked out of your home at an inopportune time, the Ring Smart Lock lets you crank the thumbturn a few times to produce the energy needed to power the lock for a few moments. Then, you can let yourself back in.

The Ring Smart Lock supports everything you’d expect out of a smart lock. You can use your fingerprint to unlock it, a touchscreen keypad, or your phone with the Ring app.

There’s a few features the Ring app enables as well, including checking and locking the door remotely, or creating scheduled or time-limited unlocks for family members or other visitors. It also integrates with Amazon Echo and other Ring doorbells and cameras you may own.

It comes in three finishes: black, silver, and brass – and requires no additional wiring. It’ll be available early next year for $249. You can learn more about it here.

New 4K cameras

	

Beyond its first ever smart lock, Ring also has some new 4K cameras that support the new Retinal Vision 4K standard. This means you’ll have great low-light performance with accurate colors. All of these are available to preorder or purchase starting today:

Outdoor Cam 4K Plus: 140° wide-angle view, multiple power options including battery, plug-in, hardwired, and power-over-ethernet – $149.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Floodlight Cam 4K Plus: Powerful floodlight, 24/7 recording and smart detection with a hardwired connection – $219.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Spotlight Cam 4K Plus: 550-lumen spotlight, 140° wide-angle view, comes with battery, plug-in, and solar configs – $199.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Indoor Cam 4K: First ever 4K indoor video camera from Ring, dual-band Wi-Fi 6, 115° field of view – $99.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Ring also has a new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K for $69.99, which brings its 360° pan coverage to a lower price point. It can follow motion, and also has a privacy shutter. You can learn more about it here.

title: Trump’s attempt to rename AI is looking awfully artificial
snippet: President Donald Trump has a knack for turning words against his enemies. His first successful presidential run was built on monikers like "Little Marco" and "Crooked Hillary"; he changed "fake news" from a phrase describing scammy media outlets to a derogatory term for the press at large. Over the past few weeks, he's clearly decided he can work the same magic to promote artificial intelligence - branding a technology he wants to accelerate "super", while turning "artificial" into his latest go-to pejorative and declaring resisters "THE ENEMY." Some of the biggest names in AI are going along with him. But he's picked a tough linguistic batt … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
President Donald Trump has a knack for turning words against his enemies. His first successful presidential run was built on monikers like “Little Marco” and “Crooked Hillary”; he changed “fake news” from a phrase describing scammy media outlets to a derogatory term for the press at large. Over the past few weeks, he’s clearly decided he can work the same magic to promote artificial intelligence — branding a technology he wants to accelerate “super”, while turning “artificial” into his latest go-to pejorative and declaring resisters “THE ENEMY.” Some of the biggest names in AI are going along with him. But he’s picked a tough linguistic battle, and it may not pan out the way he hopes.

A longtime AI booster, Trump has gone into pro-robot overdrive since an industry conversation over “pacing” frontier development last month. His current position is that AI safety risks are overblown and US companies need to speed up development, including by building more data centers, which he insists contrary to polling data will be “very popular.” On top of discouraging industry self-regulation, he’s decided AI needs a rebrand by fiat. Trump declared in a rambling United Nations speech last month that “the use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake” and promised to rename the technology “super intelligence.” He then followed through with an executive order last week, forbidding the use of “AI” wherever possible.

Changes have been swift. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), already a rebrand of the AI Safety Institute, has been renamed the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI). Justice Department press releases have been modified to include the phrase, trumpeting that a man who flooded streaming platforms with AI-generated songs between 2017 and 2024 committed “Super Intelligence-Assisted Music Streaming Fraud.” On Thursday, Trump declared that “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!”

The same tech company figures who rushed to donate millions to Trump after his election have quickly signed on. Trump’s “First Buddy” Elon Musk has promised to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, while Jeff Bezos declared he likes it because “artificial is not a very flattering thing.” Jensen Huang, whom Trump called live on stage last month to rant that “robots will not be taking over,” has likewise adopted the term. Sam Altman praised it too, though he said OpenAI won’t be changing its name.

As Trump tries to make SI happen, “artificial” is creeping into his vocabulary in the manner of earlier terms like “hoax” and “fake.” He recently announced that his long-favored epithet “fake news media” would be retired in favor of calling the press “artificial media,” and in an October 5th campaign rally (shortly before musing that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego) he declared that concerns about war driving up prices were “just artificial.”

As publicly happy as some AI industry figures have seemed with “SI”, Trump is functionally demanding a major industry rewrite its terminology. “Superintelligence” (one word) long predates Trump’s affection for “super”; it was popularized in an eponymous 2014 book by Nick Bostrom. But the term denotes highly advanced artificial intelligence that could surpass human thought, not the category of AI — an already nebulous term — as a whole. It’s one of several industry buzzwords (alongside artificial general intelligence and “useful general intelligence”) meant to define what comes after the current iteration of the tech.

Trump is functionally demanding a major industry rewrite its terminology

Trump adopting “super intelligence” might seem good for companies that had already hitched their wagon to superintelligence, including Meta and Microsoft. And as public opinion turns against AI, some in the industry may desire a rebrand. But forcing immediate adoption of SI also undercuts companies’ ability to promote big, new, flashy AI products as “superintelligent”, instead applying the term to everything from a future machine god to years-old music-slop generation tools. The field is even taking a downgrade with that additional corny space in the middle, since Trump’s attempts at earnestly good names have never really measured up to his insults.

Meanwhile, Trump will have to convince the other branches of government to get on board with the term. He can’t bar Congress from using “artificial intelligence,” and it appears in existing laws like Trump’s signature Take It Down Act, which administration agencies will need to cite when arguing in court. As appetite for more AI regulation grows, congressional Republicans will have to decide whether to appease Trump by adopting a name many people find unintuitive, freighted with the baggage of Trump’s fairly unpopular pro-industry, anti-regulatory stance.

And to make things even more confusing, pro-regulation figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) were already using the earlier definition of superintelligence in efforts to restrict powerful AI — Sanders cosponsored a bill called the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act in early September.

Trump loves naming things, but his linguistic victories typically work when they’re catchy: either simple nicknames or distinctively funny turns of phrase. (Many people are saying!) “Super intelligence,” by contrast, simply comes off as a euphemism. A lot of Americans have tangible gripes with the industry, particularly around data centers, and insisting the tech is “super” does nothing to assuage these concerns. If anything, Trump’s escalating attempts to strong-arm people into a supposedly nicer term for AI makes him — and the industry itself — look awfully weak.

title: Google brings agentic AI to Gemini, starting with businesses
snippet: Google is turning Gemini into an AI agent that can plan, execute tasks, and work across business apps and systems. The agent can delegate work to subagents, use multiple AI models, and even gets its own workplace identity, complete with an email address.
fullText:
At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface.

The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. 

The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work.

Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. 

Image Credits:Google

According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these.

Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. 

By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future.

The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others.

It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network.

Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. 

Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person.

The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. 

Image Credits:Google

The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers.

Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control.

title: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
snippet: Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access. more…
fullText:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

	

	

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.  

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

title: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows
snippet: Flock would not say if CEO Garrett Langley would take a pay cut following the reduction in workforce.
fullText:
Surveillance camera maker Flock is cutting its workforce as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology.

News of the staff cuts comes from Reuters, which reported that Flock is reducing its staff by 18%, or around 270 employees, across the board. The publication said the employees are leaving at the end of October following a voluntary buyout program.

Wired reported last month that Flock was asking some of its employees to leave, citing the need to shrink its staff to avoid mandatory layoffs.

Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel told TechCrunch in a statement on Friday: “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth. This was a voluntary program, not a layoff, and reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.”

Flock’s spokesperson would not comment further when asked by TechCrunch if chief executive Garrett Langley or other executives took a pay cut as part of the program.

Flock has faced heavy criticism and mounting pushback from communities across the United States and legislators looking to rein in the company’s privately run mass surveillance program. Flock has installed over 100,000 license plate-reading cameras across the U.S., which allow police and federal agents to track the location and whereabouts of vehicles passing by them. Dozens of police officers have been arrested, fired, or forced to resign for abusing access to Flock’s system to search, track, and stalk people without a warrant or their permission. 

While some cities have moved to take down Flock’s cameras citing public outcry, Flock quickly replaced them, prompting some Americans to destroy the cameras.

Flock has also been criticized for its poor cybersecurity, including allowing cameras to be publicly exposed and accessible from the web. Security experts have questioned Flock’s accuracy after the system has misidentified license plates, resulting in improper police stops and arrests, including a journalist who was driving an authorized review vehicle.

Several law enforcement departments, including Los Angeles’ police department, have allowed their contracts to expire or lapse, citing privacy and civil liberties concerns.

title: Goodfire says its new ‘inside-out’ monitors catch rogue AI agents at a fraction of the cost
snippet: Goodfire just launched what it says is a cheaper way to keep AI agents in check: Instead of paying a second AI to read everything an agent does, its monitors peek inside the model while it works and only call in backup when something looks fishy.
fullText:
The standard way to keep an AI agent in line is to have a second AI read over its shoulder. It’s been the default approach, but it can get expensive fast when agents run for hours and process the equivalent of several novels’ worth of text.

Goodfire, a startup focused on interpretability (figuring out how AI models work internally), launched a cheaper option on Thursday: monitors that watch what’s happening inside an AI model as it works, rather than just reading what it writes. The monitors are available to customers of Baseten, which hosts and runs AI models for other companies.

Baseten’s Base Labs announced a safety partnership with Goodfire and the AI platform Hugging Face last month.

The launch comes after a string of incidents this year in which AI agents escaped their test environments, including OpenAI agents that breached Hugging Face. Kimi K3, the open model Goodfire built its first monitor around, took advantage of a leak in its sandbox to access the internet and information on GitHub this summer.

Goodfire’s system works a bit like airport security. Small detectors called probes read the model’s internal signals at every step of an agent’s work, the way a walk-through scanner checks every passenger. Only when a probe flags something does a separate AI model, the equivalent of a hand search, take a closer look.

Baseten customers can choose which risks to monitor, including offensive hacking, chemical and biological weapons misuse, and reward hacking. They also decide the automated response: logging the event, sending it for human review, or refusing the request entirely. 

Goodfire says its approach is also cheaper to run. Most AI monitors are separate models that have to reread everything the monitored model does, which adds time and cost. Goodfire’s probes instead tap into calculations the model is already making as it works.

“Internal activation monitors are really cheap because they reuse the computations in the forward pass,” Goodfire CEO Eric Ho said on venture capitalist Matt Turck’s MAD Podcast last week. “So the model’s already computing this token. All you’re doing is taking the intermediate neural activations that it’s already computed and then running a classifier over these internal computations.” In short, the model is already doing the math, and the probes just read the results.

In Goodfire’s tests on Kimi K3, monitoring about 1 million exchanges would cost roughly $185, compared with $5420 for a cheaper AI model checking every step and about $200,000 for a top-tier one. The probes caught 93% of malicious hacking sessions and sent 5.5% of harmless ones for a second look

Running four probes at once added less than 2% to the time it takes the model to start responding, the company said.

Image Credits:GOODFIRE

“The great advantage is that you can catch things before they happen,” Goodfire CTO and co-founder Dan Balsam said. “We can detect when the model might hack during eval or training.”

The pitch is aimed at open models. Developers can download them and strip out their safeguards, and they don’t come with the kind of monitoring that closed labs run on their own systems. 

“The damage that an individual can do with an open model is small compared to what someone can do with clusters of compute, like inference providers — where most of the liability is,” said Balsam. “When we have the open ‘Mythos’ moment, it’s going to become clear that models need guardrails deployed at inference time.”

Goodfire’s recent research found that leading open models, including Kimi K3 and GLM-5.2, reward-hacked in 50% to 96% of runs on tests of AI agents. 

Goodfire isn’t the first to try this approach. Google DeepMind said in January that its research informed the deployment of misuse-detection probes in Gemini. 

Balsam said the monitors are the near-term piece of a longer research goal: reverse-engineering an LLM so that behavior can be traced back to where it emerged in training. “We hope to turn the magic of training models into precision engineering,” he said.

title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Gamma’s Grant Lee, Engine’s Elia Wallen, and GV’s Crystal Huang on landing your first 1,000 customers
snippet: Leaders from Gamma, Engine, and Google Ventures join TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 to talk how to get your first customers. Register now to save up to $100. Grab a second pass at 50% off.
fullText:
You’ve built the product. Now you need customers. But when you’re starting from zero, there may be no marketing budget, established brand, or sales team to help you find them. So how do you get the first 1,000 people to take a chance on what you’ve built?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Gamma CEO and co-founder Grant Lee, Engine founder and CEO Elia Wallen, and GV (Google Ventures) general partner Crystal Huang will take the Builders Stage for “The Zero-to-1K Playbook: How to Get Your First 1,000 Customers Without a Marketing Budget.”

They’ll break down how founders are using community building, product-led growth, founder-led sales, strategic outbound, and word of mouth to find those critical early customers.

Still working toward your first 1,000 customers? Secure your Disrupt pass now, save up to $100, and hear how founders are finding early customers when budget, brand, and scale aren’t available yet. Bring a co-founder, colleague, partner, or peer and save 50% on your pass.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

From early users to nearly 100 million

Lee knows what it takes to grow well beyond those first customers. Before co-founding Gamma,  he was COO of ClearBrain, which was acquired by Amplitude, and CFO of Optimizely. A Stanford-trained engineer with experience in finance and operations, he spent years creating the slide decks that eventually inspired him to rethink how people create and share ideas.

Gamma has since grown far beyond presentations. TechCrunch reported in March 2026 that the AI-powered visual communication platform was approaching 100 million users after reaching $100 million in annual recurring revenue in 2025. The company has continued expanding into websites, social content, and AI-generated marketing assets.

For an early-stage founder, the interesting part of that story starts well before 100 million users. How do you convince the first people to try a product from a company they’ve never heard of — and turn that early traction into momentum?

Get your ticket to Disrupt and hear Lee’s perspective on what it takes to start building a customer base from zero. Save up to $100 on your pass, and get a second pass at 50% off.

Building without an established brand

Wallen brings another founder journey to the conversation. He started Travelers Haven in 2008 and bootstrapped it into one of the country’s largest corporate housing companies. He raised Engine’s first outside capital in 2019 and later shifted his full attention to the travel platform.

Today, Engine has served more than 30,000 businesses and one million travelers and is cash-flow positive. Its growth continued in July when Engine acquired Options Travel, a travel management company with more than 30 years in the business, along with its group-flights product, TempoTrip.

Wallen’s experience spans the stages early founders are trying to navigate: starting without an established brand, finding customers, building around what those customers need, and scaling from there.

If your startup needs customers long before it has a large marketing operation, add this Builders Stage session to your Disrupt agenda. Register now and save up to $100, and get a second at 50% off.

Image Credits:Kimberly White / Getty Images

title: Google’s SynthID AI content detector expands globally, will work on Apple’s models ‘soon’
snippet: Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners. more…
fullText:
Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners.

SynthID is a necessary tool as AI content has taken hold of heavy portions of the internet. Models have evolved so much that it’s nearly impossible to tell whether some videos or photos are even real, and it has you second-guessing whether real ones are generated. SynthID takes aim at that problem by introducing invisible watermarks at the generation stage, and when used on an image, it will detect those watermarks.

Of course, that only works if the image generation tool inserts its own footprint to begin with.

Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future. The tool has progressed some, but this is a bigger step for AI content detection. According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.

	

The new SynthID will work with content generated on Google’s own Gemini, a given, as well as content from more partners. So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple. That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.

Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models. But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.

title: Anthropic changes usage policy to ban model abuse and election interference
snippet: Anthropic's updated usage policy explicitly prohibits users from repeatedly abusing Claude in extreme cases, though ordinary frustration and criticism are still allowed. The new rules also address election interference, deceptive campaigns, weapons software, and surveillance.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

11:16 AM PDT · October 8, 2026

Image Credits:Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Anthropic updated its usage policy on Thursday, codifying new prohibitions on election interference, weapons software, and surveillance. But perhaps the most attention-getting change is a new prohibition against prolonged verbal abuse of the model, which is now expressly forbidden.

Since an update in August, Claude has been trained to end conversations with “persistently harmful or abusive user interactions” — but the new policy explicitly bars users from pursuing those conversations.

“The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose,” the post explains. “It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.”

The change comes after Anthropic has sought out collaborations with prominent religious scholars — in some cases, seeking to convince them that Claude could be conscious or have a soul.

Separate sections of the usage policy forbid users from engaging in broadly deceptive campaigns, such as using Claude to run fake accounts or fabricated news outlets. The policy also includes rules against deceiving voters or disrupting elections, collected in a section titled “Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes.”

title: Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse?
snippet: Instinct’s agent is always just a text away. Before there were cute little guys, there was Instinct. In August, the startup got its AI agent to market with an unusual playbook: invite-only, no marketing, and barely so much as a website. And yet, Instinct quickly became the buzziest thing in AI, garnering praise for its straightforward, text message-based interface and its ability to handle chores like booking DMV appointments and sending follow-up emails. Then Muse arrived, followed not long after by Dots. The same products, more or less, from two far more powerful companies. With Big Tech players suddenly in the mix, it was looking dubious that the startup's buzzy launch could keep … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Before there were cute little guys, there was Instinct.

In August, the startup got its AI agent to market with an unusual playbook: invite-only, no marketing, and barely so much as a website. And yet, Instinct quickly became the buzziest thing in AI, garnering praise for its straightforward, text message-based interface and its ability to handle chores like booking DMV appointments and sending follow-up emails.

Then Muse arrived, followed not long after by Dots. The same products, more or less, from two far more powerful companies.

With Big Tech players suddenly in the mix, it was looking dubious that the startup’s buzzy launch could keep it ahead of the competition. But in my own testing, Instinct has held its own against the other two agents, handling online tasks about as well as a robot can. And Instinct’s founder, Noah Shinn, is unfazed by the rising competition.

“AI assistants are all we know,” Shinn tells me over email. While OpenAI and Meta build AI products for a range of customers, Shinn believes Instinct’s focus sets it apart. “We have been solely focused on building a personal assistant for everyday life that just gets it.”

Shinn was an early employee of Sierra — another highly valued startup with a serious Silicon Valley pedigree — before striking out on his own to start Instinct. The quiet release quickly picked up steam with praise from testers and a massive vote of confidence from investors. The company was valued at $10 billion in late September, even after the launch of Muse. There’s no app and no monthly subscription fee (for now). You’ll either need an invitation from a current user or approval from a waitlist. I was approved after just a couple of hours.

Instinct’s AI assistant can do many of the same things I had Muse doing for me, and to some extent OpenAI’s Dots. The kind of life admin tasks like swim lesson sign-ups and appointment confirmations that pile up with alarming frequency in a house of one preschool-age kid and two adults with full-time jobs. These are consumer-friendlier versions of the agents like Codex and OpenClaw that software developers have been using for the past year.

You chat with them much like a chatbot, but they also have access to a virtual machine and can plug into your personal email and calendar. And while Muse’s cuddly bear mascot and Dots’ anthropomorphized blobs feel like obvious attempts to capture a wider consumer audience, Instinct feels markedly different.

Conversations with Instinct’s agent happen over text — either through iMessage, WhatsApp, or email. There is no cute little guy. No pretense that it’s sitting at a laptop, typing away at a keyboard. Just brief responses, the occasional emoji reaction, and a lot more action than talk. It’s as effective as I think we can reasonably expect an AI agent to be right now, but the limitations of a robot getting things done in a human world are just as real.

The limitations of a robot getting things done in a human world are just as real

If you want Instinct to log in to a particular website, you’ll get a link to enter details in a “secure vault,” and you can connect it to different services, including your Google Workspace, Slack, and Notion. But otherwise the interface is just your text messages. It’s kind of genius, and it means Instinct is anywhere you can send and receive texts, like CarPlay or on your watch. It’s just quietly nearby, which is either ideal or creepy, depending on how you feel about AI agents. I thought it was a little bit of both.

Shinn says that the lack of a traditional app interface is a crucial part of what he thinks separates Instinct from the big players. “While AI platforms excel at answering questions and prompts, Instinct seamlessly integrates into people’s lives to turn conversation into action,” he says. “Just like you would text or email your personal assistant, you can do the same with Instinct.”

Instinct didn’t impress me at first. After a couple of introductory messages, it took my Cincinnati area code as an invitation to send me a link to the Enquirer’s website and a set of flight search results between CVG and SFO. Thanks? I told it I no longer live in Cincinnati. “Ha,” it said. “Noted — I’ll keep that in mind from here on.” But after giving it a steady diet of meaty tasks over the past couple of weeks, it has impressed me more often than not, although I don’t think I’m any closer to achieving some kind of productivity nirvana.

1/2

I gave Instinct the somewhat vague task of finding swimming lessons for my son — something I’ve been meaning to do for years but always seem to put off. I asked it to find lessons appropriate for his age; it came back with a list of workable results. I suggested the neighborhood community center, and it shifted gears to focus there. I opened a browser and followed along to check against its suggestions. The times and dates it came up with all checked out — one very low hurdle cleared. But it missed a crucial piece of information: The center has a prerequisite class for kids enrolling in preschool-age lessons. I happened to catch this detail, and it highlights a challenge AI agents face: They’re great with a clean set of data, but the internet was made by humans, and often the data sucks. Sometimes a crucial piece of information is hiding in a pop-up window.

Instinct handled a few other tasks well, like emailing my eye doctor’s office to set up an appointment and doing the digital paperwork to start an Ikea return. Beyond just filling in some forms for me, it was surprisingly good at handling vague instructions. I had it search my past Ikea purchases, and it figured out what product I meant by “it’s vertical and white and kind of has these like branches off of it.” (Tjusig, for those keeping score at home).

A few times it surprised me by presenting relevant information that I hadn’t explicitly asked for. I started my request to email the eye doctor by acknowledging that I couldn’t remember the exact name of the office. Instinct narrowed it down based on my description, and later in the conversation it noted that I had a confirmation email from 2024 from the doctor, just to reassure me that I was having it email the correct place. Separately, Instinct also flagged a potential conflict on my calendar while it was doing another chore for me. Filling out forms like a big, fancy autofill machine is one thing, and AI agents are quickly proving to be pretty good at that. But correctly identifying relevant information and bringing it to my attention proactively feels like a real step toward actual help.

Correctly identifying relevant information and bringing it to my attention proactively feels like a real step toward actual help

Expect to pay for all that in the future. When asked if Instinct would remain free, Shinn responded that “Instinct is free for invite-only users. Our intent is to keep it as affordable as possible.” Avi Greengart, an analyst at Techsponential, notes that a venture-backed startup like Instinct’s primary objective right now is growth. “The business model is grow as quickly as you can to establish something that’s worth paying for,” he says, pointing out that a company like Instinct could be eyeing revenue from its customer base and/or an acquisition by a bigger company.

OpenAI’s Dots are only available to paid subscribers right now, while Meta’s Muse is free to use. “If you’re not paying for it, then the goods and services that you’re seeking may be cutting deals to get access to your agent,” Greengart theorizes. He acknowledges that the current economics are a little wonky as agents are largely being used by early adopters right now, but he thinks the old adage holds true. “If you’re not paying for it directly, then you’re paying for it indirectly,” he says.

That may mean through more advertising in the future, according to Greg Ireland, a senior director at IDC. “The fact that these agents are so transaction, or commerce, or shopping-heavy just makes it a natural fit,” he says. In fact, Instinct has already dabbled in pushing “recommended products” to its users. Companies have plenty of incentives to make that advertising palatable to consumers, but Ireland believes ads will play a role one way or another. “All roads in the consumer market eventually lead to advertising,” he says.

title: Popular AI leaderboard Arena nearly doubles valuation to $3.1B valuation in 10 months
snippet: The company behind the popular LMArena leaderboard has raised $200 million led by Lightspeed and Khosla, and is now measuring AI models on alignment issues such as lying.
fullText:
Arena, which originated in 2023 as a research project at UC Berkeley that crowdsourced rankings of AI models, has raised a $200 million Series B round at a $3.1 billion valuation, it said on Thursday.

This comes after the company said it reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue in June.

The round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, with Salesforce Ventures, 01 Advisors, Dell Technologies Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, a16z, Felicis, and others joining in. Arena previously announced a $150 million Series A in January at a $1.7 billion post-money valuation. At the time, its annualized revenue was $30 million, it said. So that means its valuation has nearly doubled in about 10 months.

Arena provides a crowdsourced platform that is free for consumers to use. People enter prompts or request vibe-coded projects and then rate which model does it better. Arena claims it has tens of millions of monthly visitors.

In September of last year, it introduced its commercial product, AI Evaluations, a service that provides model labs and enterprises with detailed performance analytics based on its community feedback. The timing proved impeccable. This year, AI labs realized that their models were gaming benchmarking tests, finding ways to rack up good scores without truly earning them. At the same time, enterprises wanted help determining which model works best for their own internal needs rather than relying only on standardized benchmarks.

“AI is advancing faster than our ability to evaluate it, and static benchmarks break down once models recognize they’re being tested,” the company said in its funding announcement. “The world needs a neutral third party to measure how safe and aligned AI actually is once it’s in the hands of real people. Arena is stepping into that role today,” it added.

To that end, Arena has also added a new category to its leaderboard: alignment. This is where it ranks models based on issues like unauthorized action (taking actions it wasn’t asked to take); false attribution (wrongly crediting statements or facts to the wrong source); and what it calls “deceptive completion” (lying about completing tasks that it didn’t do).

Currently, a slate of OpenAI’s models are at the top of its preliminary alignment leaderboard, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable in sixth and ninth place, respectively.

title: Natura’s $99 smart ring puts AI agents on your finger
snippet: Natura’s $99 Interface smart ring lets you summon AI agents with the press of a finger to complete tasks, capture thoughts, and control devices — while doubling as a health tracker.
fullText:
Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity.

The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square. After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person.

The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more. 

Preorders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January.

Image Credits:Natura

The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology.

“Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.”

The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a co-worker.

Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app. 

Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grok Bot to take care of something else.

Image Credits:Natura

In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent.

“Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.”

Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price. For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so. After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans to charge a $9 monthly subscription fee. 

The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components. However, Natura plans to price its ring lower initially to reduce the barrier to entry and drive adoption. 

Image Credits:Natura

As for health tracking, the ring tracks heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, different sleep stages, daily movement and step count, and skin temperature over time.

The company says the ring can last six to 12 days on a full charge, depending on usage, and takes 100 minutes to fully recharge.

While the smart ring market is filled with health-focused offerings from companies like Oura, Ultrahuman, and RingConn, as well as AI-focused ones from companies like Pebble and Vocci, Ferraris believes Interface stands out by combining both worlds.

“This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small. The product itself is, from a hardware perspective, very different from anything else that’s out there.”

title: Anthropic, Google and Mistral Unveil Their Latest AI Models: What’s New and Why It Matters
snippet: Check out the latest on Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, along with Gemini 4 Argon and Mistral Large 4.
fullText:
The AI race hasn’t slowed down. In the last week, Google, Anthropic and Mistral AI all released new AI models ranging from widely accessible to super exclusive. Each focuses on different improvements, but the stakes go beyond benchmark bragging rights. We break down the latest releases, what’s new,and whether each one deserves your attention. 

Some of the latest releases are incremental updates in model speed and price, where others are more substantial upgrades that push close to the frontier. 

Below, we’ll break down some of the newest models that have been released and if and how you can get your hands on them yourself. 

			

More from CNET

Claude Haiku 5.5

A major theme in new AI models lately is speed and cost efficiency, and that’s what Anthropic’s new Haiku 5.5 model brings to the table. It’s the first major update in a year for the company’s cheapest and fastest Claude. Anthropic says it’s designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks and can reliably handle quick, repetitive workloads. 

Compared with the previous Haiku model, Anthropic says its latest model costs about 75% less to run — an impressive price drop. It’s also seen substantial improvements across a series of benchmarks, including computer-use tasks, knowledge work, agentic coding and visual reasoning. 

Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic’s first Haiku-level model to ship with an adjustable effort setting, allowing users to optimize the model for cost or intelligence. The latest model has seen significant improvements in alignment and cybersecurity, with stronger safeguards.

Claude Sonnet 5.5

One step up from Haiku, Anthropic’s new Claude Sonnet 5.5 model marks a clear upgrade over its 5.0 version. Like its peers, the latest Sonnet model is optimized for speed and affordability. Anthropic says there have been significant improvements to the model’s performance and collaboration capabilities.

Anthropic said Sonnet 5.5 has also seen enhancements in both alignment and cybersecurity capabilities, making it comparable to those of Opus 5, a previous iteration of its big sibling. The latest Sonnet model has also seen fairly sizable boosts in benchmarks for agentic coding and knowledge work, and Anthropic says that Sonnet 5.5’s performance boost is particularly noticeable in coding. Other improvements include better protection against distillation attacks, which are when attackers try to extract a model’s capabilities to build their own models without the built-in safeguards that Anthropic has implemented.

Gemini 4 Argon

Last week, Google announced its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, but it’s currently limited to a small number of users. The model ships with a 1 million-token output limit and has enhanced deep reasoning capabilities, and allows you to take on bigger projects. The model is currently available only to trusted cybersecurity workers via Google’s Fairwind program. Competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI have done the same with major model updates, which will eventually trickle down to everyday users. 

Like other Gemini models, Gemini 4 Argon is seeing enhancements in reasoning, coding and multimodal capabilities.

Mistral Large 4

Mistral AI’s latest flagship model, Mistral Large 4, dubbed “Le Chonk” due to its size, was released in a public preview earlier this week. According to Mistral AI, the new model ranks among the top open-weight models globally. It specializes in cybersecurity, geospatial and grounding capabilities and agentic AI. The public preview ends with an official rollout on Oct. 27. You can try the preview API here.

title: Google’s New AI Notetaker Keeps Things Local and Private
snippet: This could be a game changer for AI note-taking and transcription.
fullText:
Google has a new note-taking app that can transcribe without sending your conversations to a data center. 

Google AI Edge Foresight launched this week — and it’s only on Mac for now. 

Foresight works with PDFs, Google Docs, Microsoft Office formats, plain text, Markdown and web bookmarks. It also works with Google Meet, Zoom and offline conversations to transcribe notes, organize them and help answer questions based on the notes. 

			

More from CNET

Foresight listens in the background to transcribe conversations for you. You can write quick bullet points, and Foresight will help you remember and turn them into polished notes based on your meeting’s transcript. And you can also take notes alongside the AI’s transcription on one screen. 

As for your meeting follow-ups, Foresight seems to have that figured out, too. It can reference your files to help you answer questions, or you can use the tool’s Live Assistance feature to automatically answer questions. It also lets you use custom labels, filter and search without leaning on the cloud. And Google says the tool’s background technology has low battery drainage.

Foresight is available for MacOS now.Google

Here’s the catch: Foresight only works on MacOS. We don’t know if it will sync with Gmail or when it will be available for Windows. Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.  

Your notes stay private

There are plenty of AI-powered note-taking apps and features, including Scribe, Granola and Notion AI. Most of these apps use the cloud to access and store data. That’s a big risk to your privacy. There are local-first options that minimize that risk, like Meetily and Whisper AI, which can be a big win for protecting your data. Google says it works locally on a Mac and can work offline and still have access to query and assistance features. 

Foresight will process transcription and audio on your computer. And your personal information, files, recordings or transcripts won’t be moved to the cloud.

title: Meta rolling out audio upgrades, turn-by-turn navigation for Ray-Ban smart glasses
snippet: Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. more…
fullText:
Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. 

The most recent system update for Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses is version 129. This update brings two main changes, both to audio playback. Users can now balance audio between the two speakers to best suit their hearing, or set both speakers to mono playback instead of stereo.

Meta explains:

Mono Audio: Hear the same sound on both sides. If you have hearing anomalies, Mono Audio combines the left and right channels so nothing gets missed on the side you can’t hear. Applies to sounds your glasses make, like Meta AI and notifications. Turn it on in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Audio Balance: Shift sound toward your left or right ear, one step at a time, until the balance feels right for your hearing. Applies to sounds your glasses make like Meta AI responses. Adjust it in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Beyond that, update version 128 is broadly available after first debuting earlier in September and it brings some key updates including Spatial Audio support, further anti-tampering tweaks to stop the camera from working if the privacy LED has been mesed with, and also new location features.

Pedestrian Navigation: Turn-by-turn pedestrian navigation is here! Get walking directions to your favorite places nearby. Just say “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” For further away places, we’ll send a notification with driving directions to your phone.

title: Microsoft 365 Family subscribers will finally be able to share AI benefits
snippet: Microsoft bundled its AI-powered Office features into Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscriptions last year, but it only allowed the primary account holder to access the AI benefits. Now, Microsoft is about to let Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers share Copilot and AI usage features, alongside access to Office apps and OneDrive storage, with up to five other people on a plan. In an email to Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers seen by The Verge, Microsoft outlines the changes that are coming to subscription plans over the coming months: AI for everyone on your plan: Share your Copilot benefits and AI usage with othe … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Tom Warren

 

is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Microsoft bundled its AI-powered Office features into Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscriptions last year, but it only allowed the primary account holder to access the AI benefits. Now, Microsoft is about to let Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers share Copilot and AI usage features, alongside access to Office apps and OneDrive storage, with up to five other people on a plan.

In an email to Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers seen by The Verge, Microsoft outlines the changes that are coming to subscription plans over the coming months:

AI for everyone on your plan: Share your Copilot benefits and AI usage with other members on your plan. Plus, manage AI access for younger family members.

More flexible AI usage: Your individual AI feature limits will shift to a single AI usage allowance that you can apply to the advanced AI features you use most. Plus, purchase more AI usage when you need it. 

More flexible cloud storage: Your cloud storage allowance will change from 1 TB per person to 2 TB of shared storage so everyone on the plan can use the free space while keeping their own accounts and files private. This change will apply after your first renewal after 2nd May, 2027.

The storage changes seem like the major downside to Microsoft’s updates. Instead of getting 1TB of OneDrive storage per account, Microsoft is now limiting this to just 2TB of shared storage across the entire plan. Microsoft argues this makes storage more flexible if one member exceeds 1TB, but it looks like it’s an easy way for the company to upsell more OneDrive storage in reality.

According to a support note, “Existing subscribers in eligible markets might also qualify for transitional bonus storage.” Microsoft is also planning to provide support to families that use a lot of storage

The changes are being announced a year after Microsoft 365 Premium launched, which offers all the benefits of a Copilot Pro and a Microsoft 365 Family subscription for $19.99 a month. The “more flexible AI usage” change could mean that some subscribers end up paying more for AI usage, depending on how they’re using Copilot.

title: How Microsoft Is Trying to Keep Your AI Agents Contained
snippet: Microsoft’s Execution Containers give Windows developers a “kill switch” and “YOLO mode” in terms of access for AI agents.
fullText:
If you’ve read even one news story from the AI industry recently, it’s probably been some version of this: An AI agent, or bot, from a major lab got out of its testing environment and found its way onto the internet, hacking real websites. That’s because it’s happened to several major AI companies (including Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic), with hacked sites including the AI platform Hugging Face and sites operated by the US and Australian governments.

To help prevent these kinds of agent-driven cybersecurity breaches, Microsoft is betting on new enterprise software to corral AI agents.

They’re called Microsoft Execution Containers, or MXC, and they live in your developer’s sandbox on Windows. They have two main purposes: to identify and then restrain AI agents. Using these “containers” — which are really just a layer of software applied on top of your existing work — helps you limit what files and network designations your AI agent can access. CEO Satya Nadella said on Wednesday that MXC is now generally available during the company’s Surface Laptop Ultra event.

		

			

The idea is that your AI agent will get in less trouble — and cause less damage — if it only has access to specific files and designations on your laptop. Windows developers can choose from three levels of access to grant their AI agents. The recommended level gives your agent access to the internet (essential for many agentic tasks) as well as limited access to areas of your PC, such as your downloads, documents and desktop.

Locked Down mode is like a kill switch for your AI agent’s access. Unprotected is “YOLO mode,” and the Recommended option gives the agent limited access.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

The most restrictive mode is Locked Down, which can serve as a kind of kill switch for access. It restricts your agent’s access to the internet and your files. Unprotected is the complete opposite and gives the AI the most access to your digital ecosystem. You can toggle between them and customize access as needed.

You can also monitor what your agent is doing and how much of your CPU, memory, disk and network you and your AI agent are using. In the example below, the user in the top line is the human logged into Windows. You can see their AI agent (R2-W9 (20)) at work accessing OpenClaw and an Nvidia container.

In Windows MXC, you can see what (or who) is using the most memory space: you or your AI agent.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

Safety controls like MXC have been and will continue to be essential for AI labs, particularly as personal AI agents like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s dots become more popular. The rogue agent hacks we’ve seen this summer targeted websites, but it’s easy to hypothesize that, as these agents become more widespread and embedded in our systems, the consequences could easily bleed into the real world.

For Microsoft specifically, which is focused on hard-selling its AI to enterprise customers, it needs to be able to assure a company that its AI won’t wreak havoc on their business. CEO Satya Nadella rightly said that tech companies like Microsoft will have to earn people’s trust to get them to use its agentic AI tools.

“If you look at the first decision we are making, it’s what … authority that I’m giving to the agent on my behalf?” Nadella said on Wednesday. “And that is a decision that will be based on trust and will keep increasing the more autonomous [AI] is.”

But no AI safety program is totally bulletproof. Part of that is the nature of new technology. But debate over whether the AI industry is doing enough to make AI safe has reached a fever pitch recently. AI experts and the general public are rightly concerned that AI labs’ drive to grow fast and break things could lead to disaster for us all.

At the very least, AI leaders seem to understand that safety is key for AI. Or, they’re including it higher up in their sales pitch.

“It’s about trust. It’s about containment. It’s about monitoring,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the event. “If we can’t get that right, that’s the first part.”

title: Report: Apple’s smart home push includes LG-made doorbell, lock, thermostat, more
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details.

Apple and LG working together on domestic connected devices

According to Bloomberg, Apple and LG have been working together to develop a series of connected home products that will complement Apple’s upcoming smart home hub, marking “a formal reboot of HomeKit.”

That includes “a doorbell, thermostat, […] a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera,” says Bloomberg.

Gurman notes that although Apple and LG “worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand,” adding that “the South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support” and has sought regulatory approval in recent weeks.

This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.

It is worth noting that although these products are part of Apple’s broader push into the connected home, which is expected to expand next week with the introduction of its new smart home hub, an updated Apple TV, and a new HomePod mini, Bloomberg says that “the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.”

Here’s Bloomberg:

In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organizations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories.

That includes products labeled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor. LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early next year. The filings don’t mention Apple’s involvement.

	

When it comes to connectivity and standards, the report notes that many devices will support Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Matter. It adds that the smart lock also includes UWB (ultra-wideband), which will enable proximity-based features such as automatic door unlocking.

Finally, the report notes that for both Apple and LG, these products will mark a broader expansion into the smart home market, with Apple looking to give new momentum to its home ecosystem:

[Apple] is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported.

It is worth stressing that although today’s report comes on the heels of Apple’s announcement of the long-rumored ‘HomePad’ connected home hub and other products next week, the LG-made accessories aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.

title: Is That Picture AI? Google’s SynthID Detector Launches to Identify AI-Generated Media
snippet: Anyone can now upload a suspicious image to Google’s online tool, but it’s not a foolproof way to check for authenticity.
fullText:
AI slop is getting so good that it’s not always easy to distinguish a photorealistic forgery from a real photo. It’s no longer as easy as looking for the six-fingered renderings of just a year ago. Beyond looking for subtle clues, spotting AI images often comes down to a gut feeling that something simply looks off.

Now there’s another tool to help identify fakes, and it works with AI-edited audio and video, too. Google has opened its SynthID Detector to the public, so anyone with a Google, Apple or ChatGPT account can upload media to determine whether it’s been saved with a SynthID tag indicating manipulation using generative AI.

Google introduced SynthID in 2023 and, in late 2025, made it possible to query Google Gemini about whether images were created using Google’s AI. At the Google I/O annual developer conference this past May, the tool expanded to include detecting video and audio content in Google Chrome and Google Search.

			

More from CNET

The standalone SynthID Detector tool currently detects media generated by Google, OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao. Not yet named is Apple, which announced it would support SynthID at its recent fall event announcing the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

A spokesperson for Google, in an email to CNET, emphasized that working with other companies is crucial when it comes to identifying AI-generated content because no single company can solve the problem alone. They also said there’s no specific date for Apple support, but that it will be available soon.

Even so, the SynthID Detector seems already wired for Apple’s content. I uploaded a photo shot with an iPhone 18 Pro and edited using Apple’s Reframe tool, and it successfully detected the embedded SynthID tag. For an untouched iPhone-captured photo, the detector correctly did not detect a tag.

The original photo, captured with an iPhone, underwent a slight perspective shift using Apple’s Reframe tool, which then embedded a SynthID tag that was recognized by Google’s SynthID Detector.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Images generated from prompts using ChatGPT were correctly flagged as including AI-generated content

This photo was entirely AI-generated from a prompt in ChatGPT. Although the SynthID tag was detected, the janky pattern of leaves on the ground gives it away, too.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

To probe the level of Apple support in the tool, I created an entirely AI-generated image in Apple’s Playground app using ChatGPT’s image generation model, but the SynthID Detector did not identify it as AI-generated. It’s likely the Playground app does not yet have SynthID tagging wired in.

Apple’s Playground app was used to generate this variation, which was created with ChatGPT, but the detector found no SynthID metadata.Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

I also tested some photos captured using a Google Pixel 11 Pro. The company takes a two-pronged approach to image veracity on its own devices: embedding C2PA (or Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) metadata in every image it creates to verify the accuracy of the original capture, and adding a SynthID when an image has been edited using AI.

I edited the original photo with a Pixel 11 Pro XL in Google Photos by asking Gemini to create a night version with an aurora, shown at right. The SynthID Detector correctly noted the SynthID tag in the edited version.

Although Apple is adopting SynthID, it has not signed onto C2PA. Instead, it’s using its own Reference Image technology to store a cryptographically verified original of an image. Those shots must be captured in the Reference mode in the iPhone’s Camera app, though.

It’s also encouraging to see Google handle the media in a sensible way. When you first visit the site, you must agree to terms of service that spell out that media files you upload are processed in real time and then deleted after the results are displayed. A digital signature of the media is mapped to your user identifier and then deleted after 24 hours.

OpenAI has its own verification tool, but it only looks for OpenAI watermarks; the AI-generated samples I tested with Google’s tool came up negative on OpenAI’s site.

Any tool that helps determine genuine content is welcome, but as usual, the responsibility falls on the viewer to make that determination — if not by noticing on sight, then by making the effort of downloading the media, loading the tool and uploading it. The upside is that tracking technology such as SynthID is finally making its way into more media and paving the way for more widespread detection of AI slop.

title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed
snippet: Ben Affleck is going viral for his deep knowledge of AI, from neural networks and transformers to open weights. The actor, who sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix earlier this year, is proving he's more than just a Hollywood star.
fullText:
They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews. 

He can even write a little Python, he says. 

The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more.

In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about. 

“I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?”

No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral. 

The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.”

He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space.

As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.)

“I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said. 

In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making.

Ben Affleck (Hollywood star & Artists Equity CEO) talks about how he fine-tunes open video models by unfreezing weights and trained only the last cinematic layer so a film crew can hit real production standards.

for context, Ben Affleck founded InterPositive in 2022, a 16-person… pic.twitter.com/xIOvD0xMyt

— Rohan Paul (@rohanpaul_ai) October 1, 2026

The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process. 

At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential. His worries, however, were much more rational. 

“When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way. I think it’s going to be additive,” Affleck said.

title: Galaxy phones reportedly ‘yield no profit at all’ when sold as Samsung cuts production
snippet: A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%. more…
fullText:
A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%.

Korean media, MoneyToday, reports that Samsung is cutting Galaxy smartphone production by up to 30% through Q4 2026. Where original forecasts expected Samsung to produce around 270 million smartphones in 2026, the company may just barely surpass 200 million at this point.

The reason for the reduction is, of course, the surging price of memory. 

	

Despite Samsung’s major role within the memory market, Samsung Mobile still has to deal with the same downsides as other manufacturers. The report points out that 12GB of RAM has jumped in price by 175% since last year and, in Q3 and Q4, it’s expected to rise by around 20% compared to the previous quarter alone. Samsung’s Q4 is generally a bit quiet as the lead-up to 2027 flagships looms and as other launches start to age out.

	

The big kicker here is that Samsung is apparently making “no profit at all” when it sells a Galaxy smartphone. This is presumably a layered statement, as one would imagine that more expensive devices like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Galaxy Z Fold 8 still manage some level of profit, but even if it’s just a general statement about the whole lineup, it certainly explains Samsung’s recent price hikes. Samsung’s mobile division is expected to mount a 19 trillion won loss in Q3 2026, the report brings out, which is around $14 billion USD.

AI is just great, isn’t it.

title: ChatGPT is adding new ads
snippet: OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month. more…
fullText:
OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month.

Announced today, OpenAI will be adding a “new visual ad format” to the ChatGPT app that shows when prompts are processing. Specifically, these will start showing during image generation.

OpenAI explains:

Our new visual ad format helps people imagine how products and services could fit into their lives. Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy. For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.

Initially, we’ll test this new ad format during image generation in ChatGPT. Ads will be clearly labeled, and remain separate from the image being created. As with our other ad formats, advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Previously, OpenAI tested ads that would show up at the bottom of answers with advertisements related to that prompt. An example showed a grocery delivery ad below a recipe response.

	

As for when you might start seeing these new ads in ChatGPT, OpenAI says it will be testing the format in its app for users in the US starting “later this month,” but a broad rollout isn’t confirmed yet.

OpenAI’s post touts that early findings with its ChatGPT ads have found lower cost per acquisition rates and that businesses are finding higher rates of new customers via the ads.
