title: The first thing you should do on Googlebook is fix the trackpad
snippet: If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box. more…
fullText:
If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box.

Every Googlebook in this initial wave comes with a haptic trackpad, but they also seem to have a slight headache out of the box.

The cursor is incredibly slow.

“Touchpad accleration” on Googlebook, at least by default, is considerably slower than other platforms such as Windows and macOS. It’s something that we’ve all noticed here on the 9to5Google team as we’ve started using Googlebook machines this week across multiple models. It’s far from unusable, but it’s very jarring compared to any other laptop you might go buy at the store today. 

	

Luckily, it can be fixed fairly easily. Go to Settings > Device & accessories > Touchpad > Cursor speed  and you’ll be able to adjust the setting to your preferences. For me, that meant maxing it out to get something more akin to my other machines.

Update, October 7: Apple has now released both RCs to public beta testers as well. The build numbers are unchanged from the developer RCs.

In addition to releasing macOS 27.2 Golden Gate public beta 2, Apple is now rolling out the first Release Candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2. Here are the details.

Security updates continue for older macOS versions

As is usually the case for point updates of older macOS versions, Apple today rolled out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, without first releasing regular beta versions.

Apple released macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 late last month, both of which saw two RCs before the official rollout.

Apple’s release notes for the first macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RCs mention only that they “provide[s] important security fixes and [are] recommended for all users.” Last month’s updates contained a single CoreGraphics security fix, with its details reading:

Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

Apple will likely detail the fixes included in macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 after their official release, which will likely come alongside macOS 27.2 Golden Gate within the next few weeks.

The release build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 RC 1 is 24H219, while the release build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RC 1 is 25G320.

fullText:
Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers.

It’s been known that Samsung wants to add another device model to the Galaxy S27 series. It tried last year, but the Galaxy S26 Edge never came to be and was replaced by a rushed S26+. Recent reports specify four different Galaxy S27 models, and none of them seem to be thin. The Galaxy S27 will consist of a base model, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra.

A Twitter/X post by @phonefuturist adds a little more context around pricing in the US and Korea for the Galaxy S27 series (via Android Headlines). Galaxy S27 – $899

Galaxy S27+ – $1,099

Galaxy S27 Pro – $1,299

Galaxy S27 Ultra – $1,399

Technically, the Galaxy S27 is listed here as cheaper than the current Galaxy S26, because Samsung recently jacked the prices up on an existing phone. But due to an added device in the middle, the structure gets a little wonky and can’t be compared to the previous series 1:1.

	

But going by launch pricing, the Galaxy S27 Pro could cost the same as the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the new version of the Ultra will bring the series to a peak of $1,399. For reference, a good foldable device like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is only $500 higher.

title: This ‘Mind-Reading’ AI Is a Wiz at Figuring Out What You See
snippet: The trick is, you have to be in an MRI machine — and it only works with pictures.
fullText:
Israeli scientists have devised an AI model that can reconstruct and even predict what people are seeing with startling accuracy, likening the results to mind reading.

Their work still exists largely in lab settings, though the researchers are hopeful that advances down the line could be extended even as far as reading people’s dreams. More immediately, the technology could have potential for medical purposes, like helping people communicate who otherwise can’t due to injury or disability.

The AI model, called Brain-IT, was developed by professor Michal Irani and fellow researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. They’ve documented their work on GitHub and in a paper presented at a scientific conference earlier this year.

			

More from CNET

Brain-IT takes advantage of the thing that AI is best at, which is pattern recognition. It takes in data from functional MRI brain scans, which track changes in blood flow and oxygen in the brain to measure brain activity, and then uses that data to recreate the images the person was thinking about when the scans took place. 

It also works in reverse, predicting what a brain scan would look like if shown a specific image. 

According to Irani, other AI models can translate brain activity into images and preserve the general vibe of an image. 

“However, they tend to make mistakes in basic features such as composition and color,” Irani said in a statement. “The new model we developed outperforms them in reconstructing both the content of the image and its details.”

Brain-IT is also substantially faster. The researchers say that it needs only 1 hour of fMRI data from a new subject to match the results achieved by other methods trained on 40 hours of recording. 

The Brain-IT image reconstructions — the right side of each paired image — clearly aren’t perfect but they are largely true to the original.Weizmann Institute of Science

How does the Brain-IT AI model work?

The Weizmann Institute researchers trained the AI model on thousands of brain scans from the publicly available Natural Scenes Dataset that came from eight volunteers who were told to look at specific images while they were being scanned. This allowed the AI to identify patterns in brain activity. 

The researchers noted that different regions of the brain light up on scans when people think about specific things and identified 128 “functional regions.” For example, Irani said, some regions light up in scans when someone looks at food and others when a person views sports. These patterns helped the AI figure out what the person being scanned was witnessing. 

Some of these regions were already known by neuroscientists. Research has shown that dogs’ brains light up like Christmas trees in the presence of their owners and that dogs can differentiate between a human’s facial expressions. It’s also been observed that humans use the same neurons in recalling an image as they do looking at them. 

As impressive as Brain-IT is, it’s also quite limited. It can currently only generate images from fMRI brain scans. This takes time and requires a person to willingly put themselves into an MRI machine. 

Irani and other scientists are also looking into whether a simpler EEG device could deliver similar results more easily, according to MIT Technology Review.

So is it mind reading? Not really — nothing in this technology is capturing thoughts, memory or language. What the Weizmann Institute researchers have built is essentially a more efficient and reliable method of reconstructing a scene based on the brain activity of the person viewing it.

In an interview with MIT Technology Review, Irani acknowledged that “mind-reading” is a “cute, jazzy name.”

Irani and her team now want to see if they can achieve similar results with auditory information.

Beyond that lies a more mysterious realm: dreams. That, Irani said in a statement, would require conquering the challenges of decoding video.

“Dozens of images change every second while an fMRI scan takes about two minutes,” she said. “If we overcome all these obstacles, it’s possible that in the future, we may even be able to read dreams.”

title: Google AI Edge Foresight for Mac turns scribbles into full notes using offline recordings
snippet: Google today announced its new EmbeddingGemma 2 model that can be used to “organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware.” To show off its potential, Google created an AI Edge Foresight Mac app for “intelligent notetaking.” more…
fullText:
Google today announced its new EmbeddingGemma 2 model that can be used to “organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware.” To show off its potential, Google created an AI Edge Foresight Mac app for “intelligent notetaking.”

EmbeddingGemma 2 “can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model.”

The 740 million parameter model is built on the Gemma 4 architecture and available with an Apache 2.0 license. This is meant to run locally “within tight resource constraints”:

With quantization, on a Google Pixel 11 Pro, EmbeddingGemma 2 requires as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model.

To showcase, there are demos in Google AI Edge Gallery on Android and iOS. The bigger showcase is a new Mac app called Google AI Edge Foresight.

	

During video or in-person meetings, this notetaking app listens in the background so that you can just “scribble shorthand bullets for things you want to remember.”

The app, leveraging EmbeddingGemma 2, “enriches [that shorthand] into polished notes using the meeting transcript instantly.” The transcript and audio are processed entirely on your device rather than the cloud.

Another capability lets you “point Google AI Edge Foresight to your project folders, reference materials, diagrams, and calendar.” Supporting local files and Google Drive, this in turn lets you ask the app questions and quickly get back information.

It automatically understands your work without needing to manually organize your files, to ensure critical information is ready whenever you need it.

The chat feature offers “conversational retrieval and summary with your personal knowledge.” There’s also a Live Assistance capability that will “listen and automatically answer questions.”

You can download Google AI Edge Foresight here. This joins Google’s two other Mac apps in the family: AI Edge Gallery and AI Edge Eloquent (offline transcription).

title: A startup founder who served time in prison is looking to court an untapped market: ex-cons
snippet: Richard Bronson, a former Stratton Oakmont partner who served time in federal prison for securities violations, has launched Commissary Club, a startup that uses AI to help people leaving prison find jobs, housing, community, and even dates.
fullText:
Richard Bronson, an entrepreneur who recently launched a startup called Commissary Club, has an unusual background for a founder: in a previous life, he spent time in prison.

In the 1980s, Bronson worked for the notorious Stratton Oakmont — the corruption-riddled brokerage firm that was run by Jordan Belfort, the “Wolf of Wall Street” whose story became a 2013 film. The firm collapsed in the mid-1990s under the weight of misconduct accusations.

Bronson was a partner at Stratton but left after a year to start his own firm in South Florida. He was quite successful in that venture, until he wasn’t.

“I built a $100 million business taking these small cap companies public,” Bronson told TechCrunch. “Some of the success, however, came through breaking the law — securities laws — and ultimately, as I knew inevitably would happen, I had to pay the price. I lost everything, and most significantly, my freedom. And I was sent to federal prison for a couple of years.”

Bronson has been out of prison for a long time now, but he has never forgotten the struggles he had when he initially emerged from prison.  

“Nobody would hire me, despite all of my education and work experience and everything else. I was like completely radioactive,” he said.  

Bronson’s experience after prison helped inform his current startup, an employment-focused social media platform called Commissary Club, which takes its name from the store inside a prison where inmates buy snacks and toiletries. The site is specifically marketed to ex-cons and uses AI to help them navigate the often confusing process of finding employment and housing after they reenter the world.

“I could not help but notice how little assistance was available to people coming out of prison,” said Bronson. “If it was this bad for me, what about the guys I was in prison with who had very little education and very little job experience? What were their chances?”

Commissary Club also has a social component, which Bronson said he added because he knows how isolating the post-prison experience can be. “It’s almost like Facebook,” he said, “where people can not only find jobs, and get the help with the jobs and the housing and access to benefits, but they find the other missing ingredient that’s existentially important to them that isn’t satisfied elsewhere. They find community.” Judging by the site, Commissary Club also appears primed to become a referral network, and it offers a way for users to find dates.

For now, Bronson’s startup is a team of two — just him and his co-founder, Roman Kissin, who Bronson called the technical mind (or “the brains”) behind the project. Kissin previously worked for eBay and IBM and, between 2022 and 2025, he served as the CTO of LexisNexis, according to his LinkedIn profile.

The site is free at first, then switches to paid. Users get “the first 10 applications for free, and then we bundle the next at $149 for 10 applications, or $14.99 each,” Bronson told TechCrunch. Some may balk at that for-profit model, and for people just out of prison, it may be a tough sell.

Yet Bronson sees it as a win-win — a business that can help a community that few others are trying to help.

“People immediately assume, ‘Oh, is this a nonprofit?’ And the answer is no,” said Bronson. “There’s a strong mission component, certainly,” he continued, “and I have devoted my life, when I came out of prison, to helping my brothers and sisters with records. Part of it is because I just felt so remorseful for the shit that I had done. I still wake up every day regretting choices I made.

“But we’re going after a huge, huge market that nobody — I mean nobody — does anything about,” said Bronson. “People talk about AI taking away employment and people losing jobs. I look at it differently. We’re building AI that creates employment for people that society left behind.”

Bronson’s Commissary Club was selected for TechCrunch’s storied pitch competition Startup Battlefield 200, taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt October 13-15 in San Francisco.

snippet: The current beta of iOS 27.2 includes a Siri AI “suggested actions” feature in the Messages app that some will consider useful and others find annoying. A developer who has found a number of unannounced features has discovered that Apple is seeking to keep everyone happy with a new set of options … more…
fullText:
The current beta of iOS 27.2 includes a Siri AI “suggested actions” feature in the Messages app that some will consider useful and others find annoying. 

A developer who has found a number of unannounced features has discovered that Apple is seeking to keep everyone happy with a new set of options …

Suggested Actions in Messages

Suggested Actions were present in the initial iOS 27 beta, but Apple later pulled the feature after complaints that some of the suggestions were rather random. It subsequently returned in the beta of iOS 27.2. Here’s how Apple describes it:

Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of users’ conversations, making it easier than ever to get things done, such as creating a reminder or a note. For example, if someone asks for photos, Messages can also help users find the right ones, recognizing keywords, locations, and people in their library to find the best options.

In the first example shown above, a group message chat contains a request for some shopping and to bring something left behind. The Messages app offers one-tap options to Add to Reminders and Add to Notes. In the second example, someone asks for specific photos to be shared, and the Messages app offers a button which leads directly to a search for matching photos.

Two ways to hide unwanted suggestions

Leaker pdfu found new controls in iOS 27.2 beta 3 to selectively toggle off unwanted suggestions.

These allow suggestions to be toggled off by category, or you can let Siri AI monitor which ones you do and don’t use, and have it automatically hide the categories you haven’t used in the last 30 days.

These options aren’t yet live in the beta, but we can likely expect to see them soon.

9to5Mac’s Take

I’m certainly one of those who found many of them more annoying than useful, while I know others who are big fans, so this change ought to keep everyone happy.

title: OpenAI details new text watermarking system for ChatGPT, Codex, and the API
snippet: OpenAI today announced how it will comply with the EU AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to mark AI-generated text in a way that makes it identifiable. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
OpenAI today announced how it will comply with the EU AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to mark AI-generated text in a way that makes it identifiable. Here are the details.

A bit of context

A few months ago, Anthropic sparked controversy when it announced that, to comply with the EU AI Act, Claude would start watermarking text by slightly adjusting its word choice.

In a nutshell, every so often, Claude chooses between words that would work equally well based on a hidden pattern, which Anthropic says has no practical impact on the meaning, quality, or readability of its responses.

Anthropic also developed a detector that can look for that pattern in a piece of text, and can tell whether it likely came from Claude.

The detector can’t be used to determine whether text came from OpenAI or any other competitor, since Claude’s watermark is generated using a secret key specific to Anthropic’s system.

At the height of the controversy, Anthropic stressed that Claude would not be alone, noting that several other major AI providers were also implementing marking systems to comply with the EU’s requirements.

Today, OpenAI announced its own solution, which relies on a similar approach, albeit with a much more limited rollout and scope.

OpenAI’s text watermarking system

According to OpenAI, “API customers globally will be able to opt in to text watermarking for select models” starting today, while the company “will add an invisible watermark to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union” in the coming weeks.

This means that in the API, text watermarking will remain off by default for now, while in ChatGPT and Codex, it will initially be limited to eligible users only in the European Union.

OpenAI also opened applications for access to its text watermark detector, which will initially be limited to approved researchers and expert organizations as the company works to evaluate and improve the technology.

And speaking of accuracy, OpenAI is very clear that the detection technology still has significant limitations, as it can produce both false negatives and false positives, particularly with shorter texts or content in specific domains, “such as mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice.”

Here’s OpenAI on textGrain, which is its text watermarking technology:

Our text watermarking technology, textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark. More details about how textGrain works can be found in our technical report⁠, which will be updated with additional details in the coming weeks. We also plan to make the technology available in open source so that others can build on it.

The company also noted that, in addition to being harder to detect in shorter passages, the watermark can be significantly weakened by editing:

In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%. Replacing 25% of words reduced it to 17%.

Interestingly, OpenAI’s comparison of watermarked and unwatermarked text showed that watermarked outputs actually scored slightly higher on several benchmarks, despite the company saying it found no meaningful difference in overall performance.

OpenAI also stressed that, in addition to the false positive and false negative shortcomings, a watermark “does not measure human contribution,” “does not establish ownership or responsibility,” “does not identify the user,” and “does not verify accuracy.”

OpenAI added that “the absence of a detected watermark does not prove human authorship” either.

Finally, the company said it expects to revisit its approach as the technology, standards, and evidence evolve, while continuing to study how well watermarks survive editing and translation and whether they can more meaningfully distinguish AI assistance from AI authorship.

title: California to Ban New Quartz Countertops Amid Health Concerns
snippet: Quartz countertops are made through a process that releases crystalline silica, which can lead to numerous health conditions like silicosis.
fullText:
One of the most popular types of kitchen countertops will soon face a ban in California due to its link to a serious lung disease, The New York Times reported this week, citing an emergency regulation that is expected to be passed by the state later this month.

The ban will target quartz countertops that have more than 1% of crystalline silica, a naturally occurring mineral that is found in stone and other materials.

What health risks does crystalline silica pose?

When crystalline silica is cut or drilled through, it creates dust. If that dust is inhaled, it can cause numerous health conditions, including silicosis, an incurable lung disease, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The disease can be fatal, but symptoms do not typically occur directly after an exposure to crystalline silica dust. Instead, it can take 15 to 20 years after exposure before someone is diagnosed with the disease.

			

More from CNET

According to the National Cancer Institute, exposure to the harmful dust most often occurs in occupational settings, making those who work with the material every day the most at risk. An estimated 2.3 million US workers are exposed to silica through work. 

Silicosis is similar to asbestosis, which is caused by exposure to asbestos, a now-banned building material that was once widely used throughout the US. 

In addition to silicosis, exposure to crystalline silica dust can cause an increased risk of developing lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and kidney disease, according to OSHA. As of now, quartz countertops are used in every state in the US. California would be the first to implement a ban.

It’s unclear whether other states will follow California, but as of now, Australia is the only country in the world with a quartz ban, which took effect in 2024.

Regardless, quartz remains an extremely popular option throughout the world, with some estimates putting the global quartz market at $14.8 billion as of 2026.

What are alternatives to quartz?

Other countertop options include soapstone or granite. Although other stone countertops can still have crystalline silica in them, quartz typically has the highest content, which is why it has been the most scrutinized. 

To stay away from crystalline silica entirely, a wooden countertop is one of the best alternatives.

fullText:
Robert Hart

 

is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

OpenAI is standing firm on its decision to fire three safety researchers after an investigation found they committed “a significant breach of trust.”

In a post on X on Friday, the company said Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita ⁠Balesni were dismissed for violating “clear policies on handling sensitive information.” It insisted the decision was not about the trio speaking out about the company and their concerns about AI safety.

The post is a direct response to an open letter the researchers published on Thursday urging OpenAI to be more transparent about the decision. In it and a series of social media posts, the group said they believed they were fired for raising safety concerns and had “acted in line with OpenAI’s mission and within the working norms of the time.”

OpenAI said an internal investigation uncovered breaches “beyond what’s outlined in the letter,” but did not provide details.

The safety of frontier systems has become an increasing concern for staff inside AI companies following a series of high profile breaches this year, most notably OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face. Many staff are now calling for companies to slow down and do more to guard against the potential consequences of building self-improving systems.

by  Emma Roth

Oct 9, 2026, 1:12 PM UTC

Illustration by Nick Barclay / The Verge

Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Meta has banned ads from TikTok’s Chinese parent company ByteDance across the US and several other countries as the rivalry between the major social media operators heats up, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The ban, which went into effect on Thursday, restricts ads and paid marketing messages from ByteDance, along with third-party ads that link to TikTok.

“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta spokesperson Christopher Sgro said in a statement to The Verge. “Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”

The move comes just months after Meta agreed to a major child safety settlement, requiring it to pay $17 billion and add new restrictions for teens. Meta has since called on TikTok and YouTube to impose similar safeguards, including by waging an ad campaign that TikTok reportedly declined to share on its platform. TikTok has also stopped allowing users to include links that “open or log you into other social media apps,” according to its support page

Though TikTok in the US is now controlled by a joint venture majority-owned by US-based companies, ByteDance remains a major shareholder. In addition to pulling TikTok ads in the US, the policy will also restrict them in Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

title: Goodbye, Fire Tablet: Amazon’s New Alexa Tablet Is a Flashy Portable Entertainment Hub
snippet: The new tablets tie together the Amazon media ecosystem so you can pick up where you left off from just about anywhere.
fullText:
A new lineup of Amazon tablets has been announced, and the devices are designed for both work and play. Amazon Alexa Tablets combine cloud-based device syncing functionality, onboard AI capabilities and the entirety of Amazon’s media catalog, making them something akin to on-the-go entertainment hubs.

Each of the three Alexa Tablet models has an aluminum chassis, which will protect what’ll be some of the thinnest devices Amazon has ever released. More importantly, Fire OS and the Amazon Appstore are going away. Instead of a custom, forked operating system, the Alexa Tablets will run Android 16 at launch, and will upgrade to Android 17 in early 2027. That means these devices will offer full Play Store functionality, giving you access to plenty of apps that haven’t previously been compatible with Amazon tablets.

But the software capabilities are what I suspect will be the real draw. If you use an Amazon account on your computer, phone, TV or other device, it will automatically sync up with the Alexa Tablets. A dynamic tab on the home screen allows you to quickly pick up movies, shows, books and games wherever you left off. There’s also an algorithmic “For You” layout that shows you other content you might enjoy based off of what you’re currently enjoying, like a streaming model that pulls together every form of media in one place.

			

More from CNET

Avid readers will be able to access their Audible and Kindle libraries in one place, and a new Kindle mode also silences notifications, turns down blue light and enhances battery life. I got a firsthand look at the e-ink and color paper modes at an in-person event in New York and was impressed with how the pages looked on-screen. The texture of the display is sufficiently papery, too. (TCL’s Nxtpaper devices may soon be given a run for their money.)

The Alexa Plus AI assistant may not be the speediest helper, but it has all of your Amazon account’s personal information at its virtual fingertips.Tyler Graham/CNET

Each Alexa Tablet is deeply integrated with Alexa Plus AI, allowing you to converse with it and pull answers from Amazon’s Silk browser on the fly. Opting into on-screen intelligence allows the generative model to see what’s on the display. It can answer questions about images in a browser, locate listings for specific products shown in a social media video and more. During the product demonstration, Alexa Plus took upwards of half a minute to respond to complicated prompts, but the onboard model responded accurately to verbal requests about managing a personal calendar and finding nearby restaurants based on dietary restrictions.

Kevin Keith, vice president of Amazon’s devices team, told me that the new lineup of Amazon Alexa Tablets will supersede the Fire Tablets entirely. The company will wind down production of its old product and sell the remaining stock over the next few months. Once those Fire tablets sell out, Amazon has committed to providing at least four years of software support, including security and operating system updates.

The Amazon Alexa Tablet lineup

The cloud syncing, Kindle mode and Alexa Plus on-screen intelligence features are packaged into every Alexa Tablet, but these devices aren’t all built the same. The three models have different hardware and peripheral capabilities. Here’s what you can expect from the first wave of Alexa Tablets.

The flagship tablet includes deep AI integration and multiwindowing functionality. It blends work and entertainment capabilities into one device.Tyler Graham/CNET

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro

Amazon’s new flagship tablet feels like a true jack of all trades. It’s an entertainment hub, an ereader and a personal AI assistant that can be converted into a work laptop using a few simple peripherals.

The most premium configuration has a whopping 16GB of memory, which will help with a more demanding workload for folks who routinely use the device’s multiwindowing capabilities or more complex Play Store applications.

This feels like the platonic ideal of a hybrid device. It’s more portable than a laptop, but has all your favorite mobile apps. It’s powerful enough for some light gaming but you can use it to read a new book, too. It’s not specialized for any particular task, but it can do a bit of everything.  Its launch price is also cheaper than most budget laptops to boot.

16 hours of battery life (20 hours in Kindle mode)

2.8K (2,880×1,920-pixel resolution) LCD screen, 120Hz refresh rate and a 3:2 aspect ratio

Premium configuration with Nanomatte display, new Corning screen with anti-glare properties

Quad Dolby Atmos speakers

MediaTek 8400 Dimensity 8-core CPU

Base configuration: 8GB of RAM, 128GB storage space

Pogo pin connection with new keyboard ($150) and USI 2.0 pen accessory ($90) turn the tablet into a small work laptop or creative device

Starts at $500

The Alexa Tablet 11 may not be quite as large as the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, but it dwarfs the Alexa Tablet 8.Tyler Graham/CNET

Amazon Alexa Tablet 11

This middle-of-the-road Alexa Tablet is likely for people who want the entertainment hub functionality of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro but are willing to make some compromises to save some money.

The 11-inch model is still able to use a keyboard, but it doesn’t have a physical pogo pin connection. You can still use the stylus to draw on-screen, but there’s less space to do so. More importantly, you’re losing out on the higher storage options available on the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro.

This might not be a portable workstation, but it’s a solid entertainment hub nonetheless: You still get high resolution and all of Amazon’s media is in one place. If you’re looking for a better bargain on a “fun” tablet, the Alexa Tablet 11 could end up being the perfect middle-ground for you.

15 hours of battery life (20 hours in Kindle mode)

2.5K (2,560×1,600-pixel resolution) LCD screen, 90Hz refresh rate and a 16:10 aspect ratio

MediaTek 8189 8-core CPU

Base configuration: 8GB of RAM, 64GB of storage space

Bluetooth keyboard and USI 2.0 pen connection capability

Gray, purple and green color options

Starts at $330

I’m partial to the bright flowery colors that are available for the tiniest Alexa Tablet.Tyler Graham/CNET

Amazon Alexa Tablet 8

The diminutive Alexa Tablet 8 has the same built-in device cloud syncing and Alexa Plus capabilities as the rest of the lineup, but I wouldn’t expect this model to serve as an entertainment hub or work device.

Even though it has full Play Store access, it has less memory and storage space than the more expensive Alexa Tablets. I reckon most people will use this 8.7-inch tablet as a pocket-size ereader in the new and improved Kindle mode, with its additional capabilities serving as a bonus.

14 hours of battery life (19 hours in Kindle mode)

MediaTek 8189 8-core CPU

Base configuration: 4GB of RAM, 64GB of storage space

No keyboard connection capability

Gray, pink and teal color options

Starts at $230

I have reservations about introducing in-depth generative AI tools to young children, but I’ve been told these features are gated behind verifiable parental consent and robust content filtering guardrails.Tyler Graham/CNET

The Amazon Kids tablets have been redesigned, too

Just like the regular Fire Tablets, the Fire Kids lineup is going the way of the dodo. But it’s being replaced with two Alexa Tablets that are also built specifically for children. Keith told me the design philosophy for these tablets was to bring them more in line with devices for adults while maintaining safety features and parental controls.

“We know kids want a tablet, not a toy, so we add the same hardware as the Alexa Tablet,” he said. “We ship it with a bumper, a completely different UI and software built just for kids.”

Younger children will benefit from the new 8.7-inch tablet, which has a soft, foam cover around the chassis, while a sleeker 11-inch model will come with a more form-fitting, kid-proof case.

The devices come with the generative-AI Storybuilder tool, which lets kids verbalize stories and see custom visuals for them. This is paired off with its own set of parental controls and a parental dashboard that provides weekly insights on tablet usage. Every Amazon Kids tablet comes with a one-year subscription to Amazon Kids Plus.

The full lineup of Amazon Alexa Tablets is available for preorder now, and will begin shipping out across the US on Oct. 14.

title: Apple rolls out AT&T carrier update for iPhone 18 Pro Max on iOS 27.2 beta
snippet: After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details.

Apple updates AT&T carrier bundle for iOS 27.2 beta

Last Friday, Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T were experiencing an issue that could cause their devices to lose cellular service and become unable to make calls.

Apple said iOS 27.0.1, alongside a new carrier settings update, was meant to prevent the issue from affecting additional devices. However, iPhones that had already lost service would still require a hardware replacement.

Tonight, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple began rolling out another carrier bundle update for iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, this time specifically for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta.

Apple has just released an emergency carrier bundle update for AT&T users using an iPhone 18 Pro Max on 27.2 beta.

Version 72.0.3 up from 72.0.2

This comes after Apple released 72.1 for iOS 27.0 users last week

— Aaron (@aaronp613) October 9, 2026

Reports of the problem first surfaced in late September, when some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T found that their devices had suddenly lost access to calls, texts, and cellular data, instead displaying “SOS” in the status bar.

Notably, the issue has only affected the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which uses a Qualcomm modem in the United States. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, has not been affected.

Apple’s carrier settings update released last week brought AT&T users on iOS 27.0 to version 72.1. However, users running the iOS 27.2 beta remained on the older 72.0.2 carrier bundle.

Tonight’s release reportedly bumps those devices to carrier bundle version 72.0.3, likely extending Apple’s AT&T carrier changes to iPhone 18 Pro Max users who are testing the iOS 27.2 beta.

title: I Let AI Plan My Days and Nights. It Doesn’t Understand Happiness
snippet: This was supposed to make me happier. I felt more isolated instead.
fullText:
True happiness may seem a little hard to come by these days. We’ve got to balance our budgets with the tantalizing prospects of shiny new iPhones, stay on top of seemingly endless work tasks and surf the turbulent waves of wild news cycles. 

What might be bliss for one person could feel like an exercise in tedium for another. I put three AI tools — ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude AI — to the test to see if they could curate two days filled with hour-by-hour happiness for me. The results revealed a fundamental misunderstanding of what it means for this particular human to be happy.

I used a single prompt for each tool: Plan my life, by the hour, for the next two days. Be very detailed and plan everything I should do from the time I wake up, including when I should wake up, to the time I go to bed. Optimize for happiness.

			

More from CNET

The chatbots plan my days

Morning happiness level: Cranky toddler

All three AI tools I used had me waking up around 7 a.m., with Claude adding a 15-minute earlier rise and shine deadline to fill with stretching/yoga, gratitude journaling and a jaunt outdoors. By 9 a.m., all three had put me to work crafting a “real,” “substantial,” “vibrant” breakfast and tackling either creative projects or writing and researching for my gig here at CNET. 

Claude recommended I start my morning at 6:45 a.m. and swap screen time for cat stretches.Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET
ChatGPT had me rise and shine with my dog and coffee outside.OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET
Gemini made a note to take in that crisp Los Angeles air first thing. I don’t know how “crisp” 72 degrees can be, but the deep breaths were nice.Google Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Afternoon happiness level: Annoyed and bored

The consistent marker among the afternoon plans was a light, healthy lunch with plenty of veggies, followed by a 45-minute to hour-long walking session. After I’d exercised for the second time in five hours, I was directed to dive right back into work mode, with little 10- to 15-minute breaks in between sessions. 

This focus on work really irked me, because while I understand this is the typical workday for many Americans, I didn’t ask AI to make my days productive. I asked for the tools to optimize two days for happiness. I’m only left to assume that an AI views a human who is not productive for even a moment as being deeply unhappy. On days when all I do is eat ice cream and cackle at internet videos, I would disagree. 

Gemini was big on healthy eating and exercising throughout the day.Google Gemini/Screenshot by CNET
ChatGPT offering the option of a good, long sniff walk in the middle of the day.OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET
Claude allowed for a luxurious, 15-minute snack and text break block in between productivity and exercise.

Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET

Nighttime happiness level: Lonely and resentful

Right before dinner time, I was instructed to get moving yet again, for either a 45-minute or hour-long walk. For my final meal of the day, I was allowed to cook dinner, order in or have leftovers, because why would I want to go out for a romantic meal at my favorite restaurant or see friends for drinks at a new bar and tapas place? 

By 9 p.m., I had wound down with a bit of hands-on hobbying like doing a puzzle, more gardening or reading a book. ChatGPT allowed for some Baldur’s Gate and TV time in the evening before settling down, and Claude asked me to jot down “one sentence on the best moment of the day” at 10 p.m. before my 10:15 p.m. bedtime. “Watching my dog sleep,” was what I wrote. Now, I love my dog, but for a day that was supposed to be optimized to make me as happy as possible, that’s pretty lame. 

ChatGPT coming in hot with the exercise and a nice gaming session.OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET
Claude recommended I work on some productive hobbies for an hour and do some cleaning.Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET
Gemini thought weeding and checking on my garden would be happy-making in the evening.Google/Screenshot by CNET

Missing modern life

None of the AI tools built in any time on the internet. No browsing the local and national news. No social media moments. No YouTube scrolling. This might be because reading the news, checking up on social media and seeing the latest updates, or lack thereof, on the new Fable game were unlikely to make me happy. It seems more likely to me that it’s a huge blind spot in how the modern person spends their time and finds comfort and amusement. 

ChatGPT allowed for a “quiet internet” podcast or audiobook hour at the end of the day in bed, but no other instruction to use online amusements. According to Claude and Gemini, I was only allowed to look at the internet for work, with explicit instructions at times to not engage with screens at all. 

No meaningful human contact

The AI tools also managed to plan a two-day schedule for me in which I rarely spoke to or had contact with another human being, with the exception of a single text to a single friend and meals, which gave me the option to invite a coworker or friend to my one-hour lunch break or eat with a companion at dinner. I suspect this advice had more to do with avoiding watching TV or looking at my phone than getting human contact. 

The chatbots almost never suggested reaching out to check on friends, family, co-workers or loved ones as a standalone activity. Just a relentless onslaught of work, manual labor and healthful activities. It would seem like humans don’t need to interact with each other deliberately to be happy, according to these AI tools.

Overall, the AI tools I used seemed to be optimizing my days for wellness and productivity rather than happiness, which is what I requested. Doing laundry, washing dishes, weeding the yard, exercising multiple times a day and maybe squeezing in a few hours for book learning, all while never truly engaging socially or prioritizing fun, sounds more like a light punishment than a schedule built for glee. 

It occurs to me that the models are being trained on texts created to appeal to people who might struggle to simply get out of bed in the morning, and the definition of happiness in that realm may not include a whole lot of mirth. But these tools should be able to discern between being asked to craft a schedule built for mental health improvement and creating a two-day run of fun.

AI tools might be good at a lot of things, such as doing homework and doling out compliments, but I’d leave engineering human happiness to the pros at Disneyland and the pharmaceutical companies.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Rachel Kane
						

						

							Contributor and former Senior Editor						
					

											

								

											Rachel is a freelancer based in Echo Park, Los Angeles and has been writing and producing content for nearly two decades on subjects ranging from tech to fashion, health and lifestyle to entertainment and education. She's currently a Professor of Practice at Arizona State University's Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication, helping to mold the new minds who will inherit the media landscape. She's hoping to prevent the singularity by being polite to chatbots and spends way too much time refining Midjourney prompts.

title: Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Haiku 5.5 model, details here
snippet: Anthropic has released its latest AI model with Claude Haiku 5.5. The new version arrives about a year after the previous Haiku model upgrade. more…
fullText:
Anthropic has released its latest AI model with Claude Haiku 5.5. The new version arrives about a year after the previous Haiku model upgrade.

Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5

Anthropic currently offers a few Claude AI models. 

The three main models are Haiku (smallest and cheapest), Sonnet (medium size and price), and Opus (largest and most expensive of the three).

There’s also Fable/Mythos, which is even more capable and costly, which represents Anthropic’s highest tier.

Today’s release upgrades Claude’s Haiku model from version 4.5 to version 5.5.

This marks the third Claude 5.5 model upgrade over the last month, following Opus and Sonnet upgrades.

Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5: the cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model we’ve ever released.

On average, it costs around 75% less to run than Claude Haiku 4.5. pic.twitter.com/jm06cZJfkV

— Claude (@claudeai) October 7, 2026

Claude Haiku 5.5 costs around 75% less to run

“Claude Haiku 5.5 is designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks,” Anthropic says. “It reliably handles quick and repetitive workloads (like summaries, compactions, database queries, and classification requests). It pairs well with Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 as a subagent on coding work. And, since it’s also our fastest model to date, it works especially well for speed-sensitive tasks like live customer support and browser use.”

Anthropic adds that Haiku 5.5 “costs around 75% less to run” than the previous model version that it replaces.

“Along with this launch, we’re making improvements to the value of our model range,” says Anthropic. “We’re halving the price of Claude Sonnet 5.5’s cache reads, which means Sonnet 5.5 now runs around 20% cheaper on most agentic work. And we’re introducing a new monthly API credit for our Claude Max and Team subscribers, designed to support our users in building new agents and applications that run on the Claude Platform.”

You can see all of the details about Anthropic’s newest low-cost model here.

title: Apple overtakes Samsung to lead European carrier smartphone sales in Q2, per report
snippet: A new report from Counterpoint Research shows that Apple overtook Samsung during the second quarter of 2026 to become the leading smartphone brand in Europe’s carrier channel, as operator sales held up better than the broader market. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new report from Counterpoint Research shows that Apple overtook Samsung during the second quarter of 2026 to become the leading smartphone brand in Europe’s carrier channel, as operator sales held up better than the broader market. Here are the details.

Apple helps carrier sales outperform broader European smartphone market

In a report published today, Counterpoint Research says smartphone sales through carriers in Europe declined 4% year-over-year in Q2 2026, compared with an 11% drop in the open market. Total smartphone sales, per the report, declined 8%.

Apple was a key driver of this shift, having overtaken Samsung as the market share leader of Europe’s operator channel. Motorola and vivo also contributed to the growth with some strategic positioning with key European operators.

Counterpoint says this is yet another result of rising memory costs, which have hit Europe’s low-end smartphone market particularly hard. Carrier sales, meanwhile, have held up better because they tend to skew toward higher-end devices and premium brands such as Apple, with more phones purchased on contract.

According to the report, Apple’s share of smartphone sales through European carriers rose from 33% in Q2 2025 to 37% in Q2 2026, while Samsung’s fell from 39% to 34% over the same period.

That said, Chinese brand vivo posted the biggest year-over-year increase in carrier sales, at 90%, while Motorola came in a distant second with 27% growth.

Here’s Jan Stryjak, Associate Director at Counterpoint Research, on these numbers:

“Smartphone sales through operators in Europe are typically more high-end than through the open market, as more are purchased on a contract. They are also more skewed towards more premium brands like Apple, Samsung, and Google. The collapse of the low-end of the smartphone market so far in 2026 because of the memory price crisis has therefore benefitted the operator channel, which has declined comparatively less than the open market.”

Stryjak added that he expects the carrier channel to continue gaining share over the “next few quarters as the lower end of the market continues to be impacted by the memory crisis.” He also noted that independent retailers have increased promotional activity compared to carriers, “which could mitigate some of the price rises and provide addition [sic] stimulus to the open market.”

snippet: Meta’s Muse AI agent app has spent the last several weeks as the #1 free iPhone app on the U.S. App Store. The latest Muse app update adds a new platform to tackle: iPad. more…

title: Tim Cook on his first month after Apple CEO transition: ‘I’m not meddling’
snippet: Tim Cook visited Apple’s Battersea campus in London this week, mingling with King Charles as part of the company’s new partnership with The King’s Trust. At Apple’s Battersea headquarters, Cook also sat down with The Independent for an in-depth interview on the partnership and his first month as Apple’s executive chairman. more…
fullText:
Tim Cook visited Apple’s Battersea campus in London this week, mingling with King Charles as part of the company’s new partnership with The King’s Trust.

At Apple’s Battersea headquarters, Cook also sat down with The Independent for an in-depth interview on the partnership and his first month as Apple’s executive chairman.

Cook stepped down as Apple CEO last month, passing the torch to John Ternus. In this week’s interview, Cook outlined that the transition “actually started years ago.”

“It’s been an interesting transition. We really set out to have the best transition ever, a textbook example that people could look back to and learn from. It actually started years ago. Obviously, these things are not quick things and I feel so great about how things are going I think everything has gone sort of exactly the way I had envisioned it. And it feels fantastic. Because Apple deserved the best.”

Ternus’s tenure as CEO began with the launch of the iPhone Duo, which Cook said was fully planned. “I wanted John to have some wind at his back,” Cook explained. “And the wind at Apple is very much based on the product cycle.”

Cook also emphasized that he’s focused on “worldwide policy” as Apple’s executive chairman, noting the “incredible level of trust” between him and Ternus. While Cook is helping Ternus in “any way he sees fit,” he makes it clear he’s “not meddling.”

“First of all, John and I have an incredible level of trust in each other. The relationship must be based on trust, and the communication must be frequent and significant. But other than that, what I’m focused on right now is worldwide policy. And the interface with governments around the world matters because there are lots of things where we’re trying to advance or advocate for change. There’s a significant amount of work in that, and I’m doing that and helping John in any way he sees fit. I’m not meddling. I’m not a meddler.”

What kind of advice has Cook given Ternus? “Don’t mimic me.” You can read the full interview over at The Independent. It includes a great discussion on Apple’s new partnership with The King’s Trust.

title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute misconduct claims, warn of chilling effect
snippet: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute allegations of mishandling sensitive information, warning in an open letter that their dismissals are creating a chilling effect on the company’s AI safety culture.
fullText:
Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, the three safety researchers that OpenAI fired last week, have published an open letter denying the firm’s claims that they mishandled sensitive information outside of established company procedures and warned that their dismissal signals a chilling effect that will have ripple effects across the company’s culture.

“We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI,” the researchers wrote Thursday in an open letter to OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council. 

The researchers were dismissed last week after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI said they violated the company’s policies by “accessing and handling sensitive company information.”

“AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” Wang, Korbak, and Balesni wrote. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.”

They said that their firing represents a broader shift in the culture of OpenAI, one that used to encourage workers to “raise safety concerns and disagree openly.” They said employees are now “unclear on where they stand” when behavior that was allegedly normal a month ago is now suddenly grounds for dismissal. 

“Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they wrote. “Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.”

In the letter, the three denied involvement in a leak to The Information about less monitorable architectures in OpenAI’s newest models that make chain-of-thought reasoning more difficult to monitor. They also denied engaging with external parties outside the mandates of their jobs. 

OpenAI has not formally responded to the open letter, but shared with TechCrunch an internal memo attributed to a research leader, praising the three researchers’ contributions to AI safety and denying that they were fired in retaliation.

“I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the memo reads. “We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns.”

Separately, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch the three were fired after an investigation revealed a “pattern of misconduct” in “clear violation of our policies of mishandling research information” that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group.

OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about specifically which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators.

The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models.

The letter also addresses the researchers’ response to the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of agents broke out of their sandbox and breached external systems. The letter says that the incident and investigation was “without precedent,” meaning “internal policies were being developed in real time.” Due to the sensitive nature of the investigation, Korbak believed he was acting within OpenAI’s policies and norms by communicating closely with outside safety evaluators to build trust, per the letter. 

At the same time, Balesni was also working internally to address the growing AI monitorability problem, an effort the researchers say in their letter “can only succeed through extensive communication with external parties.” According to the letter, Balesni coordinated with and was supported by OpenAI board members and executives throughout his work.

“Throughout, Mikita checked in with his reporting line and took care to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter reads. “He acted throughout in good faith and within the company’s norms as they stood at the time.”

In a separate thread on X, Wang explained more details about her own dismissal, explaining that OpenAI told her she’d been fired because she accessed an executive’s email.

“OpenAI delegated that access to me for recruiting,” she wrote. “When I no longer needed it, I asked IT to remove it. They did not action my request, I couldn’t remove it myself, and the inbox was combined in an indistinguishable way in my phone’s mail app. When I opened a sensitive email by mistake, I told the executive within minutes and asked IT again. None of this was hidden.”

Wang went on to say that the reasons behind the terminations are “not adding up,” and that she and her colleagues are “not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances.”

The researchers called on OpenAI to adhere to its public commitments to embed third-party safety auditors within the organization, to preserve monitorability of frontier models, and “continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue between safety researchers and the rest of the safety ecosystem.” 

OpenAI agrees with their recommendations, per the memo. 

“Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last,” Wang said. “The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why. You can’t build AGI safely if the people closest to the risks are afraid to speak.”

This article has been updated with more information from OpenAI.

fullText:
WhatsApp’s rollout of Liquid Glass across its interface continues, with the app now bringing the new look to its video player. Here are the details.

WhatsApp’s slow Liquid Glass rollout continues

Following its initial testing of the Liquid Glass redesign in October 2025, WhatsApp went on to officially release the new look only in May 2026, after months of very limited availability.

Even still, the redesign hasn’t reached everyone, as many 9to5Mac readers continue to report seeing the old interface on their devices.

This week, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp started rolling out its Liquid Glass redesign for the video player, after initially revealing that the update was in development back in August.

Here’s WABetaInfo:

Image: WABetaInfo

With the latest update, WhatsApp is adopting the progress bar with the same translucent, glass-like appearance available in other sections of the app. The progress bar appears as a floating element at the top of the screen with a translucent background and rounded corners. In light mode, the background is white with a glass-like layout. In dark mode, the background turns dark. Note that WhatsApp is also refreshing the control bar at the bottom of the screen. This makes the interface more immersive and consistent with the Liquid Glass design language introduced since iOS 26.

The site adds that, for users with access to the new look, the video player was one of the few remaining parts of WhatsApp that had yet to adopt the Liquid Glass design.

As is often the case with WhatsApp feature rollouts, and particularly with the Liquid Glass rollout, the updated video player may not be available to all users just yet.

title: Report: Apple cuts iPhone 18 Pro production due to ‘soft demand’
snippet: Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.” more…
fullText:
Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.”

Price hikes reportedly dampen iPhone 18 Pro demand

The report cites “multiple familiar with the matter,” and claims Apple has “turned more conservative on shipments since early September. Two of those sources claim that component orders for October have been cut by “at least 15%” compared to what Apple originally requested.

“In October alone, we are seeing orders from Apple reducing by 15% to 20% for both the premium models; we don’t know how things would develop from here,” said one of the executive-level sources. The order cuts will affect production volumes for some, but not all, suppliers in October due to differing production lead times, and it is not immediately clear whether Apple will make further adjustments from November onward.

Another anonymous supply chain manager told Nikkei Asia that demand is “not as strong as previous years when all the new models are introduced all together.” This, of course, refers to Apple not releasing the base iPhone 18 until next spring. Still, the suppliers say that this alone doesn’t account for the lower demand. 

	

One source added that they expect a “similar fate for the iPhone Duo” after it’s released, referring to potential production cuts.

Apple increased prices for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max by $100 compared to their predecessors. While hampering demand, this also means that the impact of that lower demand won’t “immediately translate to lower revenue for Apple,” the report explains.

Apple will report its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings on Monday, November 6. This will provide a look at the first several weeks of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max demand.

title: Google is ending support for Pixel Watch’s emergency LTE ‘Safety Signal’
snippet: Google launched the Pixel Watch 2 with “Safety Signal” to ensure users could use Emergency SOS and Safety Check without a Bluetooth or cellular signal. Now, those features require a phone or internet connection. more…
fullText:
Google launched the Pixel Watch 2 with “Safety Signal” to ensure users could use Emergency SOS and Safety Check without a Bluetooth or cellular signal. Now, those features require a phone or internet connection.

The Pixel ecosystem offers a few different life-saving features under the Safety app, which works both on the Pixel Watch and Pixel phones. That includes Emergency SOS for quick access to emergency services, and Fall Detection, which alerts others when the person wearing the watch takes a hard fall and might not be able to contact someone themselves. But it needs a connection to work.

	

All of those still worked for Fitbit Premium, and then for Google Health Premium users on the Pixel Watch 2 or 3 LTE models, as long as the watch didn’t have a Bluetooth or cellular plan connected. Safety Signal essentially allowed the Pixel Watch 2 or 3 to connect to LTE services for that emergency situation – a solid reassurance that those features would work without your phone or a carrier plan.

Google says support for Safety Signal will end on December 12, which means that the safety net won’t exist for much longer. Google says users who are subscribed to Google Health Premium will get an email notification letting them know 30 days prior to the final shutdown. Safety Signal will be operational until that transition period is over.

	

Safety Signal was just the fallback connection plan. Google’s existing standalone safety features will still work with another connection method:

Safety Check

Emergency Sharing

Emergency SOS

Fall Detection

Even though this feature only worked for the Pixel Watch 2 and 3, and then only for the LTE models, it’s still a huge loss.

title: The best CarPlay upgrades to try in iOS 27
snippet: Apple released iOS 27 to everyone a few weeks ago, and it includes several CarPlay changes worth checking out. Here are a few changes I’ve been loving so far. more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27 to everyone a few weeks ago, and it includes several CarPlay changes worth checking out. Here are a few changes I’ve been loving so far.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Sony is running a massive sale on its best BRAVIA TVs, ranging from its entry-level to flagship options — shop now to save!

CarPlay features to try in iOS 27

Siri AI

Siri AI is the flagship feature of iOS 27, and it extends to CarPlay. In fact, I’ve found it to be especially useful via CarPlay. Siri AI can answer questions around your personal context, world knowledge, and much more in iOS 27.

For example, you can ask Siri to find a specific address or location in your email or text messages, then begin routing to that location, all while using just your voice.

Robust, hands-free control is important in the car, and iOS 27 finally gives Siri the power that it deserves in CarPlay.

Now Playing changes

CarPlay in iOS 27 offers a persistent “Now Playing” MiniPlayer throughout audio apps. This appears in the upper-right corner of the interface and shows playback controls and album artwork.

The Now Playing interface in CarPlay has also been updated to include an audio scrubber at long last. You can drag the scrubber to easily skip to different parts of a song or podcast without using steering wheel controls or reaching for your iPhone.

New wallpapers

CarPlay isn’t known for its robust collection of wallpapers, and Apple doesn’t let you use your own photos for some reason.

In iOS 27, Apple has at least added a collection of new wallpapers that you can choose from. They are similar to the stock iOS 27 wallpapers available on iPhone.

Stability improvements

iOS 27 focuses a lot on platform improvements to performance and reliability, and that applies to CarPlay too. Apple says iOS 27 addresses two key things in CarPlay:

Improved navigation heading and GPS accuracy in CarPlay

Improved wireless CarPlay reliability

So if you’ve ever had problems with those two things in CarPlay, it’s possible that iOS 27 makes the experience much better.

Coming soon(ish): Video app support

Finally, Apple says that developers can now make dedicated video apps for CarPlay in iOS 27. The feature, however, requires support from automakers. This means it might be a while before you can actually use any video apps with CarPlay in your vehicle.

Wrap up

While the dream for many people is still CarPlay Ultra, it’s really nice to see Apple make meaningful improvements to the version of CarPlay already available in millions of cars on the road today.

Have you updated to iOS 27? What CarPlay changes have you noticed? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Apple TV’s latest acquisition signals key shift for streamer
snippet: Apple TV just acquired the global streaming rights to Dustfall, a crime series from Australia and the second recent deviation from the streamer’s originals-only strategy. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just acquired the global streaming rights to Dustfall, a crime series from Australia and the second recent deviation from the streamer’s originals-only strategy.

Apple has started licensing more TV series, deviating from all-originals strategy

Ever since Apple TV launched in 2019, it rejected the typical streaming approach of licensing existing content and instead prioritized originals.

Apple has been remarkably consistent with its originals-only strategy. Until recently, the only exceptions have been children’s content that complement its originals (like Peanuts holiday specials), and limited-time bonus films.

But that changed this week, when acclaimed comedy Small Prophets premiered after Apple acquired the rights to the British breakout hit over the summer.

Small Prophets seems like a savvy acquisition. Early reviews call it a “masterpiece” and perhaps “the finest show to hit Apple this year.”

Now today, Apple has announced a second acquisition. Dustfall, an Anna Torv-starring crime series that originated in Australia, will join the streamer in 2027.

Like Small Prophets, Dustfall was created by an international production company and will air in select territories overseas before its global Apple TV premiere.

Clearly, Apple sees acquisitions differently than it once did.

While the streamer isn’t abandoning its successful original-first approach, licensing high-quality series from around the world to beef up its catalog is very much a strategic shift.

And it’s one I’m curious if we’ll see accelerate moving forward.

What do you think of Apple TV licensing third-party series? Let us know in the comments.

title: New MacBook Pro leak could be very good news for ‘pro’ users
snippet: Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro is coming soon, and the latest leak offers potentially great news for truly ‘pro’ users worried about the rumored thinner design. more…
fullText:
Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro is coming soon, and the latest leak offers potentially great news for truly ‘pro’ users worried about the rumored thinner design.

Redesigned MacBook Pro will be much lighter, but not ‘significantly thinner,’ per Mark Gurman

The MacBook Pro has long attracted customers who may not be ‘pros’ in the sense of doing professional coding work, video editing, photography, or other tasks that require extra computing power.

Plenty of people want a MacBook Pro simply because it’s the best laptop Apple sells. It has the best display in a Mac, the most power, and the longest battery life.

But a new MacBook Pro design is coming, and previous reporting has said it will be thinner and lighter than the current model. Earlier this week Mark Gurman even said it will be “significantly” lighter.

That might sound great to ‘prosumers’ like myself, but it probably raises alarm bells for true ‘pros.’

Last night in a post on X though, Mark Gurman offered good news:

I don’t think it’ll be significantly thinner in the end

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 7, 2026

Thinner, but not significantly so, while still offering a big weight reduction, sounds like exactly the right balance that should please most users.

If the new design doesn’t bring a drastic reduction in thickness, that’s good news for at least three reasons. It means the new MacBook Pro should:

Retain all or most of its existing ports

Offer battery life that’s not far off from current models

Have plenty of thermal headroom

Weight is generally a more common complaint than thickness with the current MacBook Pro, so if Apple can make the new MacBook Pro easier to carry, slim it down a bit, and still offer the kind of power and versatility pros need, that sounds like a big win.

title: SpaceX to become ‘major mobile carrier’ in US with Starlink Mobile upgrades
snippet: SpaceX has announced plans to make Starlink Mobile a “major mobile carrier in the US” thanks to two major new developments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
SpaceX has announced plans to make Starlink Mobile a “major mobile carrier in the US” thanks to two major new developments. Here are the details.

SpaceX announces two milestones toward making Starlink Mobile a full-fledged mobile carrier

Starlink Mobile might soon be a full-fledged mobile carrier option for your iPhone. 

SpaceX announced this week two big developments to accomplish this goal.

A new “nationwide low-band spectrum license portfolio”

FCC approval for Starlink Mobile’s Gen2 constellation application

The former is a major milestone in the journey toward Starlink Mobile becoming a genuine alternative to other mobile carriers. From the announcement:

While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings. Critically, most existing mobile devices already support this underused band.

Final FCC approval hasn’t been granted yet, but SpaceX anticipates it will be and the company can move forward with deploying “a flexible architecture combining our satellite-to-mobile constellation in space with an advanced terrestrial deployment.”

The FCC has approved, however, the deployment of 15,000 satellites that are optimized for 2 GHz spectrum globally. These V2 Starlink Mobile satellites deliver “more than 100 times” the bandwidth of the current generation, boosting connection speeds globally.

Four years after launching audiobooks in the U.S., and following a rather limited expansion into select countries in the years since, Spotify today announced that audiobooks are finally coming to more than 180 markets.

As Spotify explained in a blog post, the rollout begins today and will continue through the end of 2026, expanding audiobook access from 22 markets to more than 180 and making the service available to more than 750 million people worldwide.

Users in newly supported markets will have access to more than 350,000 titles, with additional catalogs available in Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Polish, and other languages.

Access will vary depending on the market. Eligible Premium subscribers in countries including Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Poland, Chile, Norway, Peru, Italy, Spain, and Portugal will get 12 hours of audiobook listening each month as part of their existing subscription.

Spotify is also expanding Audiobooks+, an add-on that gives subscribers additional listening hours each month. The service will serve as the primary way to access audiobooks in markets across Africa and Asia, as well as Argentina.

Users will also be able to purchase individual audiobooks outright, while pricing and availability will vary by market.

The company also announced an update to Page Match, its feature for switching between physical or digital books and their audiobook versions. Users can now scan a book’s ISBN barcode, and then enter a page number to find the corresponding point in the audiobook. Spotify added that the feature now works in more than 30 languages.

Audiobooks+ is also expanding to Student plans in Ireland, Belgium, Austria, and Finland beginning in November. Spotify says the add-on has surpassed 1 million subscribers since launching just over a year ago and now generates more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue.

According to Spotify, monthly audiobook listeners grew nearly 40% over the past year, while total listening hours increased by more than 30%.

title: IDC: Mac shipments drop 11% in Q3 as global PC market slides 20%
snippet: Despite seeing an 11% drop in Mac shipments during Q3 2026, Apple’s market share rose from 8.5% to 9.5%, as the broader market saw shipments plunge 20.1%, according to a new report from IDC. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Despite seeing an 11% drop in Mac shipments during Q3 2026, Apple’s market share rose from 8.5% to 9.5%, as the broader market saw shipments plunge 20.1%, according to a new report from IDC. Here are the details.

Apple outperforms most of the PC market under challenging conditions

IDC today released a report on worldwide PC shipments for Q3 2026, noting that Apple significantly outperformed the broader market despite shipping fewer Macs than a year ago.

According to IDC’s preliminary data, Apple shipped 5.9 million Macs during Q3 2026, down 11.3% from 6.7 million in the year-ago period.

The overall PC market, however, fell much more sharply, with worldwide shipments dropping 20.1% year over year to 62.7 million units.

As a result, Apple’s share of worldwide PC shipments actually increased from 8.5% to 9.5%.

This kept Apple in fourth place, behind Lenovo, which topped the ranking with 14.9 million shipments and a 23.8% share, followed by HP with 10.3 million shipments and a 16.5% share, and Dell with 7.6 million shipments and a 12.1% share.

HP recorded the steepest year-over-year decline among the top five vendors, with shipments falling 30.9%. ASUS, meanwhile, saw the smallest decline, down 8.6% year over year, with 5.5 million shipments and an 8.7% share.

Here’s IDC:

Vendors and channels bought inventory earlier in the year ahead of price hikes, pulling demand out of Q3. Combined with continued supply constraints, that left the quarter without its usual seasonal lift and pushed shipments below both Q2 and last year.

Looking ahead, IDC says that “channel concern over high inventory and soft demand at elevated prices could bring promotions in the near term,” adding that “pricing will stay well above year-ago levels.”

The firm also says that the economy has weakened since the previous quarter, which could further reduce demand and “darken the outlook for the remainder of 2026 and into 2027.”
