title: Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9
snippet: When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets. more…
fullText:
When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets.

A select group of users are starting to spot these screensavers being added to older Pixels, beginning with the Pixel 9, as reported by Android Authority. Earlier Pixels did have support for a basic screensaver tool, but with this upgrade, every option available on Google’s latest releases have finally been backported to its 2024 hardware. The update appears to include a pop-up demo of these new options, along with everything currently available as of the Pixel 11’s launch. Clock, Charge, Weather, Photos, and Home Controls are all available, and can be swiped through at will. And speaking of Charge, it too seems to be headed to the Pixel 10 series, after having been exclusive to the Pixel 11 for the past two months.

Unfortunately, it does seem like this is one of Google’s classic slow rollouts. There aren’t a massive amount of reports from Pixel 9 users that these styles are live on their devices, implying it might take a few weeks before reaching everyone. The same goes for Charge on the Pixel 10, with plenty of Redditors confirming they have yet to see that specific style arrive.

title: XREAL Aura with Android XR start at $1,279
snippet: XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279. more…
fullText:
XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279.

XREAL makes glasses that aren’t a traditional VR headset, nor are they the smart glasses we’ve imagined for the future. They sit somewhere in between, with a display that sits atop a see-through lens so you can mix the display’s content with the real world around you, no cameras needed. 

As we noted in a review of XREAL One Pro, though, the base experience of using the glasses to display content from a USB-C device like a laptop, phone, or handheld game console is a bit limited. Android XR’s promises are set to deliver a big upgrade to the experience, and that’s exactly what XREAL has been building.

XREAL Aura is effectively the same core idea, just with an included puck that has a battery, processing power, and Android XR. And it starts at $1,279, the company has today confirmed. The price of XREAL Aura was the missing puzzle piece for months, and it’s actually well below the company’s promise of “under $1,500.”

	

That’s for the base 12GB/256GB model, with an upgraded version costing a bit more:

XREAL Aura 12GB/256GB: $1,279

XREAL Aura 16GB/512GB: $1,499

There’s no charge for the medium or large size difference.

As far as actually putting in an order, XREAL says the initial delivery wave will arrive “before the holidays,” with a second wave presumably arriving sometime in early 2027. You have to purchase a $199 “Priority Deposit” to place a pre-order, with the cost going towards the price of your Aura glasses.

Pre-orders open later this month.

title: Leaks reveal new Apple TV 4K and HomePod features coming next week
snippet: Apple is launching new products next week, with Apple TV 4K and HomePod models rumored to be among them. And leaks in the latest Apple software reveal several new Apple TV and HomePod features expected to be unveiled. more…
fullText:
Apple is launching new products next week, with Apple TV 4K and HomePod models rumored to be among them. And leaks in the latest Apple software reveal several new Apple TV and HomePod features expected to be unveiled.

New Apple TV and HomePod features leaked in code are expected to be announced next week

Next week, Apple will unveil a fresh push into Home products, with new Apple TV 4K, ‘HomePad,’ and HomePod mini models set to launch.

We’ve already gotten plenty of leaks around new features to expect, but yesterday’s beta 3 releases of tvOS 27.2, HomePod 27.2, and iOS 27.2 reveal even more.

Aaron Perris found references in tvOS 27.2 beta 3 to Apple Intelligence coming to Apple TV. Headlined by Siri AI, these AI features are expected to be exclusive to new hardware.

He also found code in iOS 27.2 that suggests nearby home accessories could show controls in your iPhone’s Dynamic Island.

iOS 27.2 beta 3 includes new HomeKit code suggesting nearby smart-home accessories could show controls in the Dynamic Island.

A new method explicitly references showing Dynamic Island controls through HomeKit’s proximity manager. 

This is an AI mockup of what it may look like: pic.twitter.com/szddeb2nCg

— Aaron (@aaronp613) October 6, 2026

	

On the HomePod side, pdfu posted several discoveries related to the surround sound feature he previously detailed. A couple include:

Highlights from audioOS 27.2 beta 3:

Siri can match a speaker to its surround system. Code includes the diagnostic “Accessory [X] is a speaker in surround system [Y].” Relies on HomeKit exposing the surroundSystem interface.​

When HomePod is part of a Home Theater group for an eligible Apple TV, it can now use a new proxy-activation path to pass Siri requests to Apple TV. A separate, older path still forwards microphone audio to Apple TV.

title: Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android
snippet: After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards. more…
fullText:
After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards.

The previous design made use of a carousel to show your stored payment methods. This design showed just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google allowed you to reorder cards and set a default one.

	

With this stacked redesign, the homepage shows one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen layout that shows most of each card. “Manage payment methods” at the bottom lets you arrange the order and set the default.

You select a card to tap-to-pay. To see card details and transaction history, there’s a new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This adds an extra step compared to the previous approach.

	

This approach is nice for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom. There are no other changes to the Google Wallet homepage.

This redesign started appearing in September and is now seeing broader availability. It’s rolling out via a server-side update and appeared on several devices we checked today.

title: Googlebooks can’t install the Slack web app on day one
snippet: Googlebook is now on sale and shipping to customers and, on day one at least, they can’t install the Slack web app. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is now on sale and shipping to customers and, on day one at least, they can’t install the Slack web app. 

Googlebook as a platform relies on two main forms of apps. The first is native Android apps, as Googlebook OS is, at its core, Android. That’s what you’ll use for many experiences including Gemini, Google Photos, music apps, and more. Others, like Gmail and YouTube, instead rely on progressive web apps. That term might sound familiar if you’re a long-time Chromebook user, as Chromebooks bet pretty heavily on progressive web apps (PWAs).

That history aside, Googlebooks directly tell their users to use Slack through the web app. The Play Store puts up a banner saying that Slack is “better on the website” when you try to download the Android app. 

That’s correct, frankly, as Slack’s Android app has terrible support for anything besides a standard smartphone. 

	

But the Slack web app cannot be installed on a Googlebook at this time.

	

Trying to install the Slack web app as a PWA on Googlebook results in an error message saying that “this app cannot be installed.” You can still create a shortcut that opens as a Chrome tab, but it won’t open in a window. 

Other PWAs we’ve tested including Photopea, Squoosh, SnapDrop, and others seem to be working fine. It’s unclear why Slack in particular is broken, but it’s hard to imagine it’s the only PWA not working on Googlebook on day one. More importantly, Slack is a mainstay in the modern workspace, so lacking any form of desktop-level Slack support on day one is sure to leave a poor impression on early Googlebook adopters.

Update: Google, in a statement, says that Slack is not a “compliant” PWA but that Googlebook will add support for manual installation soon.

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

snippet: Apple is widely expected to release a new touchscreen MacBook Pro as soon as this month. This will mark the first-ever touchscreen Mac, and Apple is laying the groundwork in macOS 27.2 to accommodate touch gestures. more…
fullText:
Apple is widely expected to release a new touchscreen MacBook Pro as soon as this month. This will mark the first-ever touchscreen Mac, and Apple is laying the groundwork in macOS 27.2 to accommodate touch gestures.

Apple released macOS 27.2 beta 3 to developers today, and it includes new references to upcoming support for touchscreen interactivity. As discovered by Aaron Perris for MacRumors, there are “gesture recognition tools” for several stock Apple apps:

Photos adds “PXGTouchDwellGestureRecognizer”

Notes adds “ICTouchPressGestureRecognizer”

Safari adds “a touch sentinel recognizer”

Quick Look adds a “dragTouch feature”

macOS 27.2 beta 3 also adds a new long-press animation for the Dock, which could also be a hint at the forthcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro:

Apple has gradually made a number of changes to macOS 27 in preparation for touchscreen support, including pull-to-refresh support for the first time. macOS 27 also added touch input to Sidecar, a feature that lets you use your iPad as a secondary display for your Mac.

Bloomberg has also reported on Apple’s work to optimize macOS for the impending touchscreen MacBook Pro. For instance, tapping a button or control will prompt macOS to dynamically display relevant touch options. Similarly, tapping the menu bar will automatically enlarge controls for easier touch navigation.

In addition to a touchscreen, the new MacBook Pro will reportedly have an OLED display and be “significantly lighter” than the current models.

Apple is expected to introduce the new MacBook Pro (or MacBook Ultra?) as soon as this month, though Bloomberg has cautioned it could slip to November.

title: iFixit tears down Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, finds mixed repairability results
snippet: Concluding iFixit’s teardown sequence for Apple’s September launches, iFixit today published the teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s what they found. more…
fullText:
Concluding iFixit’s teardown sequence for Apple’s September launches, iFixit today published the teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s what they found.

iFixit tears down Apple Watch Ultra 4

After applying heat to the new Apple Watch Ultra 4’s screen, iFixit’s Shahram Mokhtari uses the company’s new metal pick to pry the screen open, exposing the battery and the Taptic Engine.

He notes that replacing the 2.444 Wh battery (versus 2.313 Wh in the Ultra 3) still requires removing the screen, which remains a significant repairability drawback. The four screws on the bottom of the case provide access only to the sensor assembly on the underside of the back cover and the S11 chip on the case itself.

Once the screen is unglued, though, removing the battery and disconnecting the display’s press connector seems straightforward enough, provided that the initial step was done carefully enough to avoid slicing through any of the flex cables underneath.

That said, with no significant improvements in repairability, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 scored 4/10 on iFixit’s repairability scale, the same as its predecessor.

iFixit tears down Apple Watch Series 12

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 revealed a slight repairability improvement, with Apple adding stretch-release adhesive and a pull tab that make the 1.461 Wh battery (versus 1.403 Wh in the 46mm Series 11) easier to remove.

Still, as with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, the Series 12 also requires prying off the glued display to get inside, which remains the biggest obstacle to repairs. Mokhtari noted that the tolerances around the Series 12’s display are even tighter than on the Ultra 4, requiring enough force to make him concerned about potentially damaging the screen.

Mokhtari also noted that Apple replaced the ZIF connector and tape used for the display on previous models with a simpler press connector.

The tradeoff is that replacing the screen now also requires removing and replacing the battery, “which, if you’ve come this far, why wouldn’t you?” he adds.

All in all, the modest repairability improvements were enough for iFixit to give the Series 12 a 4/10 repairability score, a 1-point bump from the last base-model Apple Watch it scored.

For comparison, iFixit gave Google’s Pixel Watch 5 a 9/10 repairability score, noting that its display can be removed with just two Torx screws and a gasket, while its battery can also be removed without dealing with adhesive.

title: From Zuck to Musk: Big Tech’s Scandals and Scammers Are Coming to the Big Screen
snippet: Here are the movies to keep an “AI” on through the rest of the year.
fullText:
Hollywood is unleashing a handful of movies this fall, pulling the curtain back to shine a light on some of the big names in tech: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg; Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk; Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes; and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Plenty of movies have tackled themes of techno-pessimism and dug into the deep well of science fiction. Remember 2001: A Space Odyssey? Blade Runner? M3GAN? But apocalyptic threats and human-versus-machine scenarios feel much more prescient in 2026. 

What’s changed is that there seems to be an appetite for Big Tech to get its comeuppance. The movies being released are real stories about the scandals and scammers affecting our daily lives.  

			

More from CNET

The Social Reckoning (Oct. 9)

The Social Reckoning continues the story Aaron Sorkin began with the 2010 film The Social Network about Facebook. The Oscar and Emmy-winning screenwriter stepped behind the camera to helm the movie, which he once again wrote.

The Social Reckoning highlights the societal damage caused by Zuckerberg’s social media empire. Based on thousands of leaked documents from former Facebook engineer Frances Haugen, the movie draws inspiration from the 2021 Wall Street Journal article The Facebook Files, which documents the whistleblower’s actions and the subsequent fallout.

Succession star Jeremy Strong now plays Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg played the bright-eyed college student 16 years ago). The film also stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Billy Magnussen, Bill Burr and Betty Gilpin.

The Social Reckoning hits theaters Friday.

Musk (Oct. 16)

The upcoming documentary Musk is by lauded filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose work includes Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley. 

Running about 4 hours, the movie delves into the life and legend of Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, and (cue Dr. Evil’s theme music) the richest man in the world. Given that the film seems to dismantle the mythos he built and sold along the way, Musk hasn’t had kind words to say, calling the movie a “hit piece” and Gibney a “douchebag” in a social media rant.

For a brief period, ads for the movie were barred from social media platforms Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. Google and Meta have since cleared the way for promotional materials for Musk, while the other platforms have remained silent.

Musk hits theaters on Oct. 16 and will stream on HBO Max next year.

You Can See Everything (Oct. 16)

In case you’re unfamiliar with the story of Holmes, Gibney’s 2019 movie is a good place to start. You could also try the 2022 Hulu original series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried. Holmes, who was the face of Theranos, a short-lived blood-testing company, was indicted in June 2018 for fraud and conspiracy.

You Can See Everything is a nearly 3-hour-long documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (the director of the Chris Hanson drama Primetime), which appears more like a psychological horror film than a nonfiction narrative. The new movie follows Fielder into the private life of Holmes and her family, roughly a month before she was to report to prison. You Can See Everything has a hefty amount of buzz behind it and is turning into one of fall’s must-see theatrical releases.

You Can See Everything is released Oct. 16. 

Artificial (Dec. 25)

Italian film director Luca Guadagnino (Call Me By Your Name and Queer) turns his eye on OpenAI’s Altman in his upcoming biopic, Artificial. Just like The Social Reckoning, this isn’t a documentary, and it’s already generating substantial Oscar buzz.

Artificial takes place in 2023 and follows the tumultuous period when Altman was fired by OpenAI and then rehired five days later. Amazon MGM Studios was originally set to distribute the movie, but after signing a multiyear partnership with OpenAI, it stepped away from the project. Neon came in and picked up the film, which also stars Billie Lourd, Monica Barbaro, Chris O’Dowd, Jason Schwartzman, Zozia Mamet and Ike Barinholtz (who plays Musk).

Artificial will premiere in theaters on Christmas Day.

What to stream

If you’re watching from home, you can also cash in on the Big Tech dystopia genre. 

AMC’s The Audacity is a fictional account of the Silicon Valley tech bubble. Netflix has the documentary The AI Doc or How I Became an Apocaloptimist and will soon release AI Gone Wild, a new Instadoc about the rather infamous Hugging Face cyberattack. The streamer will also debut The Altruists, an eight-episode true-crime series about the 2022 collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s cryptocurrency empire, FTX, on Nov. 19. There’s even a legal procedural called Cupertino coming to CBS this week that is about Silicon Valley lawyers.

fullText:
A new leak reveals that Google’s upcoming Fitbit Edge tracker will probably have a price somewhere around $180 and offer 7-day battery life.

Having first appeared in a marketing leak and, more recently, a set of leaked images, Google’s Fitbit Edge tracker is a middle ground between the Pixel Watch 5 and the screen-less Fitbit Air. It has a smaller size than the Watch, but has a screen to display notifications and other features beyond what the Air’s minimalist experience delivers.

Today, a second major leak reveals more details about the Fitbit Edge, including its price.

Dealabs reports that the Fitbit Edge will have a price of €179 in Europe and £159 in the UK. By comparison, Fitbit Air costs €99 and £85 in those regions, meaning the Fitbit Edge will likely cost around $180 in the United States.

	

The report goes on to offer more detailed specs for the tracker, including its 1.34-inch display, detailed battery life estimates, and more. Here’s the breakdown.

Fitbit Edge Specs

Display: 1.34-inch AMOLED

Battery Life: 7 days without always-on display, 2 days with always-on display

Charging: 24 hours of battery in 5 minutes

Water Resistance: IP68/5ATM

Phone Compatibility: Android 11+, iOS 16.4+

Bluetooth 5.4

Fitness tracking: SpO2, steps, heart rate, blood pressure/insulin trends, ECG, VO2 Max, more

Weight: 17.7g

	

The report also mentions support for Gemini, some form of Google Play integration, and that the battery is user-replaceable. 

Also notable here is that Fitbit Edge is apparently compatible with iPhone, something that it shares in common with Fitbit Air, but that the Pixel Watch series lacks. 

A release date for the Fitbit Edge remains unknown at this point, but it’s clear that the tracker is making its debut in the very near future.

title: Google Wallet for Android getting vertically stacked card list [U]
snippet: Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list.

Update 10/6: This revamp is not yet widely rolled out, but we’re slowly seeing it on more devices.

With this stacked redesign, you’ll see one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you can tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen view (as seen below). After selecting a card, you can tap-to-pay.

To see card details and transaction history, select the new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This is more cumbersome than the current design. 

	

	

Original 9/14: The current design shows your saved credit and debit cards as a carousel at the top of the screen. You swipe horizontally to browse, with this approach showing just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google lets you reorder the payment methods and set a default card. This interface allows passes to share the homepage.

The new design uses a vertical list, like the Wallet app on iPhone, that really benefits those with multiple saved cards. Google is showing much more of the card design than Apple, which is a nice aspect of the current look.

This approach is definitely friendlier for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom.

There are a handful of reports about this rollout over the weekend, with most coming from international users.

title: Apple partners with The King’s Trust on new Creative Labs initiative in the UK
snippet: Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details.

Apple’s partnership with The King’s Trust dates back to 2019

In a Newsroom post published today, Apple and The King’s Trust announced the “Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs” initiative, which will “offer young people meaningful engagement with Apple experts across industries as they explore a variety of career pathways, equipping them with the technology, resources, skills, confidence, and expertise needed to realize their potential.”

According to Apple, the program’s immersive educational experience began earlier this week with “music industry and creative workshops, aligned to the recent opening of Apple Music Hall.”

Apple says the first cohort will include up to 20 participants aged 18 to 30, with additional sessions and cohorts planned over the next year.

Here’s Alisha Johnson Wilder, Apple’s senior director of Global Community Impact, on what the initiative means for Apple and its partnership with The King’s Trust:

“At Apple, we believe education is a powerful force for equity and opportunity. […] For years, we’ve been proud to work alongside The King’s Trust to spark creativity and open doors for young people across the UK. With the launch of the Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs, we’re taking that commitment further, connecting the next generation of creators and innovators directly with our experts, technology, and mentorship to help them build vital skills, discover their passions, and thrive in the workforce.”

Jonathan Townsend, The King’s Trust’s UK chief executive, also commented on the initiative, calling it “an exciting new chapter in our partnership that will help even more young people develop the confidence and creative digital skills they need to take their next steps toward employment.”

In the announcement, Apple said it is also working with The King’s Trust on resources to improve AI literacy and help educators incorporate new technologies into their teaching.

title: Why did it take so long for someone to make a magnetic USB-C port? [Video]
snippet: In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything. more…
fullText:
In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a full-on powerhouse with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chipset, up to 128GB of RAM, and plenty of ports. But it’s one of those ports that is the most unique new features.

“Magnetic Connect” is Microsoft’s name for “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C” charging port. The USB-C port itself functions as normal with any standard cable, but the included charger is specially designed to magnetically attach akin to Apple’s MagSafe or any other number of magnetic charging connectors.

I want it.

	

The “how” here is that the charging portion of the cable uses super-strong magnets to align and latch on the charger so the port connects properly, but the charger itself also tapers the edges of the USB-C port so it can more easily slide into place. As such, that end won’t securely connect to your phone or other devices, as it needs that magnet to hold itself in place. 

	

The Verge shows it in action in a video on YouTube:

Microsoft is apparently hoping this idea will catch on and show up on other laptops, and I sure hope that’s the case! As for phones, the size of the magnets implies it probably won’t be feasible in a standard smartphone, but I really hope this idea starts showing up everywhere! Certainly I hope it at least shows up on a laptop that doesn’t cost $2,600 — Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders are open now.

What do you think?

Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support.

This is the second time we’ve heard this rumor, but both times it has come from the same source: the yeux1122 account on Naver. This account has a very mixed track record with Apple rumors. It often seems to regurgitate information from unnamed sources rather than provide its own.

Nonetheless, the latest post from yeux1122 claims “there is mention of 120Hz in some overseas sources” for the new OLED iPad mini, but “domestic production volume has already confirmed” it will use a 60Hz display.

Again, I’m treating this rumor with more than a healthy dose of skepticism, since no other reliable sources have corroborated it.

However, if it does come to fruition, this will be a disappointing limitation for iPad mini buyers. This iPad mini upgrade is expected to bring a number of other notable improvements, including:

An OLED display.

Apple’s A20 Pro chip, up from the current iPad mini’s A17 Pro chip.

A refreshed design with smaller bezels that could be more water-resistant.

The FaceTime camera will be relocated to the horizontal bezel, similar to Apple’s other iPad models.

	

If Apple made all those changes but stopped short of upgrading the display to ProMotion with a 120Hz refresh rate, it’d really sour the launch of the new iPad mini.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 12th digital state ID
snippet: Following the last launch at the end of August, Google Wallet is rolling out support for Oklahoma state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the last launch at the end of August, Google Wallet is rolling out support for Oklahoma state IDs on Android.

Open Google Wallet on your phone and tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom > IDs & personal info > Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Oklahoma as the 13th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the American Bison (state animal) and the scissor-tailed flycatcher (state bird).

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the SOK. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet at any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Tap Personal Info.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

Confirm that you want to delete your ID from your device and Google Account.

title: Fantastical’s long-awaited Android debut begins today on Googlebook
snippet: Fantastical has long been hailed as one of the greatest calendar apps available today, but if you’re an Android user, there’s a good chance you’ve never used it. Despite a move from Apple exclusivity to cross-platform availability on Windows, Android has long eluded the attention of development team Flexibits. Today, that’s finally changing, as Fantastical is headed to Google’s mobile OS platform — but not precisely in the way you might expect. more…
fullText:
Fantastical has long been hailed as one of the greatest calendar apps available today, but if you’re an Android user, there’s a good chance you’ve never used it. Despite a move from Apple exclusivity to cross-platform availability on Windows, Android has long eluded the attention of development team Flexibits. Today, that’s finally changing, as Fantastical is headed to Google’s mobile OS platform — but not precisely in the way you might expect.

Beginning today, Fantastical is now available for Google’s new laptop initiative, Googlebook. Existing Fantastical users who rely on the app on different platforms (like iOS or Windows) can access Fantastical on Googlebook at no additional charge, while new users coming to Fantastical for the very first time can likewise also use the application on any of their other supported devices.

While the underlying OS on Googlebook is Android, Flexibits’ co-founder and CEO Michael Simmons stressed that the application isn’t quite ready yet to debut on phones, tablets, or foldables. Those versions are on the way — bucking what Simmons himself said back in 2024 when he declared the app would never find its way to the Play Store — but they won’t be ready for launch until sometime in 2027. Likewise, today’s announcement does not include bringing the company’s contact management app, Cardhop, to Android; Simmons tells me they have “no announcement” about that app at this time.

Fantastical began life on Mac back in 2011, offering calendar creation tools via a straightforward ordinary language-based interface that isn’t all too dissimilar to today’s LLMs. Though Flexibits unveiled a Windows variant in late 2024, today’s move marks the first step towards compatibility with Google’s mobile OS, and you can thank Googlebooks for building that bridge. Simmons told me development began after Google showed the Fantastical team a demo of its new laptop platform, and he found himself impressed enough to take a chance on finally expanding the app to Android.

	

While most users will have to wait until next year to get their hands on Fantastical, all you early Googlebook adopters out there have the chance to begin using a brand-new calendar app starting today. Individual pricing starts at $57 per year, with family plans starting at $90 annually. A free, less powerful tier is also available.

title: Apple must pay Masimo an extra $184M for Apple Watch patent infringement
snippet: It’s almost a year since Apple was found to have infringed a Masimo patent for low-power pulse oximeter features used in the Apple Watch. At the time, the company was ordered to pay $634 million in damages, but a federal judge has now ordered it to pay an additional $184 million in interest … more…
fullText:
It’s almost a year since Apple was found to have infringed a Masimo patent for low-power pulse oximeter features used in the Apple Watch.

At the time, the company was ordered to pay $634 million in damages, but a federal judge has now ordered it to pay an additional $184 million in interest …

Apple had been fighting with health tech company Masimo on a couple of fronts. The more serious of them was an International Trade Commission ruling that Apple must remove the blood oxygen feature in two Apple Watch models back in 2023 in order to allow them to be sold in the US. The Cupertino company was forced to redesign the way the feature worked in order to be allowed to bring the devices into the US.

But the company also faced a lawsuit from Masimo, seeking damages for the use of its patented approach to measuring blood oxygen in a power-efficient way. Apple was found to have infringed on this patent and ordered to pay damages amounting to the license fees it should have paid.

Bloomberg Law reports that Apple has now been ordered to pay an additional £184 million in interest on this sum. 

Judge James V. Selna rejected Apple’s argument that awarding interest would constitute a windfall for Masimo, citing US Supreme Court guidance that “interest from the time that the royalty payments would have been received merely serves to make the patent owner whole.”

There was some good news for Apple. Masimo had asked for interest calculated at 7%, but the judge rejected this, saying that the interest rate should instead be equivalent to that paid on Massimo’s own borrowing. However, annual compounding still added a total of $184M to the amount due.

fullText:
You only have to read some of the comments right here to see that there’s a vocal minority of people rejecting all AI tools, including Apple Intelligence. That’s led to an unofficial tool enabling people to turn off the feature on their Macs and remove all downloaded Siri AI models.

We warned yesterday that this could be a risky thing to do, but it’s now being suggested that Apple may have to officially support an AI removal feature in order to protect hardware sales …

There’s been growing pushback against generative AI in general, with opponents citing reasons ranging from fearing for the survival of the human species down to simply not wanting unwanted AI features to take up storage space on their devices.

The latest Apple Intelligence models can require up to 14GB of storage, so there’s a significant hit to 256GB machines if you don’t want the features. That led indie developer Om Lahore to create a project called RemoveMacAI.

	

We warned yesterday that using this is not without risks. Given how deeply Apple Intelligence is embedded into macOS 27, it could have unwanted impact on even quite basic functionality.

But some are arguing that Apple may have to introduce an official way to remove Apple Intelligence from Macs. Daring Fireball’s John Gruber points to organizations banning the installation of AI tools.

There are institutional groups that have rules against AI — these places aren’t allowing Golden Gate at all until and unless Apple Intelligence can be removed. And that means not buying new Mac hardware that only runs Golden Gate.

To be clear, Apple does offer a great many controls to organizations using device management. Currently, Apple says they can “restrict the use” of certain Apple Intelligence features, and there are individual toggles to enable or disable features one at a time. What’s currently lacking is a single switch to disable all Apple Intelligence features in one hit, together with the option to remove the downloaded models.

It’s not a live issue yet, but as future generations of Macs start dropping support for older versions of macOS, failing to allow the easy removal of AI models could start to hit Apple’s hardware sales.

10 years ago today, Google launched the first Pixel smartphone and, at the time, teased it by saying we’d still be talking about it years later. And, yeah, we still are, and this is a Google project that shows no signs of slowing down.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Google has a bit of a reputation for churning through projects. If something isn’t a hit, it either gets canned or converted into something else. And that’s what many assumed would happen to Pixel, especially during the lean years in the middle of the series. While Pixel hit the ground running with great first impressions, missteps on the Pixel 2 XL’s display, the Pixel 3 XL’s funky bathtub notch, and the Pixel 4 series just, as a whole, left room for plenty of doubt.

Prior to the first Pixel’s launch, Google’s at-the-time head of Android, Hiroshi Lockheimer, said that we’d still “be talking about October 4, 2016.” And, 10 years later, he wasn’t wrong. 

	

Google has stuck to its guns around Pixel, and perhaps expanded the project more than anyone might have thought. Investments like a mid-range lineup, Tensor chips, and a whole ecosystem of accessories weren’t really in the thought process a decade ago. Yet, here we are. 

We’ve revisited several of Google’s Pixel devices this week and asked our readers what they think the best Pixel of all time is. So far, Pixel 10 Pro XL is winning that poll.

title: Pretend you’re sitting at Elizabeth Holmes’ desk on this weirdly detailed website
snippet: With over a thousand emails, slides, texts, and documents from the United States v. Elizabeth Holmes trial, Extend engineer Bo Lau created a website that simulates what it might have been like to rifle through the Theranos founder's desk.
fullText:
With over a thousand emails, slides, texts, and documents unveiled during the United States v. Elizabeth Holmes trial, Extend engineer Bo Lau created a website that simulates what it might have been like to be the chief executive of Theranos before everything came crashing down.

(Every day, I am grateful to the American legal system for making the discovery process public.)

i built a website where you can sit at elizabeth holmes’ desk

open her macbook, scroll her iphone, run the theranos edison machine

her texts, emails, slides, documents, and theranos machine records are real, sourced from exhibits in the united states v. holmes criminal trial pic.twitter.com/5At9T5m3UV

— bo lau (@bolau_) October 8, 2026

The environment that Lau created is ambitiously detailed, taking you right back to 2016, a time when iPhones had home buttons, and you had to slide your finger across the screen to unlock it. Even the MacBook Air is running OS X El Capitan. 

You can click around the environment, which lets you look through the documents made public from the court case on Holmes’ iPhone and laptop screens. You can even run the Theranos Edison machine, the company’s ill-fated device that was supposed to be able to extract large amounts of health data from one drop of blood.

The project seems like it was mostly made for laughs, but it’s actually an interesting way to peruse the documents from one of the most infamous court cases in tech history — it’s a lot easier to navigate this than to source thousands of PDFs from court websites.

There’s another agenda, though. Lau is promoting a watch party that her company is throwing for Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything.” 

Also, of course, she’s promoting the company itself. So, what exactly does Extend do? Apparently, it can “parse, extract, and split your hardest documents with unmatched accuracy.” (I’m not really sure what that means, but if it makes something like this Holmes desk simulator possible, then I guess that means I’m bullish on B2B SaaS.)

title: Google’s original Pixel Fold was the right idea years ahead of its time
snippet: Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time. more…
fullText:
Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time.

Foldables were still very much going through growing pains in 2023 when Google stepped up to the plate with its first foldable, the Pixel Fold. At the time, I called it “better than it should be, but far from perfect,” and I stand by that. Even with hindsight of three more Google foldables and the rapid improvements of the rest of the industry, the Pixel Fold managed to do a lot right at the time. It offered sturdy hardware, respectable cameras, and less compromises than most other foldables of the time.

Has it aged well? Not particularly. The glossy finish to the metal frame remains a fingerprint magnet in the worst kind of way, and the sheer heft of this phone is wild. I don’t often take issue with a heavy smartphone, but especially compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using the past couple of months, the original Pixel Fold is noticeably heavy in the hand. The crease down the center is huge, and it’s a thick device too. And, three years later, I can only imagine how bad Tensor G2’s heat management issues have become – that was ultimately the deal-breaker for me when I was using the device last. 

Yet, for everything it got wrong, the Pixel Fold got one thing right, the form factor.

	

In the wake of Apple’s debut in the foldable market, brands are quickly pivoting to wider form factors, and they seem to be resonating with customers. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a smash hit, and I bet we’ll be seeing a lot more of these wide foldables over the next year. 

But the Pixel Fold did it three years ago, albeit with a lot less flash. 

Google’s foldable looks almost normal compared to a Galaxy Z Fold 8, but the core idea is the same. The wider canvas is designed for better multitasking and tablet apps, something that I pointed out in my original review. Where Samsung’s foldables were really good at using phone apps on a bigger canvas, the Pixel Fold was far more likely to trigger a proper tablet version of an app instead. 

	

Google ultimately threw that away. Why? Android apps simply weren’t ready at the time. While Android apps have always been designed around scaling to form factors, bigger and wider canvases were still in the minority, and most apps didn’t fully support them. As such, the taller and squarish design just made more sense.

Arguably, it still does, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has shown that it works when you do it “right.” Two months into using it, I’m thrilled with this form factor, and a bit annoyed that Google gave up on it so quickly even though, at the time, it probably made sense. Unfortunately, that’s a bit of a trend in the Pixel’s legacy and Google’s as a whole – Inbox, Stadia, etc. It doesn’t take much to find a Google idea that was left behind too quickly.

It’s anyone’s guess when Google might revisit this design, but I hope it happens.

title: iOS 27.2 release date: When to expect new iPhone features
snippet: iOS 27.2 is coming surprisingly soon. iOS 27.1 will focus on iPhone Duo changes only, so new features for everyone else will arrive in iOS 27.2. Here’s when to expect the update’s release. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is coming surprisingly soon. iOS 27.1 will focus on iPhone Duo changes only, so new features for everyone else will arrive in iOS 27.2. Here’s when to expect the update’s release.

iOS 27.2 confirmed to launch in October, likely late in the month

Apple is currently beta testing iOS 27.2, and has been for several weeks now. It’s being tested much sooner than a x.2 release normally would, but for good reason.

iPhone Duo launches October 23 running iOS 27.1. And all indications are that no other iPhones will get that update, instead jumping straight to 27.2.

By keeping iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, Apple can keep more details of the software experience under wraps by not potentially exposing them during a beta process. That’s why iOS 27.2 is currently in beta instead.

When will iOS 27.2 launch? We know it is coming in October.

Last month when iOS 27 debuted, Apple said that Siri AI would add support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish “next month.”

Those new Siri languages are included in iOS 27.2, thus confirming an October release. Additional new features coming with iOS 27.2 include:

user profiles in the Apple TV app

Dual Capture for Group FaceTime

new Suggestions feature in Messages

Up Next overhaul for Apple Podcasts

design updates for Apple Books

Historically, Apple has shipped its first feature update after a major new OS version in late October, and that’s what we’re expecting this year too. The week of October 26 is the most likely launch window.

iOS 27.2 could always arrive slightly sooner, especially if new hardware introduced next week ships with it pre-installed. But the rumored Home products likely won’t ship right away. Instead, the first orders could deliver during that final week in October, right when iOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, and HomePod 27.2 all ship too.

snippet: Apple TV announced a new comedy series coming—The Choir—that reunites Ruth Jones and James Corden, the duo from beloved UK sitcom Gavin & Stacey. more…
fullText:
Apple TV announced a new comedy series coming—The Choir—that reunites Ruth Jones and James Corden, the duo from beloved UK sitcom Gavin & Stacey.

The Choir is new Apple TV series from Ruth Jones and James Corden, reuniting the ‘Gavin & Stacey’ duo

Last year reporting indicated that Apple had struck a deal with Ruth Jones and James Corden for a new comedy series.

Now Apple has made it official: Jones and Corden are reuniting for The Choir, a new Apple TV series coming in 2027.

The duo might not be as well known to US viewers (though Corden has an established US track record), but they starred together in the massively popular UK sitcom Gavin & Stacey. For context, its series finale in 2024 became the UK’s most watched scripted show ever.

Here’s the official series summary for The Choir:

Brother and sister Ben (Corden) and Lisa (Jones) haven’t seen each other for several years. Ben has been living abroad, while Lisa has carried on in their small English town, where nothing ever happens. But when events take a sorry turn, Ben is forced to return to a life he never wanted, a town he never liked and a family from which he’s estranged. Can the unlikely healing of a rift with his big sister come in the form of a struggling local choir and the ensemble who sing their hearts out each week?

Guest stars include Hannah Waddingham, James McAvoy, and Jim Broadbent, and there’s a strong supporting cast too.

Apple describes the show as being a comedic drama about “family, friendship, love and music,” with a seemingly similar heartwarming feel to that of Gavin & Stacey.

Are you a fan of Gavin & Stacey? Is The Choir of interest to you? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple TV just unveiled the new season of last year’s hit comedy
snippet: One of Apple TV’s hit comedy series from last year, Stick, is coming back for season 2 soon. Here’s the new trailer for Stick’s highly anticipated return. more…
fullText:
One of Apple TV’s hit comedy series from last year, Stick, is coming back for season 2 soon. Here’s the new trailer for Stick’s highly anticipated return.

Stick season 2 is coming November 4, here’s the trailer

Ted Lasso just wrapped up its fourth season, but Apple TV has another heartfelt sports comedy ready to take its place.

Stick returns for season 2 on Wednesday, November 4, with two episodes available initially then weekly releases through December 30.

Watch Stick on Apple TV

For the unfamiliar, Stick stars Owen Wilson as an ex-pro golfer—Pryce Cahill—whose career ended prematurely. But after helping train a 17-year-old golf phenom in season 1, the new season sees Cahill get back to the game himself.

And he’ll do it with the help of a new coach played by Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”).

Here’s Apple’s official season summary, followed by the new trailer:

In season two, Santi takes the next step in his pursuit of professional golf, only to discover how quickly the game changes when talent becomes expectation. As Santi chases his dream, Pryce finds himself wondering what might still be possible for him. Urged on by his former rival Clark Ross (Timothy Olyphant), Pryce does something nobody expects: he bets on himself, launching an improbable comeback in hopes of becoming the oldest golfer ever to win a major. But the road back proves far harder than he imagined. And the closer Pryce gets to the golfer he once was, the more he is forced to confront why he never fulfilled the promise everyone once saw in him. With brilliant new coach Amanda (Rhea Seehorn) and trusted caddie Mitts (Marc Maron) in his corner, Pryce sets out to prove — to the golf world and, more importantly, to himself — that maybe he really was as good as everyone always said he was.

In my experience, you don’t have to care about golf at all to enjoy Stick.

The show feels similar in spirit to other Apple comedies like Ted Lasso and Shrinking. In my view it especially hit its stride near the end of the season, so I’m excited to see it return.

If you’re looking for more Apple series to check out, Small Prophets just premiered and is being hailed as a “masterpiece” and in contention for the streamer’s best show this year.

title: I Asked Meta Muse to Fix an Issue With My Phone Provider. It Got Blocked at Every Turn
snippet: This tech to-do has been on my list for too long. Can an agent do it for me?
fullText:
Something weird has been happening with my phone for years. I thought I’d fixed the issue, but it always comes back. Years ago, I bought a SIM-only plan through Visible, Verizon’s cheap sibling. $25 a month gets me unlimited calls, texts and a decent amount of data… and a lot of spam calls and messages looking for someone called Andrew. 

Given Visible is all-digital with no number to call, it’s a pain to wrestle with a customer service chatbot to fix it. I’ve tried before, and it said the number is in my name, but I’m not convinced. I still receive multiple messages per month from people trying to reach Andrew. 

These messages almost always have something to do with a home trades project. Weird, I know.

			

More from CNET

Screenshot by Amanda Smith/CNET

It’s one of those life admin tasks that just never gets done because I can easily ignore these messages – making it the perfect job for a personal AI agent like Meta Muse. I want to make sure my name is formally listed as the number owner, as I don’t want people thinking I’m this elusive Andrew. 

I tried using Meta Muse as my personal shopper, which was fun, but I ran into an issue at checkout. Let’s see how it can handle an annoying task like this, without a number to call. One AI agent versus another.

Setting up Meta Muse with the task

I opened the Muse app and started a new conversation, instead of picking up on my previous chat with the AI agent. Keeping tasks and chats separate prevents context overload and helps Muse stay focused on the specific objective at hand. Just hit the new side chat button. 

Here’s how I instructed it: “I am a Visible customer on the $25 per month plan. I often get calls and texts looking for someone called Andrew. I think he was the previous owner of my number. It’s not a coincidence, because every time someone reaches out, they always ask for Andrew. I’ve contacted Visible before, and it said I own the number, but can you check I’m formally listed as the number owner? Check government websites, etc.” 

I also uploaded an example of a text I got. 

This was Muse’s response:

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I told Muse to talk to the Visible chatbot, search my number online and find anywhere that references Andrew. Within seconds, it found a link where my number showed up on a data broker page.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

But Muse couldn’t get through, as Visible blocks bot visits. Muse suggested changing my number (no) and making some changes on my phone to minimize unknown senders and silence unknown callers. This wasn’t super helpful either, as I often receive work calls from numbers I haven’t saved. 

I told Muse I didn’t want to change my number. It advised me against claiming the number, as that can encourage spam calls directed at me instead of Andrew. 

It said the Andrew data will go stale at some point. 

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I had to take over the browser for Muse to chat with Visible. That was taking forever, so Muse did a workaround via the guest option. This took a good 10 minutes, which I spent cleaning the kitchen. But it had no luck.

“Quick honest update,” Muse told me, “I got into Visible’s guest chat, but their send button wouldn’t submit my message, and then their help pages temporarily blocked me.”

It advised me to paste the following chat into my Visible app: “My number is recycled — I get monthly spam calls and texts for ‘Andrew,’ the previous owner. I don’t want to change my number. What are my options? Do you offer spam/scam protection, and how do I turn it on? Can I report the number as recycled?”

Of course, such advice could have been delivered to me by a regular AI chatbot like ChatGPT or Gemini. The advantage of using an AI agent like Muse is that it’s supposed to do all of that for me.

But with a lot of these websites blocking AI agents, it makes autonomous task completion a challenge. I attempted to take over the browser again, but got a 403 forbidden error.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

Muse told me the 403 error is a dead end and that my taking over the browser didn’t change the network address, which was annoying. Muse said it’s the bot protection that’s the problem, not Muse. It drafted a message to send to Visible chat manually, via a live agent.

Screenshot by Amanda Smith/CNET

While I chatted with Visible, Muse gave me a link that showed Andrew and my number. What’s interesting is that the last reported date was when I owned the number. 

When I ran a quick manual search on my phone number, the top two websites referenced Andrew. I asked Muse how to update these, and it gave me good advice, like requesting a suppression or removal of records from WhitePages and FastBackgroundCheck, but no instant resolution. 

Muse said this would clean the public record, but the messages are coming from old marketing lists, so it said I should keep reporting those as junk. Brokers re-scrape, so it should resolve in time. 

I tried it via WhitePages, but quickly hit a roadblock. It wouldn’t let me click Next.

I couldn’t follow the second instruction as I don’t have Andrew’s email address. It advised me to use my email (no thanks) or to call the number.

In another browser, I got escalated to Visible’s “advanced” support. Its instruction was to keep the browser open for 4 to 24 hours.

At this point, I gave up. 

The verdict on Meta Muse for this task

I wouldn’t say this was Muse’s fault specifically. It seems most websites have mechanisms in place to block any bots. Most AI agents would struggle to complete this autonomously. For me, in this situation, Muse still feels like a regular chatbot, giving guidance for me to follow. 

While I better understand the issue — spammers using outdated data — it still didn’t fix the problem. I’m hoping Visible pulls through with a solution and, if so, this was still time well spent. Without testing Muse to see if it could do it for me, I wouldn’t have prioritized this task. 

So, that’s a win, I guess.

title: Googlebook gets Luminar photo editing app with ‘Continue On’ support
snippet: One of the biggest questions around Googlebook is what app support will look like and, as the platform officially arrives for customers this week, Luminar is debuting a rebuilt photo editing app for Googlebook. more…
fullText:
One of the biggest questions around Googlebook is what app support will look like and, as the platform officially arrives for customers this week, Luminar is debuting a rebuilt photo editing app for Googlebook.

Luminar is a photo editing app that’s available across desktop platforms like Mac and Windows, but it’s also on Android, iOS, iPad, and ChromeOS. Now, it’s also making the jump to Googlebook.

The Luminar app has been rebuilt with support for Googlebok OS and meets “Tier 1” quality standards for the platform including keyboard shortcuts, resizable windows, drag-and-drop, and more. 

That’s on top of Luminar’s existing Android support for photo editing which includes the ability to adjust qualities of your photo, handle RAW edits, and use AI for features such as swapping out a background, masking, and more. You can even start edits on your phone and finish on your Googlebook as Luminar supports “Continue On.”

	

Luminar explains in a press release:

Luminar for Googlebook is fully adapted for large screens, meeting Google’s Tier 1 quality standards and introducing capabilities such as drag-and-drop, keyboard shortcuts, and resizable windows that weren’t previously available on phones and tablets. After several rounds of testing, Luminar has built a range of capabilities specifically for Googlebook OS:  

Built for the laptop: resizable windows, full mouse and keyboard support, shortcuts, hover states, multitasking, drag and drop, and file handling

New for launch: Generative Erase, HDR Merge, and batch editing – features usually associated with professional editing

One app, one subscription: use Luminar on an Android phone and on a Googlebook with the same account. [If available at launch:] With Continue On, you can start an edit on your phone and finish it on the laptop

Googlebook owners can download Lunimar via the Play Store. A temporary offer gives 12 months of access to Luminar for free, with a later one-time purchase unlocking the app’s premium features permanently.

title: Googlebooks with Intel chipsets might have trouble with ‘complex’ Android apps
snippet: According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps. more…
fullText:
According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps.

When Android apps made their debut on ChromeOS, one of the big downsides was that ARM-based machines ran those apps better than those using Intel chips. It was never a surprise given that Android apps are generally designed for devices running on an ARM architecture vs the x86 used on Intel chips.

Yet, the problem remains on Googlebook.

Despite the whole platform being Android-based this time around, Google confirmed in a statement to Android Authority that Intel-based Googlebook machines will still run into the occasional hiccup with “complex” Android apps and games, though the company emphasizes that “the vast majority” will work just fine.

	

The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box.

Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio.

Update 10/6: In an email to 9to5Google, Google further clarifies that “96.6% of the top 10k+ most-used applications” in Google Play work “flawlessly” on Intel-powered Googlebooks. 

The company stresses that 32-bit x86 emulation is not to blame as Googlebooks use a “highly advanced binary translation layer that dynamically compiles modern 64-bit Arm (arm64-v8a) code directly into native 64-bit Intel (x86_64) instructions” and that apps not compatible with Googlebook are “primarily due to app incompatibility with large screens for all platforms (eg require gyroscope).”

	

Still, this is noteworthy as the first wave of Googlebook hardware includes mostly Intel-based machines. Laptops from Lenovo, Asus, and Acer all run on Panther Lake-generation Intel chips, while Dell and HP machines both use the Snapdragon X Elite (the 2024 chip, not the newer version).

Another chip used for Googlebook from MediaTek is also in the works, though no machines are using it just yet.

The first batch of Googlebook laptops are all available as of today.

title: Gemini for Android Auto is just giving up on answers for some drivers
snippet: The promise of Gemini for Android Auto is huge, as the AI assistant is theoretically more capable than Assistant was. But, as it’s now becoming the only option, a weird issue is leaving Gemini for Android Auto perhaps less than useless, as it just gives up on answers from drivers. more…
fullText:
The promise of Gemini for Android Auto is huge, as the AI assistant is theoretically more capable than Assistant was. But, as it’s now becoming the only option, a weird issue is leaving Gemini for Android Auto perhaps less than useless, as it just gives up on answers from drivers.

To say Gemini’s launch on Android Auto has been riddled with issues is a bit of an understatement. For months users have reported problems with various commands and just overlooked bits of functionality. I’m personally still waiting on Google to fix the issue where Gemini just keeps on talking or waiting for a response after I’ve completed a task via the touchscreen instead.

A new issue popped up this week, though, that’s not only frustrating, but just a waste of time.

Users report that Gemini for Android Auto is hearing commands, processing them, and then just giving up entirely on the answer. A Reddit user shared a video of this and several others chimed in with the same problem, and it’s one I’ve also personally encountered just this week. 

	

	

The issue doesn’t seem to have anything to do with signal strength or the question being asked. Gemini just sits there thinking for a few moments before giving up.

The video above demonstrates the issue when paired to a Pixel phone, but users report the same issue when paired to Samsung and Motorola devices too; I’ve noticed it with my Galaxy Z Fold 8. Google has, so far, not acknowledged the problem as far as we’ve been able to find.

Are you running into this problem?

title: How to Disable Some Apple Intelligence Features on Your iPhone or Mac and Reclaim Valuable Space
snippet: The new AI features could be taking up a lot of storage on your device.
fullText:
Apple launched iOS 27 and MacOS 27 in September, and those updates introduced a revamped Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence to Apple devices. While the new Siri was better at most tasks in my testing, it can still take up a significant amount of on-device storage space. On my iPhone, for example, it takes up about 6.4GB of data, while it takes up about 17.9GB of space on my MacBook Neo.

If you aren’t using the new AI features, you can disable some of them, and depending on what system you’re on, you can reclaim some of that valuable storage space. That way you can stave off for a little while the dreaded pop-up that tells you your storage is full – I need that extra storage for photos of my wife, son and dog.

		

			

Here’s how to see how much storage Apple Intelligence is taking up on your devices and how to disable – or at least limit – it on different operating systems. And don’t forget, Apple Intelligence is only available on certain devices.

How much space is Apple Intelligence taking up on your device?

How much space Apple Intelligence is taking up on your device is easy to check. If you’re on iPhone, go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage > iOS. From here, look for the Apple Intelligence tab to see how much space it takes up on your iPhone.

On a MacBook, click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then go to System Settings > General > Storage, and click the i next to MacOS. A new pop-up will open to show you how much space Apple Intelligence uses on your MacBook.

Disabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone that’s running iOS 27 or later is straightforward. Go to Settings > Siri > Turn Off Siri and follow the on-screen prompts. You can then go back and check your storage, and Apple Intelligence should be gone from that menu.

Disabling Siri AI can free up a few gigabytes on iOS 27.CNET

If you’re running iOS 26, you can disable Apple Intelligence by going to Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri and tapping the toggle next to Apple Intelligence. This should free up some space on your iPhone.

You might also have to disable other Apple Intelligence features across your iPhone. To do this, go to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions and tap the toggle next to Content & Privacy Restrictions. Then, tap Intelligence & Siri. From here, you’ll need to tap into Image Creation, Writing Tools and Intelligence Extensions and tap Don’t Allow in each one.

This should free up a few gigabytes of space on your iPhone.

You can free up a few gigabytes of space in iOS 26 by disabling Apple Intelligence features.CNET

How to disable Apple Intelligence on your Mac

Disabling Apple Intelligence and freeing up storage space on your device can be weird, depending on which operating system you’re using. For instance, if you’re on MacOS 26, it’s easy to disable the feature and free up space. If you’re on MacOS 27, it’s a little more complicated. 

We’ll start off with the easy one. To disable Apple Intelligence on MacOS 26, first click the Apple logo in the top left corner of your screen. Then go to System Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri and click to toggle next to Apple Intelligence. That should free up a few gigabytes of data on your device.

Disabling Apple Intelligence on MacOS 26 frees up a little bit of storage.CNET

There are a couple of potential ways to disable Apple Intelligence on MacOS 27. The easiest way I found to free up a few gigabytes of space is to click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then go to System Settings > Siri and change your language to something like English (Irish). Siri AI isn’t available in every region yet, so changing your Siri language to a language from one of those regions could trick your device. Granted, it freed up only about 4 GB for me.

I changed my Siri language, and it freed up a few gigabytes of space.CNET

CNET’s sister site PCMag has a more in-depth way of turning off Apple Intelligence and freeing up some space. However, I couldn’t get this method to work. I’m not sure why I couldn’t get this method to work, other than that my device is running MacOS 27.0.1 and not MacOS 27. Maybe this will work for you, though.

According to PCMag, you have to go to System Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy. Then, toggle Content & Privacy off. Click Siri and change it to Siri Classic. Then go through the list of Capabilities and turn each feature off.

You’re not finished yet. Then, go to System Settings > Siri and select Don’t Allow Siri or Siri Classic.

Finally, you’ll need to go into individual Apple Intelligence settings and disable those features. Some easy ones include going to System Settings > Notifications > Summarize Notifications and turning the toggle off, or going to System Settings > Messages > Settings and turning off Message Summaries.

You could do all that work, or you could just switch your Siri language as I did. The choice is yours.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and iOS 27.0.1.

fullText:
MacRumors reports that in addition to Apple’s expected event on October 13, the company is planning to unveil another batch of new products in the final week of the month. Here are the details.

New Macs and OLED iPad mini expected before year’s end

Over the weekend, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman claimed that Apple will, in fact, hold an event on October 13 to announce “its long-awaited smart home hub with a screen, the new HomePod mini and an updated Apple TV.”

Gurman’s report came amid uncertainty over whether Apple would hold an event or announce the new products through videos and press releases, as it has done in the past. That said, these announcements at the end of the month would cap off an unusually busy October for Apple, with the iPhone Duo launching on October 23 and the company also expected to report its quarterly results before the month is out.

snippet: I have been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, dating back to the original Sonos One. fullText:
I have been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, dating back to the original Sonos One. So, about two years ago, when I heard that Sonos was entering the over-ear headphone market, I knew I had to give it a try. The Sonos Ace looked great, was very comfortable, and brought some cool Sonos ecosystem features. But for a premium pair of headphones, there were still a few areas that left me wanting more, like strong bass, better ANC, and a better app experience. But now, the new Sonos Ace Ultra feels like they went down that list and addressed nearly every complaint that most customers had, including me. I have been using them as my main headphones for almost a month now, for travel, video editing, workouts, walks, and everyday listening. So I have a good grasp on them now, and here is what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video review for the Sonos Ace Ultra below:

Sonos Ace Ultra

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra does not look much different from the original Sonos Ace. They decided to keep the same clean, understated design with a few differently placed chrome accents and some additional colors. But the biggest differences are inside these headphones. 

What’s new versus the original Sonos Ace

Here are some of the biggest changes from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

Redesigned 40mm drivers

10-microphone array, up from eight mics on the original

Improved adaptive ANC, stating up to 2X more effective and being able to adjust to things like glasses, hair, and changes in the seal around your ears

Longer battery life with up to 35 hours with ANC turned on

Bluetooth 6.0 versus 5.4 on the older generation

Expanded EQ controls with three and an advanced eight-band EQ options

Headphones linking with the Sonos Ecosystem

User-replaceable batteries

Updated ear and headband cushion materials  

More rotation of the ear cups so they can sit flat when around your neck

Two new colors: Agave and Sand

The main things that I noticed in these changes are the redesigned acoustics, better bass response, and stronger ANC. With the original Sonos Ace, I would sometimes get this hissing noise when I was in ANC mode. This would rarely happen, but I did notice it. So far, the new Sonos Ace Ultra has alleviated that issue. You also still get some of the great specs from the previous model like:

Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos

Dynamic head tracking

Lossless audio on supported devices

USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio support

Bluetooth multipoint

Fast charging with up to three hours of playback from a three-minute charge

TV Audio Swap with compatible Sonos soundbars

They still have the same super high-quality design, combining plastics and metals to give you a premium, lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra also keeps the magnetically replaceable ear cups, and one of the best things that I have noticed is the new EQ settings that really let me hone in on how I like to listen to my music. But how were they as an everyday pair of headphones?

My experience

Again, it’s easy to put specs on paper, but the biggest reason I’ve enjoyed the Ace Ultras is that they actually sound noticeably better. My biggest complaint about the original Sonos Ace was the lack of bass depth. The bass was not bad, but for a pair of $450 headphones, I felt like they were lacking a bit. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop music, so bass is important to me. I wanted more low-end impact and to feel the bass. The Ace Ultra finally delivers the experience that I wanted. 

There is substantially more punch and depth at the low end. But one thing to note here is that Sonos hasn’t achieved that by simply turning up the bass slider. Any headphone brand can crank up the bass, but the difficult part is maintaining separation so that the bass doesn’t overwhelm the vocals, instruments, and higher-end frequencies. That is where the Ace Ultra has really impressed me. The bass hits harder, but the vocals are still clear, crisp, and easy to listen to. And it’s not just for music; all media sounds better, like podcasts, movies, and all the YouTube videos I watch. They have sounded fantastic in all media listening situations. 

The improved ANC is something else I noticed immediately. The new 10 mic array allows even more sound to be dynamically pushed away from the headphones. Even when there is no media playing, it’s insane how quiet the headphones are in so many different environments. It’s almost too good! The biggest improvement to ANC is the unpredictable noises. It’s one thing to block out a consistent noise like an airplane engine, but another to block out passing cars, construction, sirens, or sudden loud sounds while walking outside.

Two final things I want to bring up are comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These headphones are the most comfortable headphones I have worn. Even on a long 8-10-hour airplane ride, I wore them 95% of the time, and I felt no aches, pain, or heat at all. Lastly, I have a lot of Sonos speakers around my house, and they introduced a new feature that lets you move music from a speaker to your headphones with the press of a button. It’s a very cool feature, but I personally haven’t used it much.

My only complaint is that they need a new zipper or mechanism for the headphone case because that sticker gets stuck way too often!

Pricing and availability 

The Sonos Ace Ultra is available today on Sonos’s site and Amazon for $449, keeping the same launch price as the original Sonos Ace. They come in four colors: Black, White, Agave, and Sand. I also noticed that the original Sonos Ace is available on Amazon for $239 while supplies last. At $240, now that could be a good choice as well.

At $450, the Sonos Ace Ultra is firmly in the premium noise-canceling headphone category alongside options from Apple, Bose, and Sony.

Final take

The original Sonos Ace felt like a good first-generation product. The Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete and finished product. As we saw, they did not reinvent the look or design, but they improved in all the areas that mattered and even added a few new cool features. The sound is noticeably better, the ANC is strong and smarter, battery life lasts longer, the app experience is smoother, and that Agave color is amazing.

If you already own the OG Sonos Ace, I actually think there is enough here to justify the upgrade, depending on what you value. If you are in the market for a premium set of headphones, I think the Sonos Ace Ultra needs to be on your shortlist. At $449, they are certainly not cheap, but if you want one of the best premium headphones and are a Sonos fan, then you will love these.

fullText:
Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching soon, its first new design since 2021. Here are three design changes reportedly coming.

#1: No notch

One of the defining traits of the current MacBook Pro design is its display cutout: the notch.

The MacBook Pro introduced the notch to the Mac line in 2021, and the redesigned model that’s about to launch will reportedly remove it. Instead, the new MacBook Pro will have a small camera cutout and Dynamic Island built in. Per Mark Gurman:

The Dynamic Island on the Mac will be built around a hole-punch-sized cutout for the computer’s camera. It’s smaller than the pill-shaped notch in current iPhones.

It sounds like the notch replacement could be similar to iPhone Duo’s hole-punch camera on its outer display.

#2: Thinner and lighter

The current MacBook Pro is a hefty powerhouse, but Apple reportedly has a thinner, lighter design coming for the new MacBook Pro. Per Bloomberg earlier this week:

The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry.

It’s unknown whether slimming the MacBook Pro will result in any ports being removed. Apple’s current MacBook Pro design brought back many ports that had been removed in the prior iteration. It would be surprising for the company to strip ports yet again.

#3: Slightly larger displays

An Omdia report this summer said the redesigned MacBook Pro will come in two screen sizes:

14.3 inches

16.3 inches

	

If accurate, this is a very slight increase over the current 14.2- and 16.2-inch sizes. It’s possible Apple will reduce the bezels a bit to achieve a larger usable display area.

It’s also possible that the overall form factor will get slightly larger to help provide extra space for components despite the thinner body. But there are no specific rumors around these details yet.
