title: Upgrade to Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4? Here’s how to get the most out of it
snippet: Upgrade to a new Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4? Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 bring upgraded performance and new health sensing features. Still, they can feel like the same watch in day-to-day use unless you know where to look for the changes. From new health complications to automatic Shazam recognition, a few setup changes can help you get more out of your upgrade. Here’s what to try. more…
fullText:
Upgrade to a new Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4? Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 bring upgraded performance and new health sensing features.

Still, they can feel like the same watch in day-to-day use unless you know where to look for the changes. From new health complications to automatic Shazam recognition, a few setup changes can help you get more out of your upgrade. Here’s what to try.

Refresh your watch face

Start by adding exclusive new complication options only supported on the new Apple Watch models. Series 12 and Ultra 4 can display your live heart rate, steps count, and readiness score on your watch face.

You can add these complications to your favorite watch face to unlock new insight into your health and fitness. 

For me, live heart rate data has been an essential new complication, using a single slot with better data compared to the old wide slot with less current data. Step tracking has also been a big motivator for getting activity logged earlier in the day. 

And since readiness score can change throughout the day based on your vitals and activity, displaying readiness on your watch face can be a great tip.

And while it’s off by default, you can enable quick switching between watch faces with a swipe at Settings > Clock > Swipe to Switch Watch Face.

Turn on automatic Shazam

Your new Watch can identify music around you without a request to Siri or a tap on Shazam.

On Apple Watch, open Settings → Smart Stack and enable Music Detection. When you open the Smart Stack, Music Recognition can show the song title and artist.

It’s a small setup change with an obvious payoff the next time something unfamiliar plays at a restaurant or coffee shop.

Try Siri Modular

Siri Modular comes to every Apple Watch running watchOS 27, although Series 12 and Ultra 4 have more complication options.

Something I love about the Siri Modular face is how you can style it. For now, I have a few instances of the Siri Modular face in my rotation using different colors, fonts, layout styles, and complications.

Give readiness time to work

Adding a readiness complication is only part of the setup. You also need to collect the data behind the score.

Apple says to complete your Health Details, set up Activity and overnight vitals, enable Sleep, and wear your Watch while sleeping for at least seven nights. You also need sleep data from the previous night.

Find a charging window during the day so overnight tracking becomes easier to maintain.

So far, readiness has been an interesting experiment, but I think it’s still too early to call it useful for me. 

Daytime vitals

Lastly, the Vitals app has more insight with Series 12 and Ultra 4 hardware.

You can see daytime vitals, not just overnight, in the Vitals app. This is based on heart rate and recovery heart rate variability. Overnight vitals also factor respiratory rate and wrist temperature.

Looking ahead, there’s more to come for Series 12 and Ultra 4 with Siri Recap and Live Rewind on the way.

What are your favorite ways to get the most out of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4? Share your ideas in the comments.

title: Google Pixel at 10: Successes, failures, and fun along the way [Video]
snippet: A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though. more…
fullText:
A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though.

Look back at the line-up, and it’s still hard to believe we’ve had a decade of Pixel. If you asked me back in 2016 whether Google’s in-house hardware experiment would stick around long enough to reach fully custom 3nm silicon, I’m not sure I’d have believed you.

To say that Google was late to the market is an understatement. By 2016, Apple and Samsung were already well into the swing of things. To be fair, that still is the case a decade later, but now with an even tighter iron grip over the space. I was personally distraught when the Nexus lineup was canceled to the point that I actually went with the Galaxy S8 rather than wait to see what Google had in store next.

	

Google’s answer to the ‘big two’ was Pixel. A phone not “officially” made by partners, but still sort of relying on OEMs while the production pipeline or groundwork was laid.

Pixel and Pixel XL (2016)

The original Google Pixel was built in a close manufacturing partnership with HTC, featuring a wedge-shaped profile that famously tapered down to eliminate any camera bump. 

Let’s be real, the hardware wasn’t tearing up trees, and it looked more than a little similar to the iPhone 7/8 series. It was a conservative design, but pretty darn self-assured.

The main thing that helped differentiate the device was its built-in Google Assistant integration and HDR+ image processing pipeline for photos. Rightly or wrongly, this simple formula has more or less defined the Pixel for the past decade of Google’s mobile computing efforts.

Smart, simple software and artificial intelligence have been at the forefront from the very beginning and will remain so over the next 10 years.

Pixel 2 series (2017)

With the second generation, Google finally figured out design. The LG-made Pixel 2 XL gave us the iconic “Panda” colorway with its stark black-and-white glass back and the bright orange accent power button. You’ve told us time and time again that it’s a personal favorite for Pixel fans. It also debuted the Pixel Visual Core, Google’s first attempt at custom co-processing to let apps like Instagram use HDR+.

Add single-lens Portrait Mode that put dual-camera rivals to shame, squeeze-to-activate Active Edge, ambient Now Playing track identification, and the persistent At a Glance widget, and the Pixel 2 series genuinely felt like magic in your hand.

The first major problems started to appear, though. The blue shift on the 2 XL meant that viewing from an angle is not recommended. Screen burn-in was also something people suffered.

Pixel 3 series (2018)

The Pixel 3 era was peak camera software dominance mixed with a few just flat-out bizarre hardware choices. 

That Pixel 3 XL “bathtub” notch was an absolute eyesore and was thoroughly roasted by the tech community and reviewers alike. I think in some ways, once you fired up the camera, all was forgiven. I’ve taken some incredible photos with the Pixel 3. Pictures that I still look at very fondly 8 years later.

This was the first Pixel to come with Night Sight, which arrived via a software update and single-handedly changed low-light smartphone photography forever. It wasn’t the first, but it was one of the best implementations.

You could shoot in near pitch-black conditions and walk away with a clean, detailed photo without ever touching the flash. Pair that with yet more AI-powered functions such as Call Screen, which handles telemarketers and spam in real time, and the software was doing all the heavy lifting.

In trademark fashion, the Pixel 3 had issues with RAM management and poor battery life. It was a mixed bag, but it was followed up by something truly interesting because the Pixel 3a is one of the best midrangers ever. It set the stage for a change of pace…but that wasn’t for a couple of years.

Pixel 4 series (2019)

Let’s be honest, Google swung for the fences with the Pixel 4, but it didn’t quite land. 

It is almost the least Pixel-y of the entire lineup because it stands apart from all that have since followed. The black sheep in many ways. It ditched the trusty rear fingerprint scanner, they threw Project Soli into a chunky top bezel for wave-to-snooze Motion Sense gestures and 3D Face Unlock.

We also got a silky smooth 90Hz display and a telephoto lens rather than the industry-preferred and marginally more flexible ultrawide. It felt like a zig to everyone else’s zag.

Alas, it was a big risk and one that ended up compromising the most. The small Pixel 4 had a tiny 2,800 mAh battery that struggled to get through an afternoon, let alone a full day. High launch prices and Soli radar frequency restrictions in key markets meant commercial success was hard to come by, and the negatives really held back the lineup. It actually triggered a reshuffle in Google’s hardware team.

Pixel 4a, 4a 5G and Pixel 5 (2020)

Faced with global disruptions in 2020 due to the emergence of COVID-19 and maybe due to some, at the time, unknown future plans, Google completely pivoted with the Pixel lineup. The Pixel 4 was a big swing, but the follow-up series went in a very different direction.

The mid-range Pixel 4a launched at just $349/£349 and became an immediate hit because it kept that flagship-grade camera performance in an understated, no-nonsense plastic body. This was an appetizer for what was to come.

Then came the flagship Pixel 5, but this wasn’t the premium phone that many expected. It skipped top-tier Qualcomm silicon entirely for the upper-mid-range Snapdragon 765G. It was the same chip used by many cheaper phones and even the more affordable Pixel 4a 5G, which was basically a bigger, bolder version of the 4a.

The 5 was coated in a bio-resin finish over a recycled aluminum frame, it brought back the rear fingerprint scanner, swapped the telephoto for an ultrawide lens, and gave us uniform bezels with reliable battery life. It lacked raw processing grunt, but it earned a cult following for simply being a reliable, compact everyday phone.

On one hand, it was good to see Google right some issues with the previous generation. On the other hand, it was confusing as it sort of signaled that maybe Pixels were not high-end phones. It was a reset.

Pixel 6 series (2021)

After a fairly unassuming and, arguably, boring preamble, 2021 was without a doubt the biggest turning point in Pixel history. 

Google overhauled the design, introducing the now iconic camera bar running across the back, creating a silhouette you could spot from a mile away. We were given a proper two-tier lineup with a Pro phone that packed in a triple camera system, a larger 120Hz display, and a cheaper but still competent base model. 

Most importantly, though, was the debut of original Tensor (now G1) silicon. Moving away from standard Qualcomm chips meant Google could tailor hardware directly for on-device ML—powering features like Magic Eraser, Live Translate, and Material You dynamic color themes.

As well-received as it was at launch, the Pixel 6 had some serious growing pains with a slow optical fingerprint reader, terrible modem performance, and overheating issues galore, but despite what were fairly major issues, the foundation was set.

Pixel 7 series (2022)

The Pixel 7 and 7 Pro took the foundational groundwork of the Pixel 6 and smoothed out the rough edges. Visually, the camera bar evolved into a seamless piece of 100% recycled aluminum that flowed directly out of the side rails, swapping out the all-glass visor for a sleeker metal shell with pill-and-cutout camera cutouts.

Under the hood sat Tensor G2, which paired with an upgraded Samsung Exynos 5300 modem. This finally resolved the signal drops and battery drain that plagued the previous generation. While raw computational gains were modest, Tensor G2 unlocked key software capabilities: Photo Unblur in Google Photos (which could restore old, blurry archival photos taken on any camera), Macro Focus via the ultrawide lens, and the return of a fast 2D Face Unlock system.

Mid-2023 also saw the Pixel lineup expand its footprint. The Pixel 7a raised the bar for mid-range phones by bringing a 90Hz refresh rate and wireless charging to the A-series for the first time. Meanwhile, Google made its long-awaited entry into new form factors with the original Pixel Fold, showcasing a short, wide “passport” design that prioritized a usable outer display over tall, narrow screens. It was a bit of a “fail” in the sense that it didn’t move the needle and was quickly overshadowed by others due to launching with the previous-generation processor and, admittedly, strange aspect ratios.

Pixel 8 series (2023)

In my mind, the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro were the moment the lineup transitioned from an enthusiast recommendation with caveats to a phone you could comfortably recommend to everyday consumers. Never perfect, but quietly the last Pixel that felt truly like a Pixel. These are bubbly, friendly phones in all the ways that matter.

A few more AI functions made their debut: Best Take, Audio Magic Eraser, Video Boost, and, as a headline addition, 7 years of full updates for the first time. Basically, making these the industry standard for smartphone support. Google leapfrogged Samsung and even Apple for software support windows.

No, no reinvention of the wheel. Tensor still didn’t hit the heights many wanted, which is to say it was fine.

Pixel 9 series (2024)

The Pixel 9 was a rapid design departure in a number of ways. Firstly, it ditched the friendly, playful looks that had been a trademark of the series. Instead, it took a very boxy route that instantly felt familiar to anyone who may have tried an iPhone.

It was a really polished upgrade and sort of put to bed some of the tricky hardware issues that plagued many of the older Pixel models. Google also began leaning into yet more AI-powered functionality, with Gemini now being a key component.

Google unified the launch across all phones, coming on day one, but also switched from the standard October release cadence to a late-summer August release. Pitching the Pixel ahead of the iPhone has been a huge change. Allowing the company to lay out plans and getting even more hype around a launch lineup.

Pixel 10 series (2025)

Although on the surface, almost the exact same, the Pixel 10 was the first 3nm chip for the lineup, and it was the first to be fabricated by TSMC. It signaled the end of the Samsung Foundry partnership that was the start of the Tensor era.

Any lingering thermal issues were gone, Gemini was integrated even further and into even more places, like the camera, and the first steps of multimodel intelligence were added with Magic Cue. I’d stop short of saying the Pixel 10 delivers on some of the promises made way back on October 4, 2016, but it came as close as it ever had until that point.

Finally, we had a flagship-level device with Qi2 magnets at the back too. It took until 2025 for one of the biggest Android brands to adopt Magsafe or, in this case, Pixelsnap. With that one move, the Pixel 10 opened up a whole world of accessories to be attached without the need for a case. It’s so elementary, it’s a wonder we haven’t seen more try to do it.

Pixel 11 series (2026) and beyond

A decade later, we’re here with the Pixel 11. The peak of the Made by Google series thus far. There are still pain points, namely a design that hasn’t evolved too drastically, performance from the Tensor processor still feels decidedly mid-range at times, and a heavy emphasis on AI functionality to make up for this raw performance gap.

A sometimes lazy observation of the original Pixel was that it was the “iPhone of Android,” but that seems to have been taken to heart, and a decade after launch, we have the most “iPhone-y” Pixel to date. Maybe that is a symptom of where smartphones have stalled, but it’s a really interesting evolution. The advantage is that you know what to expect. Gemini is becoming more and more prominent and yet a more integral component in Pixel phones, and that isn’t likely to cease any time soon.

What’s easy to see is that Pixel has been a bigger success than the Nexus lineup. Getting hold of the full end-to-end user experience has helped drastically. I don’t think anyone can argue that the best Nexus phone is easily surpassed by the best Pixel phone.

It would be remiss of anyone talking about Google products without some fears over whether we’ll get another decade of Pixel, but with so many internal changes at the company and bigger marketing budgets thrown at actually marketing the devices, it seems that, at least for now, the Pixel is here to stay. 

The past decade has proved that Google was never really trying to build the highest-spec hardware on the market. Instead, Pixel has always been an engine designed to deliver Google’s software vision. From early HDR+ algorithms on single camera lens setups and now to custom TSMC Tensor silicon wired for Gemini integration, it’s hard to argue that Google’s Pixel has succeeded in changing how we evaluate a smartphone: not by how fast its CPU clocks, but by how helpful it is throughout the day.

Maybe sales will eventually catch up, but the main thing is to keep making solid devices, and playing the long game might start to be the best decision Google could have made after entering the market late.

There have been plenty of bumps in the road along the way, but here’s the next decade of Pixel. I’m sure it’ll be a wild ride.

title: These are the best times to save money on your next flight, according to Google Flights
snippet: Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price.

With surging fuel prices have also come much higher plane ticket costs and, with that, everyone’s looking for a deal. In a blog post this week, Google Flights details the best times to book your next flight.

For domestic US flights, the best time is apparently 39 days prior to departure, but the lowest price can fall anywhere between 57 days prior and 22 days prior to the actual flight date. International flights should be booked much further out, with 89 days being the magic number there.

Thanksgiving and Christmas flights bend the rules a bit. Thanksgiving flights are actually cheapest 34 days prior to departure, but Christmas flights need to be booked much earlier at around 56 days.

	

Here’s the full breakdown from Google:

Domestic flights: 39 days before departure (low price range is 22–57 days)

International flights: 89 days before departure, but the average price drop during the low range (50–133 days out) is insignificant

Thanksgiving: Lowest prices hit 34 days before departure (low price range is 21–57 days)

Christmas: 56 days before departure (low price range is 33–67 days)

Spring break: 50 days before departure (low price range is 29–64 days) for trips in March or April

Summer vacation: 21 days before departure (low price range is 20–47 days) for trips in July or August

Trips to Europe: 49 days or more before departure

Trips to Mexico or the Caribbean: 43 days before departure (low price range is 24–69 days)

The post goes on to detail trending destinations for the 2026 travel season, with Hawaii being the top Thanksgiving destination and international trips to Greece and Canada trending around Christmas and New Year’s Eve.

title: Google confirms Android Auto updates & fixes for media apps – the squiggly line is here to stay
snippet: New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay. more…
fullText:
New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay.

In a Reddit post by Google’s “Community Engagement Manager” for Android, five recent Android Auto updates are confirmed as either rolling out or widely available. The first is the ability to control media from any app, including YouTube and others. We noticed this rolling out back in March of this year for YouTube, and it has since rolled out to more apps. Today’s post confirms it is available for “browser audio streams, and niche media apps” and is designed to work with “any media app.” You can use it for play/pause and skip controls, but you can’t open an app to browse any other data.

Next up is the redesigned media app player that applies to apps like Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pocket Casts. The new design makes it easier to access playback controls and also better fits on a variety of different screen sizes.

This one has been showing up all year and started rolling out more broadly in July. Today’s post confirms that the in-app UI for media apps on Android Auto will start changing for some apps “in the next few months,” as announced in May.

	

Another new media-focused feature on Android Auto that’s been rolling out is the ability to swipe between active media sessions from the dashboard widget. If you start driving with one app and then switch to another, both will stay readily available for easy access.

A background improvement, Google’s post adds, has been made to autoplay. This includes making it so media apps that you haven’t recently used will “no longer be selected for autoplay,” while Android Auto will also now recognize if you frequently stop autoplay and offer a pop-up that lets you turn off the feature quickly. If you’ve ever noticed issues with autoplay starting even when you have it turned off right after your vehicle turns out, Google also says that a fix is being applied.

Finally, the post also confirms that the “squiggly line” media player design is here to stay. This one has been showing up for months, but has come and gone for many. Especially in the past few weeks, there have been dozens of reports of the redesign simply vanishing.

The updated design is apparently meant to “make it easier to see where you are in a track at a glance,” but Google is apparently listening for feedback on it – it’s been a rather divisive change among the Android Auto community.

title: Gemini app gains new ‘Map’ tool, replacing ‘/’ with ‘@’
snippet: Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills. more…
fullText:
Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills.

On mobile (not available on the web), you can find “Map” at the end of the carousel alongside Photos, Camera, Avatar, Files, Drive, and Notebooks. 

This launches a live map of your current location with a circular focus area. You can pan and zoom in/out as needed, while the magnifying glass icon in the top-right corner lets you search for any location. Once you’ve made a selection, hit “Explore this area.”

This adds “Map Area” to the prompt box where you can append text. The Map tool is widely rolled out.

	

With the latest Google app beta (version 17.63), Gemini is replacing the forward slash (“/”) to invoke skills with the “@” symbol that’s already used for Connected Apps, which will soon be renamed to “Connectors.”

Google just announced on Wednesday that skills will replace Gems and that you can use a slash in the prompt box to activate. We’re seeing the following prompt when entering a slash: 

/ is now @. Access your skills, connectors and more from a single place.

The box that appears is slightly wider than before, with skills appearing first and a shortcut to create new ones. This change is not widely rolled out yet.

More on Gemini app:

Google details Gems to skills migration, including free access

Gemini app adding Google Wallet integration for ‘personalized insights’

Gemini app starts rolling out big side panel simplification, settings redesign

title: New Xbox Division XP Will Adapt More Video Games for Movies and TV
snippet: Xbox already had success with A Minecraft Movie and Fallout.
fullText:
The Xbox reset continues. Despite a rough year of revenue losses, layoffs and major restructuring, the Microsoft gaming division announced Thursday that it’s going big into the entertainment industry and elsewhere.

After the resounding success of A Minecraft Movie and the Fallout TV series — both of which are longtime video game titles — Xbox is creating a division called XP to expand its video game brands into movies, TV, merchandise and even live events, the company said.

Xbox has hundreds of games in its catalog, with only Minecraft, Fallout and Halo adapted for film and TV. But there are a few other adaptations in the works — movies for Call of Duty and Gears of War, and a Netflix animated series for Diablo.  

			

More from CNET

“Our ambition at Xbox is to be the number one entertainment company in the world,” Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball said in the announcement.

XP, which refers to “experience points” in the gaming world, will consist of four departments. Xbox Pictures will create more film and TV adaptations; Xbox Products will develop licensing and merchandise; Xbox Places will host live events and broadcast events in theme parks and other locations; and Xbox Partnerships will collaborate with creators and brands to make new experiences.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma named Kayleen Walters as president of XP. Walters was executive producer of A Minecraft Movie, which led all movies in US ticket sales and grossed $424 million in the US last year. She is now a producer for the sequel, A Minecraft Movie Squared, scheduled for release in theaters on July 23, 2027.

Before joining Xbox’s Mojang Studios in February 2025, Walters spent 13 years at Lucasfilm running successful global marketing campaigns for the Star Wars franchise.

Sharma also announced Maria Angelidou-Smith, a former VP at Meta and chief product officer at Reddit, will become CEO of Mojang and Minecraft.

It’s been an eventful tenure for Sharma since becoming Xbox CEO in February. Revenue dropped $1.7 billion, or about 7%, from July 2025 through June 2026. On July 6, Sharma announced a reset — “the most significant restructure in Xbox history” — laying off 3,200 people by mid-2027 and moving four studios out of Xbox and under new management.

Expansion is smart, analyst says

With its gaming business struggling, Xbox is making a smart move, says streaming media analyst, author and speaker Dan Rayburn. 

“They have to expand outside of the core gaming audience,” Rayburn told CNET. “They’re realizing, with how much content is being licensed these days and all the different platforms out there, let’s create more content off our brand that others might want to license for their streaming services.”

Moving beyond the confines of the console definitely worked for A Minecraft Movie and Fallout, and their success on screens boosted Xbox’s gaming business. There was a 75% increase in weekly active users of Minecraft after the movie’s release in spring 2025, and there was a fivefold increase in hours played on the various Fallout game titles during the TV series’ first season on Prime Video.

But whereas Minecraft and Fallout found enthusiastic audiences in the entertainment world, that won’t be true for all of Xbox’s games, Rayburn said.

“They’re going to know that certain brands aren’t going to resonate with certain individuals outside of gaming, so you have to pick and choose the right content,” Rayburn told CNET. “That’s why hiring someone from the film business (Walters) is the key point here. They took a film executive as opposed to a gaming executive. You can’t have a gaming executive running that.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Alex Valdes
						

						

											

								

											Ever since being admittedly fascinated by the Cambridge coffee webcam from the 1990s, I've written about VPNs, the NFL, smartphones, living wages, over/unders and everything in between.
															
						See full bio

iOS 27.2 beta 3 details

Apple released iOS 27.2 beta 3 on Monday for developers, with build number 24B5099f. It comes two weeks after the release of the second beta. A new public beta was released on Tuesday, ahead of a final release to everyone before the end of the month.

What’s new in iOS 27.2 beta 3?

New Apple Music logo

Apple teased a new Apple Music logo when it announced Apple Music Hall last month, and iOS 27.2 beta 3 suggests it’s about to roll out everywhere. The new logo uses a bolder typeface than the old logo, plus a lowercase “m” in “music.”

Apple has also started rolling it out to the Apple Music sign-up flow in iOS 27.2 beta 3.

New Messages settings in the works

Code references in iOS 27.2 beta 3 suggest Apple is working on a new setting that gives users more control over the suggested actions that appear in the Messages app, such as the “Add to Calendar” button.

The code hints that you’ll be able to disable suggested actions for individual apps, including Calendar, Reminders, Notes, and Maps. The change isn’t actually enabled yet, and it’s possible Apple scraps it before releasing it.

Apple Books design tweaks

As spotted by Beta Profiles on X, iOS 27.2 beta 3 brings new Liquid Glass design changes to the Apple Books app. There’s also a new progress bar for tracking your progress when reading a book.

Ryan has some more details on it here.

macOS 27.2 beta 3: Touchscreen Mac hints

Apple is expected to unveil the touchscreen MacBook Pro as soon as this month. macOS 27.2 beta 3 includes even more hints at Apple’s work optimizing macOS to support touch interactions. The update includes new “gesture recognition tools” for several stock Apple apps.

There’s also a new long-press animation for the Dock that seems perfect for touch interaction:

More tidbits

As spotted by Aaron Perris, iOS 27.2 beta 3 includes code that suggests “nearby smart home accessories could show controls in the Dynamic Island.”

As spotted by Beta Profiles, the new beta slightly redesigns the battery icon in the Settings app and elsewhere throughout iOS.

There are new splash screens for the Apple Fitness and Apple TV apps.

Wrap up

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

YouTube, Twitch, Meta, and X aren’t saying whether they’ll allow the US government to livestream an execution on their platforms. The four companies didn’t respond to The Verge’s requests for comment after an unnamed Pentagon official said yesterday that the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of a mass shooting at a Texas military base in 2009, will be livestreamed.

Two platforms responded to The Verge’s inquiries. Jamie Favazza, a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations, pointed to the platform’s policies banning “shocking and graphic content,” including “the moment of someone’s death.” Kick, a platform known for taking a hands-off approach to content moderation, confirmed that such a livestream would violate its policies. “If this was livestreamed on KICK, it would breach our Community Guidelines,” Kick spokesperson Audrey FitzGerald writes in an emailed statement to The Verge.

Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3rd at 2PM ET. YouTube, Meta, and Twitch’s community guidelines suggest that this type of content wouldn’t be allowed on their platforms, but it’s unclear whether they would make an exception for the US government.

Meta, Twitch, and X’s community guidelines explicitly state that violent content involving death isn’t allowed, while YouTube bans content that “encourages dangerous or illegal activities that risk serious physical harm or death.” YouTube says livestreams that “feature someone holding or handling a firearm” aren’t allowed, either. Rumble, an online video platform known for hosting far-right influencers, also didn’t respond to a request for comment.

title: A week with Googlebooks: four notes from our testing so far
snippet: Software, software, software. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Google's new operating system is off to a rocky start. The five newly launched Googlebook laptops have hardware that ranges from great to excellent, but the software in its current state is the weak point. There are four of us on staff at The Verge actively testing Googlebooks and, frankly, our internal Slack discussions have been mostly filled with collective venting of frustrations, disappointments, and bewilderment. The promise of Googlebooks as a fresh and smartly designed alternative to Windows or Mac for Android phone owners sounds great, but there's more than just a few kinks and quirks to work out. Some of its issues and challenges … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Google’s new operating system is off to a rocky start. The five newly launched Googlebook laptops have hardware that ranges from great to excellent, but the software in its current state is the weak point. There are four of us on staff at The Verge actively testing Googlebooks and, frankly, our internal Slack discussions have been mostly filled with collective venting of frustrations, disappointments, and bewilderment.

The promise of Googlebooks as a fresh and smartly designed alternative to Windows or Mac for Android phone owners sounds great, but there’s more than just a few kinks and quirks to work out. Some of its issues and challenges in the road ahead are systemic to Android.

While we’re actively testing each and every Googlebook from all of Google’s partner OEMs, we thought we’d come together and share a glimpse of where our heads are at with these new laptops.

This should be better than ChromeOS, but right now it feels worse

Why does this Clear all button exist? Why can’t you swipe between active desktops or move windows between them? And why wasn’t that ready on day one?

While a lot of my thoughts are well documented in our initial hands-on article, I keep coming back to what a Google rep told me at the Googlebook launch preview: Replacing ChromeOS with Android will allow for much faster development. That’s great, but why does Googlebook OS feel like a bit of a set back from ChromeOS at launch? It shares some of ChromeOS’ flaws, like not allowing you to run Chrome with separate Google accounts. And many Android apps feel as clunky to run on a Googlebook as they did on ChromeOS. (Google even put Android’s navigation buttons on the Googlebook keyboard — seemingly in part as a fallback option for misbehaving apps.)

Every day I come across new oddities in any of the three Googlebooks I’m testing. The Signal Android app linked to my phone with ease, but I have to hit Ctrl+Enter to send messages and can’t highlight text — clicking and dragging scrolls up and down instead. Photoshop and Lightroom are passable for the simplest image editing, but I’d take a cheap Windows laptop with the proper desktop apps over these mobile-first versions. You can’t drag and drop windows to other virtual desktops, and scrolling to the left of your desktops reveals a Clear All button that just kills all your apps at once. That’s straight out of the app switcher from Android on phones, but if I’m closing all apps at once on a laptop I’m either rebooting or shutting down.

Even something as simple as installing the progressive web app version of Slack isn’t working properly. So who should I be mad at? Slack or Google?

If I bought one of these Googlebooks I’d be mad at myself for being a paying beta tester for Google. I know that’s often the case for early adopters on a new OS, but these days I have less time and patience than when I bought my T-Mobile G1 / HTC Dream, Nexus 7, etc. There’s something cool here for sure with Googlebooks, but we need that “faster” development to go into warp speed.

— Antonio G. Di Benedetto, currently testing the HP Googlebook 14, Lenovo Googlebook 15, and Acer Googlebook 14

Google has a big, big developer problem

Streaming apps like Crunchyroll are basically tablet apps. The keyboard can’t pause or rewind, and you have to click or touch the screen for those playback controls.

One of the reasons Googlebooks exist is that Android has become a mature, useful platform across a lot of screen sizes. It’s true: Android now works relatively well on your phone, tablet, TV, even your car. The apps are another story. Over and over in my testing so far, I’ve been amazed at the number of apps that seem to have no idea what to do with a Googlebook.

Take Netflix, for instance, which was one of the first apps I downloaded because I have some travel coming up and I’m psyched to finally be able to download movies for plane rides. The app works well enough, I suppose (and it does download movies!) but it launches as a full-screen, tablet-style version of the app. Basically every streaming app does so. If you hover over the top bar, the windowing option appears, but none of that is obvious. And launching and windowing app after app gets tiresome.

There are a few apps that are properly optimized for Googlebooks, and they make the device feel more like a proper laptop. But even they have some problems: many do that weird thing where they don’t show the app content when you’re resizing the window, for instance, which feels broken on a laptop. Even some of Google’s own apps do this, while others, like YouTube and Messages, scale more naturally. Some apps respond naturally to the keyboard and mouse; others don’t. Virtually everything is better optimized for a touchscreen. A note to developers: If I can’t pause the movie by whacking the space bar, your app doesn’t work with keyboards.

For the most part, I actually like the Android-ification of Google’s laptop strategy. Connecting deeply to your phone, running and syncing all your apps, even some of the phone-style interface decisions make sense to me. But just about every time I open an app, my Googlebook starts to seem like an Android tablet pretending to be a laptop. (And don’t forget: nobody has ever really wanted Android tablets.) Google’s going to need developers to get with the program, or it’ll never be more than that.

— David Pierce, currently testing the Dell XPS Googlebook

Linux apps (probably) can’t save Googlebook OS

Apps in the Googlebook’s Linux virtual machine don’t show up in the taskbar or app tray.

A string of little annoyances has chipped away at my hopes for the new Googlebooks over the last few days. Some are more frustrating than others — losing a normal Caps Lock key isn’t a deal breaker, but getting stuck with only mobile browsers just might be. Android app compatibility seems to always be a roll of the dice, and so far Linux apps don’t seem like a viable alternative.

Slack was one of the first apps I tried installing from the Play Store, but it ended up being the mobile app awkwardly resized for a larger screen. So, I tried installing the Linux version of Slack through the Debian virtual machine that lives in the Googlebook’s Terminal app. I got it working, along with GIMP and Steam.

But the big catch is that anything you install on the virtual machine only lives there. So, none of those apps have app drawer icons like my Android apps, and they don’t pop up in my taskbar when they’re running. I have to manually switch my mouse and keyboard between the VM and the rest of Googlebook OS, which makes jumping between Linux and Android apps slow and awkward. Since the Linux and Android apps are running in different environments, they don’t automatically share files or clipboard content, either.

I’ll have a dedicated write-up on the Googlebook gaming experience later, but the virtual machine hasn’t been great for that, either. I got Steam running, but the games I’ve tried (none of which are particularly resource-hungry) have been too laggy to be playable.

I’ve liked some parts of the Googlebook so far, but it’s hard to appreciate them when friction keeps popping up from Android and Linux apps alike.

— Stevie Bonifield, currently testing the Asus Googlebook 14

The best bit of Googlebooks only works half the time

The obvious selling point of the Googlebook, for me at least, has always been the “seamless” Android integration. And I’ve had a few moments this week when my phone and laptop have come together in a truly delightful way: replying to a WhatsApp message directly from the notification on the Googlebook; dipping into an app cast from my phone to quickly use it without reaching for my pocket; opening Quick Share to move files between the two devices in seconds.

But even here, so much of the experience right now sucks. My phone connection drops in and out from the laptop, and I can’t for the life of me figure out how to connect a second phone or tablet. I used Quick Share for file transfer because using the Files app to browse the phone’s drive is painfully slow, taking minutes to open or transfer a single photo. Opening a notification to the phone-cast version of an app when you have it installed natively will never stop feeling awkward. And some apps cast terribly anyway: Bluesky renders text illegibly; my banking app won’t cast for security reasons; and my credit card one won’t because it just breaks.

Seamless, this is not. It’ll get better, I hope. It has to get better. When the Android integration works, it feels a little bit like magic. But that’s only because it happens so rarely — Google needs to make this reliable enough that it feels mundane instead.

— Dominic Preston, currently testing the Asus Googlebook 14 and HP Googlebook 14

Google’s new operating system is off to a rocky start. The five newly launched Googlebook laptops have hardware that ranges from great to excellent, but the software in its current state is the weak point. There are four of us on staff at The Verge actively testing Googlebooks and, frankly, our internal Slack discussions have been mostly filled with collective venting of frustrations, disappointments, and bewilderment.

The promise of Googlebooks as a fresh and smartly designed alternative to Windows or Mac for Android phone owners sounds great, but there’s more than just a few kinks and quirks to work out. Some of its issues and challenges in the road ahead are systemic to Android.

title: The humble Playdate has become one of gaming’s best deals
snippet: The Playdate, Panic's tiny yellow handheld that launched in 2022, has slowly but surely become a great deal - which is a good thing, because everything else in gaming has only gotten more expensive. fullText:
The Playdate, Panic’s tiny yellow handheld that launched in 2022, has slowly but surely become a great deal — which is a good thing, because everything else in gaming has only gotten more expensive. Despite being a weird device with a black-and-white screen and a crank jutting out the side, the Playdate has managed to cultivate a strong and constantly growing library of games. And with the handheld’s new season 3 of games, the deal has only gotten better.

Playdate’s “seasons” are basically curated collections of games that are released over a short period of time. For season 3, there are eight games in total, with two launching weekly over the span of four weeks. The whole thing costs $39, and the season is off to a pretty good start with two games that are indicative of what the overall Playdate experience is like.

Image: Panic

One is called Soggy Froggy, and it’s an arcade game about giving a frog a bath. The little guy sits in a cauldron over a fire, and your job is to keep the water at just the right temperature to keep him warm and cozy. Do nothing and the water quickly heats up, but turn the crank and you can cool things down. If the water gets too hot, well, the poor little froggy boils to death. The goal is to keep him alive for as long as possible, making it a game about chasing a high score that’s both cute and morbid. I can’t stop playing.

The other new release is a dungeon-crawling RPG called Gloom Gate. Here the goal is to traverse a sprawling castle, defeating all kinds of monsters and gathering gear and experience points to get stronger. What’s most notable about the game, though, is its 3D graphics, which feel like they shouldn’t be possible on the underpowered Playdate. In each battle you enter into a small arena with an enemy, and you have to dodge, parry, and attack while keeping a close eye on your stamina, which depletes with every action you take. It’s kind of like a stripped-down version of Dark Souls (there are even campfires to rest at), but it also really reminds me of Epic’s long-lost mobile series Infinity Blade, which was similarly a technical showcase centered around surprisingly deep combat.

Image: Panic

The full lineup for season 3 hasn’t been revealed yet, but it’ll also include a word game, hide-and-seek for two players on the same handheld, and a classic Mac-style point-and-click adventure (a trend I can really get behind). It seems like there’s going to be quite a bit of variety, and that really captures what the first few years of the Playdate have been like so far. Between its seasons and the Catalog store, as well as the ability to sideload games from platforms like Itch.io, the handheld has built up a very strong lineup that covers just about every genre you can think of: daily puzzle games, demonic pinball, Monument Valley-style adventures, even an MMO. It’s impressive both how much developers have been able to squeeze out of the device as well as how expertly Panic has managed to curate the platform. Every time I check out the shop it seems like there’s something new and interesting to try.

The Playdate hasn’t been totally immune to the steadily more expensive nature of the world. Last year, it got $30 more expensive due to increased production costs. But when compared to everything else going on, the current $229 price tag feels like a drop in the bucket, particularly when most new games for the Playdate only cost a few bucks. For comparison, the special edition of Grand Theft Auto VI — which, to be clear, doesn’t even include the game — costs $399.99.

Obviously the Playdate isn’t a one-to-one replacement for a new PlayStation or Switch. You can’t play the latest big-name releases — you’re going to miss out on a very busy November, for instance — and outside of a few titles, it’s a mostly solitary experience. But even still, in an era of rising costs and formulaic games, the Playdate remains a breath of fresh air, a comparatively affordable platform that’s home to games that are inventive and surprising. And it’s a platform that only seems to be getting better with time.

title: Xona’s commercial GPS alternative is about to go live
snippet: Xona's precision timing and navigation service will enter beta testing after SpaceX launches six satellites designed by the company.
fullText:
The first precision commercial alternative to GPS is preparing to go live when six satellites designed by the startup Xona Space Systems launch into orbit this month.

A service that competes with free signals provided by governments around the world may seem foolhardy, but Xona is hoping to add navigation and timing to the list of de facto government space monopolies disrupted by venture-backed startups.

Xona was founded in 2019 by a team of five engineers who originally met at Stanford University’s aerospace engineering graduate program. One, Tyler Reid, went on to earn a PhD, writing his thesis on the possibilities of using satellites in low-earth orbit to improve navigation.

GPS and analog satellite networks built by Europe, China, and Russia provide huge value, but are also easy to jam and aren’t precise enough to be used alone for applications like farming robots or self-driving cars. Over “pizza and beer chats,” the friends mulled whether fixing those problems could be a business.

“My knee jerk was like, this is dumb,” Xona CEO Brian Manning told TechCrunch during a recent visit to the company’s headquarters. “Why would anybody replace GPS? It’s free, right? And I started digging into it. People think of GPS as a free service, but the market isn’t the service. The market’s the hardware, and you have billions of devices being sold every year; those things aren’t being given away for free. There’s an immense market that is desperately looking for better performance.”

That didn’t mean the road to delivering such a service was simple. Improving GPS with a stronger signal that offers more precise timing and location data remained a technical challenge. The company needed to develop a unique architecture that would allow its satellites to keep time without expensive atomic clocks onboard, taking advantage of the spacecraft’s proximity to Earth and close communication with ground-based sources of truth.

The other technical challenge the company solved was making sure its signals could be received by existing GPS receivers with a relatively simple software modification. That gives Xona immediate access to the market and smoothes the way through the regulations for broadcasting navigation signals.

Later this month, a SpaceX rocket is scheduled to launch six satellites for Xona. Four are similar to a prototype the company launched last year that proved its technology; those satellites are built around a satellite platform from Aerospace Labs. The other two satellites were built entirely by Xona at its Burlingame, California, headquarters, and are intended to be the foundation of the company’s 258-satellite operational constellation, called Pulsar.

Xona’s Pulsar satelliteImage Credits:Xona Space Systems under a Xona Space Systems license.

Pulsar will offer centimeter-level precision for geolocation, instead of the meter-level precision provided by GPS, and its signal is strong enough to be detected inside buildings and in urban environments. Manning also believes its signal is powerful enough to deter would-be jammers and spoofers, too.

Xona can begin beta-testing Pulsar with real customers once its satellites are in orbit and passing overhead the mid-latitudes about eight times a day. 

Ian Gough, the CEO of TimeBeat, a company that specializes in electronic timing, says the initial pilot will allow his engineers to check and correct the timing provided by its devices around the world. By 2028, Xona hopes to offer full coverage in the U.S., Europe, Japan, and South Korea.

Xona has raised just over $300 million from venture investors since its founding, including $20 million from the U.S. Space Force. While the company is focused on offering a commercial service, the U.S. government is clearly interested in the technology, as jamming and spoofing of satellite navigation services become increasingly common in conflicts.

While there are literally billions of potential users for a new precision timing signal, Xona is also looking ahead to a world of growing autonomy. Reid, whose thesis inspired the company and who now serves as its CTO, worked on self-driving cars at Ford and saw that a service like Pulsar would be needed to realize the potential of autonomous vehicles of all stripes.

Xona’s headquarters boasts an incredible view of planes landing at San Francisco International Airport. Watching the jets come in, Manning points out that among “all the forms of mass transportation, the gold standard for safety is civil aviation. We see Xona and what we’re building being able to play a big part in that … to provide the service to a car, so you can feel as safe taking your hands off the wheel as you are laying back in an airliner.”

He has closely covered the rise of the private space industry and is the author of  Rocket Billionaires: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and the New Space Race. Formerly, he was a senior reporter at Quartz, the global business news site, for more than a decade, and began his career as a political reporter in Washington, D.C.

title: Apple may soon track when Google promotes Chrome inside Safari
snippet: Apple may be preparing to track when Google promotes Chrome or the Google app to users browsing in Safari, and how users react to those promotions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple may be preparing to track when Google promotes Chrome or the Google app to users browsing in Safari, and how users react to those promotions. Here are the details.

Since iOS 27.2 beta 2, Apple has been testing code in Safari that can detect when Google shows banners promoting Chrome or the Google app on its search pages, as well as whether users interact with those promotions.

While this does not mean that Apple will ship this telemetry feature when iOS 27.2 officially launches, it does suggest that Apple is at least experimenting with a way to measure how often Google promotes its own apps to Safari users and how those users respond.

It is currently unclear why Apple is testing the feature. However, the new code comes amid heightened regulatory scrutiny of competition between Safari and rival browsers, including how users are steered toward alternatives such as Chrome.

In the UK, for instance, Google has specifically cited its efforts to promote Chrome to iPhone users as evidence that it continues to compete with Safari, while regulators have examined whether the companies’ search agreement reduces their incentives to compete in browsers.

In the European Union, in turn, Apple is also subject to Digital Markets Act requirements around browser choice and defaults, with the European Commission previously investigating whether its Safari choice screen complied with those rules.

	

So whether Apple intends to collect and use this data for its own benefit or as part of an effort to address growing regulatory scrutiny over browser competition remains to be seen.

What the code does establish is that Apple has built Safari to detect and log those interactions, and the system works like this: Safari injects a .js script into certain Google home and search results pages, which looks for visible promotional banners or other Google page elements intended to encourage users to open or install Chrome or the Google app.

Safari then looks for links associated with either app, including their custom URL schemes and App Store IDs. If it detects a promotion, it can log certain events, including whether the banner was shown, whether the user appears to be signed in to a Google account, and whether the user interacted with the promotion. This allows Apple to categorize the interaction as either accepted or dismissed and log that result.

As of iOS 27.2 beta 3 and Safari 27.2 beta release notes, Apple has yet to publicly document the feature.

title: Apple TV reveals ‘unconventional’ rom-com show with The White Lotus star

fullText:
Apple TV just debuted the first look at Prodigies, a new series from The White Lotus star Will Sharpe that offers an “unconventional take” on the romantic comedy genre.

Prodigies stars Will Sharpe and Ayo Edebiri and premieres February 10, 2027

Apple has officially set its Valentine’s Day offering for 2027: a new romantic comedy series named Prodigies.

Prodigies will premiere February 10 with its first two episodes, followed by weekly releases every Wednesday through March 17.

The series stars Will Sharpe (“The White Lotus”) and Ayo Edebiri (“The Bear”), and was created, written, directed, and executive produced by Sharpe.

Here’s Apple’s official series summary:

“Prodigies” follows Didi (Edebiri) and Ren (Sharpe), two former child prodigies now in their 30s, as they reexamine the relationship they’ve been in since they were nine. From London to Tokyo by way of Virginia, this unconventional take on a romantic comedy explores ideas of potential, ambition and the universal complexities of long-term relationships. As they begin to question whether their very ordinary existence is living up to the extraordinary promise of their childhood, they find themselves in a new and terrifying kind of chaos.

The ensemble cast is a strong one, headlined by John Malkovich, Tobias Menzies, Yumi Asō, Maria Bakalova, and more.

Apple’s slate of originals is currently light on romantic comedies, but the talent behind Prodigies gives the show a lot of promise. I’m excited to learn more as February draws closer.

title: Acclaimed British comedy series ‘Small Prophets’ now available on Apple TV
snippet: The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below. more…
fullText:
The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below.

’Small Prophets’ now streaming on Apple TV

Earlier today, my colleague Ryan covered the raving reviews for “Small Prophets,” a British comedy series Apple TV acquired for international distribution earlier this year.

The move marked a first for Apple TV, as the streamer had never previously acquired an existing English-language series that had already aired elsewhere.

“Small Prophets” premiered on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two in the U.K. earlier this year, before Apple picked it up for international distribution in August.

It is now available to Apple TV subscribers globally, except in the U.K., where it will arrive on the service in 2027.

“Small Prophets” was created, written, and directed by Mackenzie Crook (Detectorists), who also stars alongside Pearce Quigley (The Way Back), Lauren Patel (The Effects of Lying), Sir Michael Palin (Monty Python), Sophie Willan (Ludwig), Jon Pointing (Big Boys), and Paul Kaye (Game of Thrones), among others.

Following the two-episode premiere, the show will run every Wednesday through November 4.

Here’s Apple TV’s synopsis of “Small Prophets”:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

Michael gets help from his young coworker Kacey (Lauren Patel), an unlikely friendship that blossoms partly (but not wholly) through their mutual dislike of store manager Gordon (Mackenzie Crook). Their friendship adds to the frustration and intrigue of his nosy neighbors (Sophie Willan, Jon Pointing) who are obsessed with trying to find out what the hell is going on in the garden shed.

title: Google seems to finally understand why it bought Fitbit
snippet: Good morning! Today, I’m searching for Prime Day deals, watching Chris Rock masterfully dodge questions about The Slap, questioning Sam Altman about whether we have to accept “some bad things” to justify AI’s exponential growth, and brushing up on my chess game after many years of neglect. fullText:
Good morning! Today, I’m searching for Prime Day deals, watching Chris Rock masterfully dodge questions about The Slap, questioning Sam Altman about whether we have to accept “some bad things” to justify AI’s exponential growth, and brushing up on my chess game after many years of neglect.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

When Google bought Fitbit back in 2019, it wasn’t clear that the brand had a future. 

As many companies are wont to do, Google had good reason to ingest the accessory maker’s IP and set fire to the rest — but that didn’t happen. After a few fallow years, Fitbit became the software powering the Pixel Watch’s health capabilities, and is now shifting once again to working as a standalone hardware brand within Google.

	

After the monumental success of the Fitbit Air in May, the company is poised to release a Charge follow-up called the Edge. The Charge series hasn’t seen a refresh since 2023, and it appears that Google is updating its design and adding a number of app-like features that should bridge the proverbial gap between tracker and smartwatch.

Of course, Google may not have known Fitbit’s true trajectory back in 2019, but it’s arrived at a place that makes sense: Fitbit’s software is now tightly integrated into all of Google’s health-related endeavors, so the brand is pivoting back to hardware where it made its mark originally.

So the question is whether the Edge, or something like it, is the right move. The Air’s success came from its accessible price ($100) and the growing trend of screenless trackers. I wear a Fitbit Air alongside either a smartwatch or a regular one, and that’s its biggest appeal. And people are going to great lengths to hide the diminutive tracker in places most wearables can’t go. 

The Edge, on the other hand, is a traditional fitness tracker with a few tricks up its sleeve. Judging from the leaks, it will offer notifications, Google Maps, music controls, along with Find My Device support. And of course health tracking that, with a Google Health Premium account, includes an AI-powered fitness coach that’s proven its mettle over the past few months.

I doubt the Edge will have the same cultural impact as the Air, but I also see its existence as proof that Google understands why it bought Fitbit in the first place. Now that it’s plumbed the company for all of its wares, Fitbit rises once again where it all started: with cheap hardware that does just enough well to keep users happy.

title: These US states just said ‘no’ to Apple Wallet driver’s licenses
snippet: Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all.

Florida and Rhode Island won’t be getting Apple Wallet driver’s licenses anytime soon, per key leaders

The number of US states offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps growing, and we even have a good idea of three states launching support soon.

Plenty of states likely intend to support digital driver’s licenses at some point, and haven’t gotten around to it. But there are two who recently indicated they have no plans to launch support.

Those two states are:

Florida

Rhode Island

Last week, Florida rolled out a brand new driver’s license and ID card. Many states take such occasions to launch digital versions too, but the state made zero announcements around digital ID.

That’s no coincidence, as Governor Ron DeSantis actively opposes the idea of digital driver’s licenses. He posted the following on X last November:

The convenience of a digital drivers license is outweighed by the potential for government to abuse it.  

Not gonna happen in FL.  

No digital ID. https://t.co/YD7J6PtBgR

— Ron DeSantis (@RonDeSantis) November 28, 2025

Florida previously did offer a digital ID but abruptly ended support in 2024. Perhaps the next governor will take a different stance.

In Rhode Island, Walter “Bud” Craddock was on a podcast last week discussing mobile driver’s licenses (“MDL”). Craddock is currently Chair of the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators (AAMVA) International Board of Directors.

	

Here’s what he said:

“I want to see more universal adoption or need for an MDL. I had one of my senators approach and try to talk me into doing it. I had to give him the old Heisman move and push him back…the main user right now is TSA. Up until recently, there was no airport in New England area that could accept an MDL. So why would I spend the money in the development of it? And also, I’m looking to do a solution that is across all platforms. Instead of just doing one for Apple or the Google Wallets, I don’t want to replicate and duplicate efforts.”

Like DeSantis, Craddock’s position of leadership is slated to end in the next few months. So depending on his successor’s stance, perhaps Rhode Island could get Apple Wallet driver’s licenses sometime in 2027.

Here’s the full list of US states currently offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses, and three expected to launch next.

title: Review: Rhinoshield’s iPhone 18 Pro bumper case is minimalist but surprisingly protective
snippet: iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case. more…
fullText:
iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case.

Apple finally got back into the bumper business with the iPhone Air last year. I was hoping Apple would expand their bumper case to the iPhone 18 Pro (like they did with the clear case and iPhone 11), but unfortunately they did not. In my search for another option, I came across Rhinoshield’s Minimalist Impact Bumper case. 

Key Details

The Impact Bumper Case has a fit similar to most other bumpers, where the lip on the screen is fairly minor, while the lip on the back is a little larger. A unique feature of this case, and one that I quite like, is that it has special supports that keep the camera plateau and lenses off of wherever your phone is resting, which I particularly appreciate considering the aluminum 17 Pro and 18 Pro. This results in a far more protective case than your typical bumper would be. It also eliminates the annoying wobble when using your phone on a flat surface.

The case’s fit, however, is not quite what I was hoping for. It’s somewhat loose, and you can easily bend the edges outward, and I do wonder if over time they may end up getting stretched out. I don’t think the phone flying out of the case when dropped will be an issue though (and I have unintentionally tested that). That said, the material of the entire case is a hard plastic rather than rubber, so hopefully it will be fine in the long run. Rhinoshield says that it is made entirely of just one material, and is therefore 100% recyclable.

The case comes in three colors, which are matched to the iPhone 18 Pro colors: white, blue, and black (sorry Burgundy fans). The blue, which is what I have, is close to Glacier but not perfect. 

Downsides

There are some downsides, however. My primary gripe with the case is that the buttons can be hard to press. For some reason they went with a nearly flush design, and the way that the buttons are designed makes them mushy. 

The material choice as a whole may be a downside. To me, it feels cheaper than the likes of Apple’s iPhone Air bumper, but some may end up preferring it. I certainly prefer it to the materials of a typical TPU/rubber clear case. The material and loose design also seem to attract pocket dust.

If you use Apple’s Wrist Strap or Crossbody Strap, be aware that this case does not have the required loop connection points. 

Conclusion

The Rhinoshield bumper is definitely not perfect, and I still hope that Apple will extend their bumpers to other iPhones. In the end though, I have decided to keep the case, for one primary reason: it lets me have a near-caseless experience without worry of the fragile aluminum getting chipped or dented. As far as I can tell, the bumper case is usually only available from their own website, so the price of about $30 matches the price of Apple’s ($39) after shipping. You can get the Rhinoshield Minimalist Impact Bumper case here. (Occasionally, an Amazon listing will pop up, so you can give that a try as well.)

title: Googlebooks don’t have the same web app or Linux app support as Chromebooks
snippet: Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either. more…
fullText:
Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either.

Googlebooks rely on Android apps and web apps for virtually all core functionality, with the Play Store actively directing users to which app is the most ideal on the platform. 

As it turns out, though, support for Progressive Web Apps on Googlebook isn’t quite at the same level as Chromebook. While most PWAs we’ve tried so far are easily installed, we ran into an issue installing the Slack PWA. Google, in a statement today, confirmed this is because Slack is not a “compliant” PWA, with Chromebooks instead relying on “manual installation.” It’s unclear what differs regarding Slack’s PWA — it functions just fine on other platforms such as Windows and ChromeOS — but it can’t be installed on Googlebook or Android devices.

Google says:

	

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

This mirrors another regression in app support compared to Chromebooks.

Googlebooks also, at least for now, lack the same level of Linux app support.

Chromebooks started adding support for installing Linux apps way back in 2018 and, after a few years in development, it became a secret super power of Google’s platform. Linux app support on Chromebook allowed users to bridge the app gap with the ability to install full desktop apps via Linux ports and, while it wasn’t the easiest process, it got the job done.

Googlebooks are in a very different state.

There’s little to no documentation around Linux apps on Googlebook right now, with Google’s only page on the matter describing how you can use the Terminal app to access a Debian command line interface. Google says:

You can use the Terminal app to access a powerful Debian Linux command-line environment directly on your Googlebook. You can install and run developer tools, code environments, and access other Linux applications. It expands your device’s capabilities for advanced tasks and software development.

But installing apps via this portal doesn’t put them within easy reach of the end user. It’s a far cry from Chromebook’s support, which placed most apps within the app drawer once they were installed. 

	

Google says that it’s possible to run apps, but that GUI apps “aren’t the main focus” of the Linux environment on Googlebook:

Just wanted to confirm that yes, there will be a Terminal app available on Googlebook out of the box, and yes it lets you run a Debian Linux environment on your device.

Also yes, you CAN run Linux GUI apps in this environment, but note that for this initial release of Googlebook, GUI apps aren’t the main focus. We’ll have more to share soon on the Terminal app!

One Linux user far more experienced than myself who dug into how Googlebook supports Linux apps, detailing that they show up in a single Terminal display window without their own Android windows or taskbar items. Another user saw the same behavior and noted reliability issues with GIMP, a popular photo editing app for Linux.

As mentioned, there’s no documentation yet on how to get Linux GUI apps running on Googlebook, so this is not functionality for the “average Joe” — not to say Linux apps on Chromebook were either, but it’s certainly odd to see that this has regressed in functionality rather than expanded.

title: Pixel 11 series still not on Android 17 QPR1 with October update
snippet: With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1. more…
fullText:
With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1.

The Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold launched in August with the base Android 17 release. In September, the Pixel 11 series received two early updates that presumably addressed issues that emerged since launch. 

	

Later in the month, Google rolled out QPR1 to all other devices. Visual changes in the quarterly release include system blur for the volume slider and power menu, while there’s an updated system media player that gets narrower when other apps are available. The Mobile Data Quick Settings Tile gets a time-saving “Don’t ask me again” toggle, while there’s now a Keyboard QS Tile.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 series did not get the initial Android 17 QPR2 Beta 6 release and had to wait a few days for Beta 6.1, which introduced HiLight support for message notifications. It did get the 17 QPR3 Beta without issue a few days later. 

	

This week’s October release does contain fixes for the Pixel 11:

Fix for issue causing the virtual keyboard to occasionally not appear when interacting with search input fields*[1]

Fix for issue occasionally causing captured photos or recorded videos to save in the incorrect orientation*[3]

It’s unlikely that we’ll get a second October release, with all eyes on November. With QPR2 just a month away at that point, Google might wait for December to align all the devices.

title: Call Screening has made a big difference to my iPhone experience
snippet: iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier. Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls … more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier.

Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls …

I’ve tried to be reasonably protective of my phone number, only providing it when it is not only demanded by an organization, but where I accept that it will be useful for them to have it. In many cases where a web form insists on it, I’ve used a fictitious number.

The UK’s telecoms regulator actually provides a range of 1,000 mobile numbers that have never been allocated so I can be sure my fake number won’t lead to someone else being spammed.

However, I’ve owned my mobile number for literally decades now, so it’s unavoidable that it has made its way onto some marketing lists, and there are also companies that use robocallers to dial random numbers. I haven’t been bothered by many of these historically, but for some reason there was a significant uptick earlier this year.

When Apple introduced the call screening feature last year, I was concerned about missing genuine calls, so didn’t immediately enable it. However, I did so earlier this year, selecting the Ask Reason for Calling option, and I have to say I highly recommend it.

	

The main spam/scam calls I received were from companies pretending to be my mobile carrier. I think some are likely third-party resellers hoping to trick me into switching network, while others are either trying to obtain payment details or carry out more general data harvesting. I’ve never let any of these calls get far enough to find out, but it reached the point where I was getting at least one of these calls every week. I’d also been getting a growing number of job scam calls.

Since switching on the feature, not a single one of these has got through to me. I think in the vast majority of cases, they immediately hang up when they get the automated response, while a few of them have bothered to give me their claimed reason for the call, and it’s been immediately obvious that I should reject it.

I also haven’t seen any indication of anyone genuine failing to reach me. I’ve had a number of genuine calls get filtered by the screening feature, but all of these have explained who they are and the reason for the call, and I’ve then been able to answer it.

If you don’t currently have Call Screening enabled, I highly recommend it. Open the Settings app, scroll down to the App section, select Phone, and then scroll down to Screen Unknown Callers.
