title: Apple may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU in a tax compromise
snippet: Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan. The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House … more…
fullText:
Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan.

The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House …

There has long been debate within EU countries about taxes on digital services, with Apple examples including iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Creator Studio, and more.

Some point to the significant revenues earned from selling subscription services to EU citizens without necessarily paying any tax in Europe on these receipts. Others are concerned that a digital tax could disproportionately hit European companies, while yet others are concerned about threatened retaliation by the White House for additional taxes on US companies.

The Financial Times reports that the European Commission has now come up with a compromise it hopes will keep everybody happy – other than the companies like Apple, Google and Meta who would be paying the new taxes, of course.

Brussels was considering changes to an existing proposal that would require all companies operating in the EU with revenue of more than €100mn a year to pay an annual lump-sum tax contribution, the officials said […] 

Adjusting the thresholds and contributions under the Core proposal to cover only very large corporates would both increase the amount raised from tech groups and defuse criticism in Europe that Core would hit many medium-sized European companies, officials argued.

The revised version of the plan would not single out companies selling digital services, but would apply to all large corporations. Since it was the former proposal that led the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes that the new version won’t provoke a new trade war with the US.

	

The amount that would be levied on each company has not yet been decided. The plan is to seek agreement on the principle across the 27 EU countries before setting a rate for the tax.

9to5Mac’s Take

This whole mess was supposed to have been resolved by a global agreement, brokered by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). This would have ensured that all companies worldwide pay at least some taxes in each of the countries in which they operate, and the plan had Apple’s support.

However, Donald Trump withdrew the US from this agreement, leading to calls for an EU-specific version. The idea that Trump won’t object to the revised plan seems to me rather optimistic.

title: Automattic loses its interim CFO just weeks after boardroom shakeup
snippet: Automattic's interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left the company less than a month after taking the role, TechCrunch has learned. Sources say his departure followed a demotion back to his previous position, marking another executive exit amid the organization's leadership turmoil.
fullText:
Image Credits:TechCrunch	

	

						

8:02 AM PDT · October 9, 2026

											

			

Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.

The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”

Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit. 

He had replaced the former CFO Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean. 

Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.

It’s unclear why Klaperman chose to leave Automattic, but sources told TechCrunch that the decision came after he was demoted back to his original role at VIP. (As an interim CFO, he could have been replaced by a permanent hire, but nothing on that front has yet to be announced.) Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure.

When Mullenweg originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.

title: Everything We Expect From Apple’s Surprise Smart Home Event Next Week
snippet: Apple is finally entering the smart home in a huge way. Here’s what will reportedly be announced, and what we think is unlikely.
fullText:
We finally have confirmation of Apple’s massive smart home event, which is happening on Tuesday. So many things are expected to be announced, centering on Apple and Siri entering the home tech space in all-new ways. The tech giant’s smart home devices will face serious competition from Amazon, Google and other players.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been collecting the reports, insider claims and possible leaks to see just what Apple could be announcing. It all points to a major shake-up for home security, smart home devices and how Siri AI can be used. CNET will be there in person to see what Apple has cooked up, but in the meantime, here are the latest rumors.

A representative from Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. 

			

More from CNET

A Siri smart display at last

An Apple smart display could allow Siri to get much more creative.Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be near the release of a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home. This display would focus heavily on Siri AI and compete with products like Amazon’s Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub line.

Smart displays can add a lot of functionality to smart speakers, if you don’t mind using voice assistants. Rumors say the display could swivel and/or be attached to a wall, be at least several inches wide and allow Siri to recognize different people when multiple users are having a conversation. 

Smart display touchscreens are great for getting visual information, watching videos or viewing to-do lists, so a display like this is likely to have a bit of Apple TV and Safari in it, too.

Is it likely? I think it’s quite likely, based on how many insider reports have mentioned this smart display, but I don’t think we have a good idea how it will look yet. 

Updates to the HomePod line

Is a new HomePod mini on the way?Chris Monroe/CNET

Along with a smart display, rumors are flying that Apple will give its HomePod smart speaker line the first major update in years. It’s the ideal time to update the HomePod line, too, although it’s possible some of these reports have confused plans for a smart display with a new smart speaker, both of which could fall under the HomePod label.

If a new HomePod speaker is on the horizon, reports indicate that it would be a new type of HomePod mini. That’s not surprising — the original HomePod has often been critiqued for being over $300, which is why Apple focused on the less expensive mini model afterward.

Is it likely? Yes, I’d say this is about as likely as a Siri smart display, if Apple wants to continue developing the HomePod line. 

A new Apple TV

Apple TV is due for an upgrade, too.Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The same reports that say a smart display and new HomePod are on the way also mention Apple is planning to release a new Apple TV model. 

It’s a product line that’s sort of connected to the smart home, especially if Apple is launching a smart display. The company hasn’t released a new set-top box since 2022, so it’s about time for another. This could also give the Apple TV new hardware for extra Siri AI tricks.

Is it likely? I think it’s less likely than a speaker or display. It’s not quite as much of a smart home gadget, and it seems to have gotten swept into the wide net of rumors, but without as many reports.

Little Apple security cams — with no recording

Recent rumors says Apple is ready to enter the home security world with its own products. Although we don’t know much, reports from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman say these will be tiny cameras that, interestingly, won’t record any video. No recording means Apple won’t have to worry about cloud storage and may be able to avoid charging extra subscriptions for them.

The cameras are rumored to have some kind of presence-sensing or human-recognizing technology as well as AI video descriptions, suggesting Apple Home will be running analysis on the video even if it won’t record permanently. The phrase “facial recognition” was also mentioned, but this doesn’t seem nearly as likely to me. 

Is it likely? I’m betting on some kind of home security announcement, and I expect Apple would like to have its own camera line, but I don’t know if this exact product will be released. However, the extra details do lend this rumor legitimacy.

An LG collab for a new thermostat

Apple may be partnering with LG for some smart home devices, and there are even reportedly leaked product concept photos circulating on the internet. One of the biggest potential releases is an Apple-friendly thermostat. The photos show a round, Nest-like thermostat dial, and rumors say it will include far-sight presence sensing, a humidity sensor and several temperature calibration options.

Alongside the thermostat, the Apple/LG combo is expected to release a sensor that can measure the temperature at specific locations and feed that information back to the thermostat hub. That would be no surprise, because models from Nest, Ecobee and others have similar satellite sensors, although Apple’s may have adhesive strips to attach its version to the wall.

Interestingly, Apple partnered with LG years ago to support Apple-friendly security cameras, but those lines were rarely updated and quickly became obsolete. Maybe Apple is ready to try again with a different approach.

Is it likely? If Apple really is partnering with LG for a new wave of home devices, I think a thermostat is likely. But this is starting to be a lot of products to announce at a single October event that won’t be publicly streamed. 

2. LG Smart Thermostat

•  Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.

•  Calibrated Temperature/Temperature Offset options. pic.twitter.com/Q8AAaxy4ey

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026

Further LG collabs for smart lock and maybe more 

The other big rumor centering around an LG collaboration is an Apple smart lock. While many smart locks work with Apple and Apple Home Keys, the tech giant hasn’t been involved in the development of a smart lock before. 

It could have automatic unlocking, tapping your phone to unlock and a variety of keypad management options. That’s not surprising, but the rumored product images show a round, twist-to-unlock, light-up outdoor keypad, and I haven’t seen anything like that before.

If Apple does release a smart lock, Ring will have beaten it to the punch with its own announcement of its first-ever lock, which will include Alexa compatibility and a unique thumbturn that can generate a charge when the battery dies.

Other rumors and purported product images suggest the LG partnership could also yield a video doorbell, floodlight camera, outdoor camera and indoor camera.

Is it likely? Now this is a lot of new gadgets to announce at once. I think a smart lock is about as likely as a smart thermostat; those are both strong fields for Apple to enter. For the rest of the cameras, I’m doubtful. The indoor camera could be connected to the rumors of Apple’s no-video model. If the LG partnership line is this large, I wouldn’t be surprised if Apple is saving it for a separate announcement later on.

What role will Apple Intelligence play in all this?

Apple Intelligence will fuel many Siri AI capabilities in the Apple Home app. That’s especially true of AI video descriptions, which Apple is bringing to supported security cameras (there are very few right now, but some of Aqara’s camera hubs are compatible). I’m testing these uses of Apple Intelligence now, but if Apple releases any of its own security cameras, you can bet they’ll use AI features in the same way.

Will there be any iPad news at this event?

There are rumors that Apple will announce an iPad mini sometime this month, but it probably doesn’t have much to do with this event. This is a strictly smart home-focused release.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: You can unlock a Googlebook’s bootloader, Magisk support in the works
snippet: Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works.

On a support page, Google details how you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook. Google says that a “developer or advanced user can unlock their device’s bootloader to install a custom version of the operating system or test an app,” but stresses that “most users don’t need to unlock their Googlebook’s bootloader.”

Like on a Pixel or other Android phone that easily supports bootloader unlock, you’ll need to enable OEM unlocking via the Settings menu and Developer options, then press and hold Esc + F2 and press the power button, releasing all keys when the screen lights up. From there, bootloader unlock is located under “advanced options.”

And, with that, root support is also coming.

	

Magisk developer John Wu confirmed on Twitter/X that support for Magisk is in the works for Googlebook. In a separate post, Wu called Googlebook “the ideal platform for Android modding” since modern Android smartphones suffer from broken apps including banking apps when they are rooted. Wu says that there are some tweaks needed to bring Magisk and, in turn, all of the benefits that come with a rooted device to Googlebook, but it’s coming.

title: Google rolling out ‘massive’ Pixel Buds Pro 2 and 2a update [U]
snippet: Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update. more…
fullText:
Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update.

Update 10/7: Google has reached out to clarify that these updates are only for the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a. The original Pixel Buds Pro, which has since been removed from the announcement, are not getting these new features.

The only feature exclusive to the Pixel Buds Pro 2 is Dynamic Active Noise Cancellation. Google will “automatically adjust audio or noise cancellation based on your ear seal.” This compensates for “subtle shifts” when the buds move in your ear.

The remaining features are available for the Pixel Buds Pro 2 (2024) and 2a (2025). When these features were previewed in August, Google did not mention that the original Pro model would be getting this update.

	

With last month’s Pixel Buds companion app update, you can turn on Active Noise Cancellation, adjust EQ, and enable touch controls with Gemini voice commands.

	

During phone calls, Tap to Mute lets you mute and unmute the microphone by tapping the buds. This gesture requires a paired Pixel phone.

Pixel Buds can now auto-pause media playback when you fall asleep, which is determined by Pixel Watch sleep sensing. This will also disable touch gestures and silence notifications.

The final update is Enhanced Live Translate that allows you to “leave your phone in your pocket and start translating instantly with a simple touch on your earbuds.”

Whether you’re conversing with someone or using listening mode to stay aware of your surroundings in a foreign language, Pixel Buds work seamlessly with the Google Translate app to make on-the-go translation easier than ever.

Make sure you’re running the latest version of the Pixel Buds app, and be on the lookout for software release_6.144. Open the companion client and scroll down for More settings > Firmware update to check.

title: Apple’s MacBook Pro overhaul is coming soon, here’s what to expect
snippet: Apple just released a MacBook Pro update in March, but there’s more coming soon. Apple is expected to debut one of its biggest MacBook Pro updates ever as soon as later this year. Here’s everything we know so far … including details on a surprising recent twist. more…
fullText:
Apple just released a MacBook Pro update in March, but there’s more coming soon. Apple is expected to debut one of its biggest MacBook Pro updates ever as soon as later this year. Here’s everything we know so far … including details on a surprising recent twist. 

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Sony is running a massive sale on its best BRAVIA TVs, ranging from its entry-level to flagship options — shop now to save! 

New MacBook Pro features

OLED display

The new MacBook Pro will switch from mini-LED to OLED display technology. This will mark the first time Apple has used OLED in a Mac, having previously used it on the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. This has been reported by sources including Ming-Chi Kuo and Bloomberg.

The MacBook Pro’s rumored OLED display would offer true blacks, higher contrast, and potentially more vibrant colors compared to today’s mini-LED screens. That’s because OLED can turn individual pixels completely off, while mini-LED still relies on a backlight system.

Touchscreen

OLED isn’t the only big display change coming with the refreshed MacBook Pro, though. It will also be Apple’s first-ever touchscreen Mac.

As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is optimizing macOS to take advantage of the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen. For example, when you touch a button or a control, macOS will dynamically adjust to show you relevant touch controls. If you tap on the menu bar, controls will automatically enlarge to make it easier to navigate with your finger.

It will also support common touch interface interaction methods, like pinching and zooming, and faster scrolling.

So, it’s a lot more than Apple simply adding a touchscreen to a Mac. It’s a rethink of macOS to make touch navigation feel fluid and natural.

Dynamic Island

Currently, the MacBook Pro features a notch cutout that houses the FaceTime camera. With this year’s MacBook Pro, however, Apple will reportedly ditch the notch in favor of a hole-punch cutout for the camera.

Additionally, Apple is planning to bring the Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. This will likely work like the iPhone, where the Dynamic Island masks the cutout for the FaceTime camera and displays software interface elements such as Live Activities and notifications.

Thinner and lighter design

With the 2021 MacBook Pro, Apple reversed course and made it thicker than its predecessor. It also added back ports, including MagSafe, HDMI, and an SD card slot. The 2016-2020 MacBook Pro’s industrial design famously had only four USB-C ports.

This year, however, Apple is reportedly planning to make the MacBook Pro thinner once again. We don’t have any specifics on this just yet, and it’s unclear whether Apple will remove any ports to accommodate this change.

One key difference nowadays is Apple Silicon. The 2016-2020 MacBook Pro models used Intel chips that were less efficient than Apple’s own M-series chips. Apple Silicon should mean Apple can make the MacBook Pro thinner without compromising on those things.

The new MacBook Pro will also be “significantly” lighter than its predecessor, according to Mark Gurman: 

But there is one other major difference, I’m told: The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior, miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry.

M5

It was widely expected that the new MacBook Pro models would be powered by the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. 

In a new twist, however, it sounds like this update will actually use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the current MacBook Pro models. 

The decision comes as Apple is reportedly skipping higher-end chips in the forthcoming M6 generation. Instead, the M6 will be available only in its base configuration, with no M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra variants. 

Apple is shifting its focus to the M7 generation, including the M7 Pro and M7 Max chips. These will reportedly focus on significant improvements to AI performance. 

MacBook Ultra?

Finally, it wouldn’t be an Apple rumor cycle without speculation about naming.

Mark Gurman has speculated that Apple might brand these laptops as MacBook Ultra. This name would “more clearly signal their position at the top of the lineup,” he reasoned.

The latest development that the new MacBook models will use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips adds a new wrinkle to the marketing decisions Apple will have to make. 

New MacBook Pro release date

Apple is expected to debut the new MacBook Pro lineup in October or November. It may seem weird that Apple would update the MacBook Pro twice this year, but it’s not unprecedented.

Wrap up

title: The Pixel 5 doesn’t get enough credit for making the best of a bad situation
snippet: In 2020, Google Pixel was in a remarkably tough spot. A flailing flagship with one of its central features effectively ruined by a global pandemic combined with massive supply shortages meant that grand plans for the future were on hold. It was always going to be a tough year to release a smartphone but, looking back, the Pixel 5 maybe doesn’t get enough credit for making the best of it. more…
fullText:
In 2020, Google Pixel was in a remarkably tough spot. A flailing flagship with one of its central features effectively ruined by a global pandemic combined with massive supply shortages meant that grand plans for the future were on hold. It was always going to be a tough year to release a smartphone but, looking back, the Pixel 5 maybe doesn’t get enough credit for making the best of it.

Our Damien Wilde reviewed the Pixel 5 and called it an “exercise in compromise,” and I think that sums up this device quite nicely, perhaps even better than we thought at the time. 

On the surface level, the Pixel 5 felt like a weird step forward after the Pixel 4 series. A much less powerful chipset wrapped up in a plastic “bio-resin” that replaced metal and glass was completely out of the ordinary for a flagship smartphone. Yet, it also addressed some of the Pixel 4’s failings by going back to a fingerprint sensor, by packing in a much larger battery, and by feeling a bit more familiar to what had come before after the prior year’s big swing on design.

The Pixel 4 is my favorite Google smartphone hardware to date, and it still holds up

And, looking back on it today, this thing aged quite well!

	
	

It’s still odd to think of this as a “flagship” as, across the board, it was a better fit in the mid-range category. Yet, through and through, it managed to nail down the fundamentals of the hardware. It feels good in a way that’s unique. Where the plastic Pixel 4a had virtually the same design, the Pixel 5’s resin material added some extra grip while managing to feel just a bit more premium. I’m not sure I ever appreciated it enough at the time, but with virtually everything going all-in on shatterable glass and heavy metal in 2026, a durable material like this is so refreshing.

Ultimately, Google’s Pixel 5 was a device that didn’t fit in. We’ll probably never know all of the details around its development, but it’s been said that, at some point, Google apparently wanted Tensor to debut in this time frame rather than ultimately launching a year later on the Pixel 6. We found evidence that suggested the switch wasn’t as last-minute as suggested, but even without such a radical change on deck, the Pixel 5 was absolutely born out of a rough series of circumstances and, looking back, it wasn’t half bad.

Did you have a Pixel 5? Do you remember it fondly?

title: Apple, Prosser, and Ramacciotti trade blame over delays in trade secret lawsuit
snippet: In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple said it is still waiting on additional documents from Jon Prosser and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again, while both defendants pushed back on the company’s handling of the case. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple said it is still waiting on additional documents from Jon Prosser and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again, while both defendants pushed back on the company’s handling of the case. Here are the details.

According to a joint status report to Judge James Donato, Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti are increasingly at odds over who is responsible for delays in the trade secret lawsuit Apple filed against both defendants in July 2025.

A bit of context

As a refresher, soon after announcing iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against Prosser and Ramacciotti over Prosser’s videos, where he leaked aspects of the system, including what turned out to be the Liquid Glass visual revamp.

Apple said Ramacciotti improperly accessed the development iPhone of an employee, who was later fired over the incident, and held a FaceTime call with Prosser to show him unreleased iOS features running on the device.

Since then, the case has had its own share of drama, with the clerk’s entry of default after Prosser failed to respond to Apple’s complaint by the deadline (although Prosser has disputed the characterization that he had ignored the case).

Then, eight months later, the court agreed to set that default aside and give him another chance to formally contest the allegations.

Court documents show that Ramacciotti, on the other hand, responded to Apple’s complaint and has largely cooperated with the company’s discovery requests.

Since Prosser retained representation and formally entered the case, however, things have taken a turn, with all three sides increasingly disagreeing over who is responsible for the alleged trade secret disclosure and for the delays that have followed.

The new joint status report

Back to the new status report, Apple says it wants Ramacciotti to update his interrogatory responses and sit for another deposition to address what it describes as “inconsistencies between his and Mr. Prosser’s testimony.”

Ramacciotti, however, says he will sit for another deposition once Apple provides “a roadmap to resolution of its claims against him, including what more, if anything, Apple needs from him.”

When it comes to Prosser, Apple says it “continues to await his production of certain additional documents that it requested over three months ago. These include revenue reports and data analytics for his YouTube channels and relevant communications with third parties that he identified during his deposition.”

Prosser, in turn, argues that “[i]t appears that the Trade Secrets at issue are no longer trade secrets and are in the public domain.” In other words, his argument appears to be that since Apple released the iOS update with Liquid Glass, the information at the center of the lawsuit is now publicly available and therefore no longer qualifies as secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti asks the court to hold a status conference this month, at which Apple would be required to explain what additional information it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to then have 30 days to either dismiss its claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial.

Apple, meanwhile, wants discovery to continue, including a second deposition of Ramacciotti and the outstanding documents from Prosser. Prosser argues that he has already complied with the discovery obligations he agreed to and pushes back on Apple’s continuing requests for additional material.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti’s request for a status conference, the parties propose filing another joint status report on December 2.

title: Apple accuses OpenAI of improperly adding new arguments to trade secrets case
snippet: A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence to its trade secrets case. Today, Apple fired back with its own accusation that OpenAI went beyond what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence to its trade secrets case. Today, Apple fired back with its own accusation that OpenAI went beyond what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details.

Apple says OpenAI went beyond objecting to new evidence

One of the many aspects of the lawsuit in which Apple accuses two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products of trade secret misappropriation involves a request for a preliminary injunction.

In a nutshell, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing that it would prevent its trade secrets from becoming further embedded in OpenAI’s hardware development while the case plays out.

As part of the legal back-and-forth over that request, Apple filed a reply brief supported by five expert declarations. That, in turn, led the defendants to accuse Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and ask the court to disregard some of the material.

In their objection filing, which accused Apple of presenting new evidence, OpenAI and the other defendants also submitted several documents countering Apple’s claims.

Today, Apple filed its response to those objections, arguing that the defendants went beyond simply objecting to new evidence, introducing new arguments and testimony of their own:

Rule 7-3(d)(1) permits a party to object to new evidence in a reply brief, but cautions that the filing “may not include further argument on the motion.” Defendants did not comply with this restriction and used their filing to relitigate the merits of Apple’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction.

For example, Defendants dispute whether Dr. Runge has a “basis to offer any analysis, adequately responds to “contrary evidence,” and demonstrates that certain Apple information is not public. […] Such arguments are not objections to new evidence. […] (“[A]rgument regarding how certain of Plaintiff’s positions are unsupported by evidence or contradicted by other testimony” is “not an objection to evidence.”).

Apple also takes exception to a new declaration from Liu, which it calls “the most egregious overreach” in the defendants’ filing:

The most egregious overreach is a new declaration from Mr. Liu, comprising eight paragraphs of new testimony. Defendants rely on this new testimony to offer excuses for why Mr. Liu “wiped” (i.e., erased) all the data from his iMac before returning it to Apple, […] argue about the meaning of certain text messages with one of Apple’s suppliers, […] and try to explain away his use of one of Apple’s confidential computer files, […] Such testimony violates the prohibition against “further argument on the motion.” Together, the filing and the declaration run 9 pages, which also violates the limitation that the objections “may not exceed 5 pages of text.” […]

It is worth noting that when the defendants filed Liu’s declaration, they argued that the court should consider it only if it also decided to consider the Apple evidence they were challenging.

That said, Apple argues that because the defendants have now presented new arguments of their own, the court should consider the full record rather than strike any of Apple’s reply evidence:

Defendants’ new arguments and evidence are more in the nature of a “sur-reply” rather than an objection. But, Defendants did not seek leave to file a sur-reply. Nonetheless, as Defendants have now adequately answered any “new” evidence from Apple’s Reply in its current filing, the Court should deny Defendants’ request to strike any of Apple’s Reply evidence, and should decide the Preliminary Injunction motion on a full record, including both the arguments and evidence in Apple’s Reply as well as the new arguments and evidence improperly submitted with Defendants’ filing.

The court is scheduled to hear arguments on Apple’s preliminary injunction request on October 14.

title: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
snippet: Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support. more…
fullText:
Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support.

Yes, a decade after ditching the “Kindle” branding in its tablet lineup, Amazon is ditching the Fire brand entirely for its new lineup of iPad competitors. That’s not me trying to write off its Android-powered rivals; rather, the sizes and designs all make for devices that, frankly, look like iPad knock-offs. Alexa Tablets come in three sizes: an 8-inch entry-level iPad Mini competitor, an 11-inch base iPad-esque slate, and a 12-inch “Pro” model that looks to be the most unique of the bunch. They’re all designed with aluminum bodies and, despite being much more expensive than the Fire tablets they’re replacing, still manage to undercut most of the market.

The 8.7-inch 60Hz Alexa Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and comes in graphite, rosette, and teal, while the 90Hz 11-inch Alexa Tablet 11 features 8GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and adds matcha and amethyst to the mix. Both run on a MediaTek 8189 8-core processor, a relatively recent chipset that appeared in a handful of seemingly-unreleased ChromeOS devices over the past year or so, before landing in these budget tablets. While I wouldn’t say there’s much to write home here about the specs — and again, the design is just absolutely a blatant copy of the iPad — it certainly sounds like a big upgrade over their predecessors.

	

And really, that comes down to the software. Despite Amazon’s current Android-less strategy on its Fire TV devices, the company seems to be doubling down on Android with its tablets. While it does have a unique launcher designed to push Alexa+, these things run proper Android, complete with the Play Store front and center on the device. YouTube is one of the highlighted apps on their store listings, and as someone who maintained Play Store sideloading guides at two different tech websites over the past decade, I can certainly say I never saw it coming. I have no idea how the actual software experience will feel day-to-day, but in terms of app support, it’s one problem that’s finally solved.

	

The star of the show, of course, is the 12-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. This is, bar none, the most premium tablet Amazon has ever shipped, with a price that matches. It combines a 2.8K 3:2 120Hz display with quad speakers, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor. That’s a real processor, and while I wouldn’t say it’s worthy of being called a flagship chipset, it’s undoubtedly the most powerful chip Amazon’s ever used. It’s a good sign when you’re using the same processor that a budget gaming-focused brand like Poco used just a year or two ago.

The 12-inch model also comes in an optional “nanomatte” version for an anti-glare experience, which also allows you to upgrade your RAM and storage to 16GB and 256GB, respectively. 16GB of RAM in an Amazon tablet — it’s a new day after all. And like its last attempt to go full-premium, the company does offer optional stylus and keyboard accessories for road warriors on a budget.

The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $230 for the base 64GB model with lockscreen ads, or $250 without, while the Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $330 for its base model, or $350 for the ad-free version. Both feature a 128GB upgrade for $50 more. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the base 128GB model; the nanomatte upgrade will run you $50 more. Meanwhile, that high-end 16/256 variant costs a whopping $680, and while that might sound pretty expensive on paper, it comes in well under Samsung’s latest 12-inch tablet for anyone who doesn’t need that level of processing power. Oh, and absolutely no ads on any of the 12 Pro models — the price you see is the price you pay, no upgrades necessary.

title: Apple TV brings back hit limited series for season 2 ‘by popular demand’
snippet: Apple TV confirmed today that what was originally planned as a limited series is returning “by popular demand.” Here are the details more…
fullText:
Apple TV confirmed today that what was originally planned as a limited series is returning “by popular demand.” Here are the details

’Imperfect Women’ is back by popular demand

Earlier this year, Apple TV premiered Imperfect Women, an eight-part limited series starring Elisabeth Moss (Mad Men), Kerry Washington (Django Unchained), and Kate Mara (House of Cards), with a cast that also included Joel Kinnaman (For All Mankind), Corey Stoll (The Many Saints of Newark), Leslie Odom Jr. (Hamilton), among others.

The story, based on an Araminta Hall novel of the same name, follows three best friends whose bond is tested when an “investigation reveals betrayals and shocking truths” after a murder.

Today, Apple TV announced that due to “popular demand,” the limited series will be returning “for a compelling new chapter set on Martha’s Vineyard that will revolve around fan-favorite character Eleanor, played by Emmy Award-winning producer and actor Kerry Washington, who will reprise her role and serve as executive producer alongside Emmy Award winner Elisabeth Moss.”

Here’s Matt Cherniss, Apple TV’s head of programming, on the return of Imperfect Women, which the platform says will be based on an original idea:

“After a wildly entertaining first season, driven by the performances of Kerry, Lizzie and Kate, we jumped at the opportunity to expand the world of ‘Imperfect Women’ through Kerry’s fan-favorite character of Eleanor. (…) Annie and Justin’s thrilling new story felt like an exciting and natural next chapter. We can’t wait for fans to experience it.”

Apple TV’s announcement did not say when fans should expect the second season of Imperfect Women, but the project appears to still be in the very early stages of development.

title: Honor’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo rival is reportedly launching in January
snippet: Honor’s first wide-format foldable is apparently coming in January, leaks suggest, to take on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Honor’s first wide-format foldable is apparently coming in January, leaks suggest, to take on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo.

“They got the aspect ratio” was Apple’s take on the trend of wide-format Android foldables, but it’s certainly here to stay following the smash-hit success of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Xiaomi’s 18 Fold, for instance, has already picked up the new form factor.

Honor might be next in line.

Leaker Digital Chat Station says that Honor’s wide foldable has a 5.5-inch outer display and 7.6-inch inner display, a 7,000+ mAh battery, and a 200MP main camera alongside a periscope zoom lens. That last bit is important – both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo lack a telephoto sensor (despite what Apple’s marketing wants you to think), so Honor is matching Xiaomi in this regard. Another leaker, Smart Pikachu, says to expect a January release date. It’s unclear if that’s just for China or for global markets as well. 

	

Honor’s existing Magic V6 was one of the better foldable releases of 2026, but with the entire market looking closer at the wide-format design, it’ll be rather exciting to see what Honor and other brands bring to the table.

title: Android Auto rolling out fix that stops auto-playing music when you start your car
snippet: Google has confirmed that a fix is rolling out for a bug that leaves Android Auto briefly auto-playing music when your car starts, even if you have autoplay disabled. more…
fullText:
Google has confirmed that a fix is rolling out for a bug that leaves Android Auto briefly auto-playing music when your car starts, even if you have autoplay disabled.

Most of the time you’d want Android Auto to start playing music as soon as it starts up. That’s one of the big benefits of the platform, after all. But if you don’t want music to start playing automatically, there’s a toggle that lets you disable autoplay.

It just hasn’t been working properly for a while.

For some, Android Auto would start playing music briefly when your vehicle starts before ending playback a few seconds later. It’s more than a bit frustrating, but a fix is apparently rolling out.

	

In a post on Reddit, Google confirmed that “unsolicited play commands” will no longer be sent during startup if autoplay is turned off in Android Auto. This is alongside other improvements to autoplay including a prompt to opt out of autoplay if Android Auto notices you frequently pause playback immediately after it starts.

We’ve made a couple of bug fixes so autoplay* works more predictably and accurately based on your listening preferences:

Autoplay app selection: Apps that you haven’t recently or ever used will no longer be selected for autoplay.

One-tap opt-out: If you prefer manual playback and frequently pause autoplay, Android Auto will notice and provide a convenient one-tap notification to quickly disable autoplay.

Infotainment startup handling: We’re rolling out a fix so unsolicited play commands won’t be sent when you have autoplay turned off.

There’s no mention of which Android Auto update fixes autoplay, but it is “rolling out,” Google says.

title: President Trump awards Big Tech donors with nation’s highest science prizes
snippet: Together, the awardees have donated nearly $6 billion to efforts tied to Trump and his administration.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

3:33 PM PDT · October 8, 2026

Image Credits:Win McNamee / Staff / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

On Thursday, at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, President Trump awarded Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sergey Brin, and AMD’s Lisa Su the National Medal of Science, the nation’s top science prize. Dell Technologies’ Michael Dell and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella also received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

Together, the awardees have donated nearly $6 billion to efforts tied to Trump and his administration, according to The New Republic. Alphabet and Microsoft, for example, donated to the president’s inauguration fund and White House ballroom. AMD gave to a pro-Trump Super PAC, and Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to help fund the Trump Accounts, the administration’s savings program for children. 

Trump said the honorees had helped “pioneer an incredible future for America,” and that because of them, “we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us.” 

Nadella received his medal right after the administration indefinitely suspended Microsoft from the H-1B program, which lets U.S. companies hire skilled foreign workers.

title: A fun night video test of the iPhone 18 Pro
snippet: After taking a series of portrait photos to test the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro, my original plan had been to hang around until it was dark in order to see whether letting in more light would reduce the duration of Night mode photos. I ended up postponing that test because something more interesting was going on: the extremely rare sight of a cruise liner passing through Tower Bridge. That provided the perfect opportunity to test the night video capabilities of the new device … more…
fullText:
After taking a series of portrait photos to test the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro, my original plan had been to hang around until it was dark in order to see whether letting in more light would reduce the duration of Night mode photos.

I ended up postponing that test because something more interesting was going on: the extremely rare sight of a cruise liner passing through Tower Bridge. That provided the perfect opportunity to test the night video capabilities of the new device …

Over the years, iPhones have evolved into extremely capable cameras, but for both still photos and videos, there has been a significant gap between the quality you can achieve in daylight and that available at night.

Apple has put a lot of work over the years into low-light still photography, and that really shows. Today’s iPhones offer incredibly impressive low-light camera capabilities given the extremely small size of the sensor. That was helped by the inclusion of Night mode portraits back in 2020.

Computational photography in general is the secret to a lot of the iPhone’s night photography abilities. While we think we’re taking a single shot, the phone is in fact taking a whole series of frames and then combining different exposures into a single image.

Video, however, is a far bigger challenge. When we’re shooting at least 24 frames per second, and most typically shooting movement, there’s very limited opportunity for the phone to capture multiple exposures of the same frame in order to combo them. That’s the reason that the quality of night videos inevitably lags significantly behind that of still photos.

Apple does, however, continue to put a lot of work into this, and night video performance does improve with each generation. The iPhone 18 Pro not only benefits from Apple’s annual enhancements to video processing, but also from a wider aperture that lets in more light. It’s less than a stop, but for video work in particular, every extra photon really counts.

The complete clip in normal speed lasted more than nine minutes, and I didn’t want to rely on the impressive video stabilization capabilities of the device for quite that long, so braced a mini tripod on top of a railing. I’ve sped up the video to 10x normal speed to reduce it to 96 seconds, but included a couple of actual-speed sections so you can appreciate the incredibly careful work carried out by the tugboats.

The result? Not perfect, but yes, another step forward in the quality evolution. Sure, people like me can go pixel-peeping and complaining that some of the details are rather muddy when viewed closely, but that’s kind of a “so what?” situation. The average person looks at a video like this and simply enjoys the spectacle, having no complaints about the quality. When I look back at low-light videos from a few generations ago, the difference is … well, night and day.

So yes, night video performance is not yet where I would like it to ideally be, but it continues to improve with each generation, including this one. In truth, we have easily hit the “good enough for most people to enjoy” point even in extremely challenging conditions like this.

title: See for yourself the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes
snippet: Alongside a variable aperture lens, the main camera of the iPhone 18 Pro also opens up to a wider aperture than its predecessors. Apple has been promoting this as enabling a shallower depth of field for portraits and similar shots. The difference, however, is less than a stop, and it’s been unclear how much real life difference this would make on such a small sensor, so I set out to put it to the test … more…
fullText:
Alongside a variable aperture lens, the main camera of the iPhone 18 Pro also opens up to a wider aperture than its predecessors. Apple has been promoting this as enabling a shallower depth of field for portraits and similar shots.

The difference, however, is less than a stop, and it’s been unclear how much real life difference this would make on such a small sensor, so I set out to put it to the test … 

Portraits, not Portrait mode

It’s important to draw a distinction between the optical shallow depth of field enabled by a wide aperture lens and the artificial effect enabled by Portrait mode.

With the latter, Apple uses computational photography and the LiDAR sensor to work out where the subject ends and the background begins in order to apply an artificial blur. The quality of this has improved dramatically over the years, but that’s not what we’re testing here. All of the background blur seen in the sample photos was achieved optically by using the widest possible aperture of f/1.48.

The simple testing method

The iPhone 17 Pro had a widest aperture of f/1.78. This is essentially indistinguishable from f/1.8, which is the second-widest aperture available on the iPhone 18 Pro. What I’ve done here is to use the new manual controls available to take the same photo twice, once at f/1.8 and again at f/1.48, in order to compare the difference. 

There are, however, three other optical factors affecting the amount of background blur of any photo:

The focal length of the lens

The distance between the subject and the background

How close the subject is to the camera

To eliminate these variables, all of the photos are taken at the same focal length (the main camera, which is the only one with a variable aperture), the same framing (ie. same background), and at the same distance. There’s a few seconds gap between the photos as I adjust the aperture, so they are not 100% identical, but both myself and my subject stood still to ensure both were taken at exactly the same distance even if he turned his head between shots.

With these controls in place, any difference in background blur is due entirely to the aperture.

The test shots

All of the test shots are portraits – that is, head-and-shoulder shots – as this is the type of photo for which wide apertures are most commonly used (hence the name Apple applies to the artificial effect available in Portrait mode). 

Additionally, by getting close enough to shoot head and shoulders, we are maximizing the degree of background blur we would expect to see. This makes for the best basis for comparing the shots, versus wider ones where the degree of blur may be harder to assess.

Finally, I’ve included a few shots with graduated backgrounds, so you can see how the focus falls away with distance.

With all of that pre-amble out of the way, let’s take a look at the results. Move the slider all the way to the right to view the f/1.78 version, to the left to view the f/1.48 shot, and anywhere you like to compare different parts of the image.

Conclusions

I think this shot provides the clearest illustration of the impact, as it contains background elements ranging from a few feet to around quarter of a mile:

	

The fountain is the closest element, at around 8-10 feet, and we can see a noticeable difference here. The tree is about 30 feet away, and the difference is smaller but still distinct. The pagoda is maybe 70 feet away, and the difference remains clear but a bit less pronounced. Once we reach the more distant elements – the bridge and buildings on the far side of the river – the difference is more subtle: we can clearly see it when actively looking for it, but I don’t think most people would notice unprompted.

In terms of practical benefit, the shot below is a good illustration. With the f/1.78 aperture, I’d describe the separation of Chris from the background as a little marginal in places, for example, the person eating in the restaurant top right and the section of building top-right of his head. With the wider aperture, the separation is definitely improved.

I’d wondered how much difference we could expect to see from a relatively small change, and now I have my answer. The significance of the difference is something you can judge for yourself from the sample shots; personally, I’d describe it as relatively subtle but in truth bigger than I’d expected – and enough to be useful in some situations. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

The wider aperture is not the only benefit of the new lens. There are other situations in which it can be useful to take manual control of the variable aperture, and I’ll be looking at these in a follow-up piece.

title: Google confirms fix for Android Auto’s missing signal icon is rolling out
snippet: After weeks of back and forth, Google has officially confirmed a fix is rolling out for Android Auto’s missing signal icon. more…
fullText:
After weeks of back and forth, Google has officially confirmed a fix is rolling out for Android Auto’s missing signal icon.

The corner of every Android Auto display is meant to show your phone’s battery status, the time, a number of notifications, and your phone’s current cellular connection status.

The last one has been in rough shape.

While it hasn’t been consistent or fully widespread, many have found the cellular signal icon on Android Auto vanishing off and on for several weeks now. Recent updates have seemed to fix the issue for many, but now Google is confirming a fix has been made. In a comment on Reddit, a Google representative explains:

	

We’re aware of reports about the missing cellular signal, and we’re actually currently rolling out a fix that should hopefully address this issue! The fix isn’t widely available yet, though, so it may take some time to reach your device – if you want to receive it sooner, though, you can enroll in the Android Auto beta

The Android Auto beta program, notably, is full at the moment, but you can sideload updates (at your own risk). 

Android Auto 17.8 seems to deliver the fix, at least in part, and is now rolling out via the stable track.

title: Pixel 12 series leak allegedly reveals model numbers, display specs, no wide Fold
snippet: Google’s Pixel 11 series has only been around for a few months now, but Pixel 12 leaks are already surfacing with some key display specs and confirmation of a familiar Fold. more…
fullText:
Google’s Pixel 11 series has only been around for a few months now, but Pixel 12 leaks are already surfacing with some key display specs and confirmation of a familiar Fold.

Citing the GSMA database, OVR+ highlights what appear to be listings for Google’s Pixel 12 lineup. As expected, there are four devices here, presumably to be marketed as Pixel 12, Pixel 12 Pro, Pixel 12 Pro XL, and Pixel 12 Pro Fold. The model numbers listed are:

Pixel 12 – GC0QU

Pixel 12 Pro – GWU59

Pixel 12 Pro XL – G7U1Y

Pixel 12 Pro Fold – G4D5D

Beyond model numbers, the listings point to the screen resolution of each device. The base Pixel 12 is listed at 1080×2400, just shy of the Pixel 11’s 1080×2424. Pixel 12 Pro is listed at 1280×2824 compared to 11 Pro’s 1280×2856. Pixel 12 Pro XL, following the same pattern of very slight differences, is said to be 1344×2952 compared to 11 Pro XL’s 1344×2992. We’d take these with a grain of salt, as the lower pixel counts would suggest a smaller panel, but it could also signal some form of redesign on the main display.

	

Pixel 12 Pro Fold’s inner display is listed at 2296×2404, a considerable bump up from the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s 2076×2152. While that’ll certainly be a welcome upgrade, it’s important to note that this means Google is looking at using the same near-square design for the fourth year rather than switching to a wide format like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or iPhone Duo – the aspect ratio is nearly identical to the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Not really a surprise, but certainly a bit of a shame given Google started this whole foldable journey off with something closer to the new fan favorite. Google is also rumored to be adopting a new display assembly on Pixel 12 Pro Fold.

	

Unsurprisingly, all four devices are listed with Android 18, which will have debuted by the time Google releases its next flagship series.

These early leaks are always subject to change, so take it all with a grain of salt for the time being.

title: ‘Fitbit Edge’ leaks as Google’s next fitness tracker with ‘Apps’ & ‘Notifications’
snippet: Following an accidental marketing leak in August and FCC listing last month, retail listings for the “Fitbit Edge” have now emerged. more…
fullText:
Following an accidental marketing leak in August and FCC listing last month, retail listings for the “Fitbit Edge” have now emerged.

According to retail assets shared by Android Headlines, Google is making a new wearable called the “Fitbit Edge.”

There is a bulbous screen that appears to go much closer to the perimeter than that of any past Fitbit tracker. We see what is essentially a Pixel Watch face that’s been adjusted for this display shape. The time and date are joined by complications for heart rate, step count, and starting a workout.

On the back, we see the band removal mechanism at the top and bottom, and a sensor stack that looks pretty similar to the Fitbit Air. Google might even use the same magnetic charger.

	
	

The left and right sides are home to metal strips that are presumably for ECG readings. It very much follows the design formula of the Fitbit Charge 6.

The Pixel Watch Active Band-esque straps and casings are available in Canyon, Obsidian, and Olive, similar to the Pixel 11 Pro.

The Fitbit Edge specs we have today come from a comparison table with the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5. “Connectivity” notes Bluetooth but not Wi-Fi and — compared to the Fitbit Air — Notifications.

Listed “Apps” include “Google Maps, Media and music controls & Find My Phone.” Battery comes in at “Up to 7 days,” with support for “Android & iOS.”

fullText:
Apple has confirmed a special ‘Welcome home’ product launch event is happening next Tuesday, October 13. But it hasn’t yet said whether there will be a keynote video. Here’s what we know.

Now Apple’s ‘Welcome home’ launch on October 13 looks set to similarly tread new ground.

Unlike a traditional event, Apple hasn’t yet added ‘Welcome home’ to its Apple Events webpage. And there’s no evidence of a livestream on YouTube or the Apple TV app.

These things could all change in the coming days ahead of the launch. However, currently they indicate there won’t be a keynote video on October 13.

However, Mark Gurman at Bloomberg says a video presentation is coming. In his report about another Apple launch coming October 27, Gurman writes:

Like its smart home event on Oct. 13, the next launch will include an online video presentation and in-person component for the press

So according to Gurman, who accurately reported the October 13 date and its focus on Home products, Apple will have “an online video presentation” next week.

title: Apple Announces Next ‘Welcome Home’ Special Event on Oct. 13
snippet: The company is expected to release a new HomePod and Apple TV next week.
fullText:
Apple rarely briefs the media in advance of new product announcements. But invitations to the company’s next event, confirmed for Oct. 13 at 9 a.m. ET in New York, are now out. 

Crystal balls sometimes show up via X — this time via Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. Joswiak’s video shows a time-lapse of needlepointing Apple’s logo with the date on it. The “Welcome Home” theme strongly suggests that the company will unveil several new Home products next week.

Rumors point to a new Home hub with a design similar to the old iMac G4 — the one modeled after the lamp in Pixar’s iconic Luxo, Jr. short from 1986. There may also be updates to the HomePod Mini and Apple TV set-top box, with new hardware targeted at handling AI and more colors for the small speaker, including pink and green.

			

More from CNET

title: I’m Way Too Excited for Apple’s Home Event and How It Will Level Up My Siri Experience
snippet: But what do we do now with these old “dumb Siri” HomePods?
fullText:
I have spent years anticipating the day Apple puts a screen on its smart speakers. It looks like the wait is finally over. Apple confirmed news is dropping Tuesday at an event in New York, and it teased us with the words “Welcome Home.”

In this week’s One More Thing, which you can watch embedded above, I talk about the rumors and leaks of what Apple will likely unveil: new HomePod Minis, a new Apple TV streaming box and a never-before-seen Hub that sits on a counter or hangs on a wall. 

I’m downright giddy. The HomePods are long overdue for a refresh to get the omg-it-actually-works-now version of Siri AI and sync better with my iPhone to have more context of my life.

But Apple is very late to this space. What will Apple demonstrate to convince homeowners to go with Siri as their future home assistant, when they might have already invested in systems with Alexa or Gemini?

For more One More Thing, subscribe to our YouTube page to catch Bridget Carey breaking down the latest Apple news and issues every Friday.

title: Apple announces special event for October 13: ‘Welcome home’
snippet: Today Apple announced a special event happening next Tuesday, October 13 with the tagline ‘Welcome home.” more…
fullText:
Today Apple announced a special event happening next Tuesday, October 13 with the tagline ‘Welcome home.”

Apple launching new Home products on October 13, as teased by Greg Joswiak

Apple is launching new products next week on Tuesday, October 13, as hinted at in a teaser video posted by Greg Joswiak. Here’s the video from Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing.

Apple is expected to launch several new Home products at the event, including:

New Apple TV 4K

‘HomePad’

HomePod mini 2

We’re also likely to see the leaked LG home accessories unveiled next week that Apple has reportedly co-developed with the company.

At the same time as Joswiak announced the date, invites went out to press for a special “Apple Experience” to happen in Tribeca, New York at 9:00 a.m. ET.

Here’s a look at the invite via Marques Brownlee:

	

When Apple launched MacBook Neo earlier this year, it hosted a similar “Apple experience” for press. At the time, that unveiling followed multiple days of product launches via press releases.

Currently though, expectations are that all of Apple’s new Home products will debut the same day.

It’s unclear if Apple will have a full-length video introducing the products that debuts online at 9:00 a.m. ET, but we’ll keep you posted as more details emerge.

Which new Apple products are you expecting to see October 13? Let us know in the comments.
